#5398. Anthropic is trying to kill traditional desktop apps with Claude-generated desktop apps

Rarely a day goes by that Anthropic PBC doesn’t announce some kind of new capability, feature or model, and today wasn’t any different. Today came the ability to use Claude to create fully functional desktop applications for Windows and Mac computers with a single prompt.

It promises to be one of its more impactful updates, fanning the flames of those who argue that artificial intelligence is ultimately destined to eat the software world.

The company said today that users can now transform what it calls “artifacts” into standalone applications that run independently of Claude and can be accessed from the desktop. Artifacts have been around for a while, and they can be almost anything, such as a simple order tracker or a meeting dashboard that pulls information from the user’s calendar and email inbox.

However, until today, artifacts were a bit tricky to access. They could be opened up only from inside Claude itself, which meant users first had to open up the chatbot, login and then find the old conversation where they originally created the artifact they want to use.

Anthropic said people are using Claude artifacts all the time for various everyday tasks, and so it makes sense to mature the concept. “If you rely on a tool for work, it should open like the rest of your apps and remind you when something needs your attention,” the company said.

That’s why Anthropic is making it possible for people to use artifacts to create, run and share desktop applications with Claude’s new “Install as App” feature, which is available in beta now on Windows and macOS.

In a video posted on X, Anthropic showed how straightforward it is to create a functional desktop app from a simple prompt. The user simply describes the tool they want Claude to create, click confirm and then sit back and wait for a few seconds as it slaps together the required code to bring that app to life.

You can now install Claude artifacts as desktop apps on Mac and Windows.

Ask Claude to build an artifact, click "Install as app", and open it like any other app. It can use your connectors and, if you allow it, send notifications or add a menu bar item. pic.twitter.com/8CBgqe5OKq

— ClaudeDevs (@ClaudeDevs) November 24, 2026

Because these are “real” apps, they come with their own app icons and they open in a dedicated Window, rather than running within the Claude interface. They also get the ability to send notifications to users, Anthropic said.

As an added benefit, Claude artifacts that are transformed into desktop apps will be able to use Claude and various third-party connectors, meaning that AI agents will be able to interact with them autonomously, Anthropic said. However, the company did warn that any requests made by an app to Claude will count toward their monthly credit usage, which means it could become expensive if an app is used excessively.

In a blog post Anthropic showcased a number of examples of what its internal teams have built, including a fully featured image editing app called Linnet, a file manager with a cinematic design called Phosphor, and a terminal application that integrates with Claude, which is known as Tern.

There is one major caveat to Claude artifacts-as-apps that sets them apart from traditional desktop applications. According to Anthropic, “you need to be online and signed in to Claude to open an app.”

That could be a pretty big downside, for many desktop applications are designed to work even if the computer is not connected to the internet. But those who lack a Wi-Fi connection will be unable to access their Claude-generated apps, even if they’re already built and configured.

#5396. Regional Spotlight: California Home Sales Hit Lowest Level as Prices, Mortgage Rates Rise

(TNS)–As the year comes to an end, California’s housing market has slowed down.

Existing home sales have dropped to their lowest level in nearly three years as high mortgage rates and affordability challenges continue.

“Homebuying activity weakened across California in October, pushing sales to their lowest level in nearly three years as elevated mortgage rates and low affordability remained significant hurdles for prospective buyers,” the California Association of Realtors said in its latest housing report, released on Tuesday, Nov. 17.

Existing single-family home sales totaled 246,830 in October.

That is a decrease of 5.2% from the 260,410 sales in September and 12.7% from the 282,760 sales in October 2025.

“When mortgage rates jumped to a nearly three-year high in late September, we saw many buyers step back and reassess what they could afford, which led to fewer closed sales in October,” California Association of Realtors President Mark Peterson said in the report.

Despite the slowdown in sales, real estate experts said, home prices remained relatively steady, while mortgage rates continued to pose a challenge for potential buyers.

What can California homebuyers expect to pay?

Here’s what to know about home prices, mortgage rates and where buyers can find more affordable options across the state:

How much does buying a home cost in California?

The statewide median home price was $886,760 in October, according to the California Association of Realtors.

That was down 1.4% from $899,720 in September but barely changed from $887,330 in October 2025.

California’s median home price previously reached a record $930,260 in May.

“Home prices held steady, suggesting that buyers are still engaged and sellers remain confident in the value of their homes despite the near-term slowdown,” Peterson said.

Still, affordability remains a major obstacle for many prospective homebuyers across the state.

How much are current mortgage rates in California?

Mortgage rates continued to climb in October, adding to the challenges facing homebuyers, according to the California Association of Realtors.

The group’s report put the average mortgage rate at 7.33%—up from the 6.86% in September and 6.25% in October 2025.

Zillow listed the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate in California at about 7.38%, as of Thursday, Nov. 19.

The combination of higher borrowing costs and economic uncertainty could continue to weigh on home sales in the coming year, according to Jordan Levine, the California Association of Realtors’ senior vice president and chief economist.

“The housing market is facing renewed headwinds as inflation remains elevated and the stock market loses momentum,” Levine said in the housing report. “Home sales will likely remain soft in the near term, but pent-up demand continues to build as many prospective buyers stay on the sidelines.”

If geopolitical tensions and economic uncertainty ease, Levine said, California “should see more of those buyers gradually return to the market.”

Where can I find homes under $400,000 in California?

Despite California housing some of the most expensive home prices in the country, some counties still have median home prices below the statewide median of $886,760.

According to the California Association of Realtors, the state’s most affordable homes can be found in Northern California, with a median price of $385,000.

However, one Central Valley county offers home costs as low as $288,000.

#5395. Compass follows through on Reffkin’s threat, sues 15 MLSs

The brokerage giant announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states.

Several weeks ago at an industry conference, Compass International Holdings CEO Robert Reffkin threatened to sue MLSs that wouldn’t change their rules. Now, the brokerage giant is taking another 15 of them to federal court.

The company announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it says can reach $15,000.

The announcement marks a major escalation in a fight that has been building since September, fueled by demand letters, legal threats and increasingly pointed public messaging from Compass execs. Eight of the 15 MLSs targeted Thursday are already suing Compass in two separate federal cases, adding another layer to an increasingly complicated legal battle.

A Compass spokesperson described the latest lawsuits to Inman as a follow-through on Reffkin’s warnings at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale in late September, noting that some MLS organizations had filed their own lawsuits before Compass took legal action.

The lawsuits target six MLSs in California, three in North Carolina and six others across the country.

At the center of the lawsuits are MLS rules that require agents to submit listings to the MLS once they begin publicly marketing a property.

Sellers can generally keep their homes off the MLS through an office-exclusive arrangement. But advertising a property on a brokerage website, social media or other public channels typically triggers a requirement to share the listing with the MLS.

Compass argues that those rules unfairly limit competition and prevent agents from offering alternative marketing strategies, even when homeowners want to advertise their properties outside the MLS first.

“Only the law and the homeowner should tell agents how to market a home, and the MLS is neither the law nor the homeowner,” a Compass spokesperson said in a statement shared with Inman. “Agents should be free to compete on the marketing strategies they offer.”

The brokerage also rejected warnings from MLS leaders that allowing public marketing without requiring listings to be shared through the MLS would harm buyers, sellers or competing agents.

Compass pointed to seven of the nation’s 25 largest MLSs that it said already allow agents to publicly market office-exclusive listings without fines. Those MLSs cover approximately 340,000 agents across 12 states, according to the company.

“If what we are asking for is so bad, why has it worked for years in nearly 30 percent of the country?” the spokesperson said.

MLS leaders counter that their rules are intended to ensure that publicly marketed homes are available to other brokers and their buyers. They argue that agents who benefit from access to shared MLS listings should also contribute their own publicly marketed properties.

California Regional MLS CEO Art Carter, who spent months negotiating with Reffkin before the dispute reached federal court, emphasized that point in a recent interview with Inman.

“At some point, you’ve got to say, this is a cooperative,” Carter said.

Carter also warned that withholding listings from MLS databases could leave appraisers and lenders with incomplete information about home sales, making it harder to determine accurate property values.

The new complaints largely echo arguments Compass made in its Oct. 16 antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, accusing MLS organizations of restricting competition through their listing rules. In the complaints filed Thursday against MLSs, Compass seeks triple damages and court orders blocking enforcement of the challenged rules.

On Sept. 8, Compass attorneys sent California Regional MLS a demand letter calling on the organization to stop fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings. The brokerage gave CRMLS until Oct. 6 to comply, warning that it was prepared to spend millions of dollars on litigation if its demands weren’t met.

Similar letters went to other MLS organizations across the country.

On Sept. 23, Compass International Holdings sent a separate letter demanding that MLS organizations stop sharing its agents’ production and listing data with third-party companies that help competing brokerages recruit agents. The letter specifically identified vendors Courted, BrokerMetrics and Brokerkit as examples of companies using MLS data for recruiting.

Compass argued that information provided to MLS organizations for real estate transactions shouldn’t be used to help competitors recruit its agents. It sought greater control over how that data was distributed, including the ability to exclude information associated with its brokerage brands from feeds used by recruiting companies.

Industry experts who recently spoke to Inman questioned parts of Compass’ argument, noting that MLS data serves purposes beyond recruiting and that access is often governed by agreements with brokerages and technology vendors.

Compass later raised the issue in its October antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, alleging it lost millions of dollars in commissions after agents were recruited away using data the MLS allegedly sold to competing brokerages.

On Sept. 30, Reffkin took his fight over private listings directly to MLS executives at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale. During a contentious session that drew pushback from attendees, Reffkin warned that Compass would begin filing antitrust lawsuits in mid-October against MLSs that continued fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings.

Photo by Michael Roberts of AJ Canaria Creative Services

He said Compass wanted to display listings on its own website without agents facing penalties, while some MLS executives questioned whether the company’s demands went further and could undermine cooperation.

The dispute reached federal court Oct. 5, when CRMLS sued Compass. Compass filed its own antitrust complaint against CRMLS on Oct. 16.

Amid the escalations, tensions and litigation in recent weeks, MLS organizations have also begun raising money to defend their rules in court. CRMLS announced plans for an MLS Cooperation Legal Defense Fund on Sept. 30, while CMLS subsequently announced a separate legal action fund to be run by an independent nonprofit.

In an Oct. 27 interview with Inman, CMLS CEO Jessica Edgerton said the organization had received preliminary financial commitments and was developing a process for reviewing requests for assistance.

The growing dispute has also coincided with changes to how Compass employees participate in industry leadership. On Nov. 9, Inman broke the news that Compass International Holdings had adopted a policy restricting salaried employees from serving in Realtor association leadership positions. The directive came after brokerage managers and other employees were instructed to step down from association leadership roles, including positions some had spent years working toward.

Compass confirmed the policy change, saying it was extending a similar approach previously adopted by Anywhere Real Estate, which merged with Compass earlier this year. The company did not clarify whether exceptions were permitted or whether the restrictions also applied to MLS boards and committees.

#5394. Zoom’s conversations-to-completion strategy is starting to pay off

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala

Zoom Communications Inc. has spent the better part of the past few years building products to become more than just the video company everyone used during the pandemic. Its fiscal third-quarter results, posted Monday, showed the strategy is working, though more work remains.

Total revenue grew 4.9%, but enterprise revenue rose 8.6%, its fastest pace in 13 quarters. Zoom raised its full-year outlook and announced its first quarterly dividend of 25 cents per share.

The acceleration should be viewed not as a one-quarter anomaly but as a manifestation of the strategy the company outlined at Zoomtopia about a month ago – moving from “conversations to completion.” That strategy gives customers a reason to buy more of Zoom and builds a competitive moat wider than most investors realize.

The concept of conversations to completion has enough merit that Microsoft used those exact words at its recent Ignite 2026 event. In fact, it held an entire session on the topic. Though having an 800-pound gorilla like Microsoft jump on a trend might seem threatening, Zoom has a significant lead and can use Microsoft’s marketing to add momentum to its current tailwind.

Nearly all work starts with a conversation: a meeting, a call, a chat thread or a customer interaction. Then everyone leaves, and the real work begins: updating the customer record, writing the follow-up and scheduling the next step. Collaboration vendors have always owned the first step, leaving the second to someone else.

Zoom wants both. “We’d like to leverage AI to transform our business from a conversation-centric vendor to a system of completions,” Chief Executive Eric Yuan said on the earnings call. He later put it more plainly: “Conversation is step 1. Step 2, AI will take over.”

His proof point was Zoom’s own sales organization, which uses ZoomMate, the company’s agentic framework. Sellers, Yuan said, “no longer log into the backend CRM system.” The agent takes over after the call ends. In enterprise software, value is shifting from where work is recorded to where it originates.

AI agents are quickly becoming a commodity, and so are the models behind them. What is scarce is context, the knowledge of what was decided, by whom, and why. Zoom sits on the richest source of it in most companies: what people actually said to one another and to customers.

“Any agent without context really cannot get work done,” Yuan said. That’s why the unified context layer Zoom showcased at Zoomtopia is central to the story. It links conversations to chats, documents and third-party systems, ensuring people and agents work from the same information.

My Notes, the company’s AI note-taker, extends that reach to third-party and in-person conversations. Yuan said it is nearing 2 million monthly active users, with one financial services firm rolling it out to 80,000 wealth advisers. Chief Financial Officer Michelle Chang added that online customers using My Notes have been associated with a 50% reduction in churn.

That is what will create a deeper competitive moat for Zoom. The more context a customer stores with Zoom, the more useful its agents become and the harder it is to leave. Zoom’s moat is not the meeting. Think of it as the memory of the meeting.

A context layer is only as good as the number of conversations it ingests, and this is where Zoom’s breadth of platforms matters. Meetings, phone, chat, contact center and now sales intelligence all feed into the same foundation, and each product gets smarter from the others.

Customers are consolidating. DSI Systems is replacing five separate products with Zoom. SolarWinds expanded its Zoom licenses while “recalibrating its Microsoft package,” according to Yuan. Enterprise net dollar expansion returned to 100%, its highest level in 11 quarters. “Strong RPO growth reflects our continued success in landing larger, longer-term multiproduct platform deals, demonstrating growing demand for our AI-first platform,” Chang said.

Customer experience is where completion gets paid for. Zoom CX recurring revenue grew in the high double digits for the seventh straight quarter, and all 10 of its largest CX deals included paid AI. More telling, Zoom said at Zoomtopia that 90% of its top 100 CX deals in the first half were with customers new to Zoom. Contact center is no longer a cross-sell. It is a front door.

Chang described the differentiation as “the ability to think about customer experience in a whole and fresh new way.” Specifically, she said, “to be able to seamlessly hand off from virtual agents to agents assisted with AI is a big winner for us.” AI-native startups have the virtual agent but not the human side. Legacy contact center vendors have the humans but not the pace of innovation. Zoom has both on one platform.

There is also an economic moat. Zoom runs most of its AI workload on its own small models and saves the expensive frontier models for harder tasks. “I fundamentally believe no single model can satisfy everything,” Yuan said. Gross margin rose even as AI usage grew, a feat that a point product reselling another company’s tokens cannot easily match.

The quarter was strong, but analyst questions revealed several concerns.

Some will read the dividend as a sign of maturity. With more than $7 billion in cash and free cash flow margins above 40%, I see a company that can fund innovation and return capital at the same time.

Although these issues came up during the call, most of the investment community remains positive about Zoom. In his note, Arun Bhatia of William Blair wrote, “Churn and downsell rates are becoming more favorable, AI usage and monetization are increasing, and adoption of new products such as Phone and Zoom CX is strong. We are encouraged by these trends and see potential for a growth uptick in the future.”

Zoom’s headline growth resembles that of a mature software vendor, but the company is in transition, so it’s important to look beyond the numbers. The underlying enterprise business is built to be a platform that uses context to drive customers toward more products and longer commitments. Investors should watch enterprise growth, net expansion and CX AI attach rates rather than the top line.

For information technology and business leaders, the lesson extends beyond Zoom. Conversation data is a strategic asset, so decide deliberately where it lives and which agents can act on it. Insist on openness so that context can feed the tools you choose. Start where completion is easy to measure, in the contact center and in sales.

That is where Zoom is proving that the conversation was never the product. The outcome is.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5392. Your ‘just sold’ posts are missing the best part of the story

Turn closings into case studies. Use ChatGPT Voice and footage you already have, plus this free Canva template, to tell the story behind the sale.

I’ve always found it interesting how much time and energy we put into selling a home, only to reduce the entire experience to a “just sold” graphic once the transaction closes.

We spend weeks, sometimes months, developing a marketing strategy, communicating with sellers, negotiating with buyers and navigating challenges along the way, but so little of that work makes it into the content we share afterward.

I don’t think there’s anything wrong with celebrating a closing. But I’ve always felt that the story behind the sale is often more interesting than the sale itself, especially when you consider what a prospective client is trying to figure out when deciding who to hire.

Most sellers probably assume any experienced agent can put their home on the market. What they don’t necessarily know is how that agent approaches marketing, how much effort they’ll put into a listing or how they’ll respond when something doesn’t go according to plan. Those are difficult things to communicate in a listing presentation when every agent is promising some version of the same thing.

For years, I’ve tried to give people a better understanding of our work by creating case studies of the homes we’ve sold. Initially, that meant compiling listing footage into a Reel with a longer caption explaining the transaction. More recently, I’ve been experimenting with carousels that tell those stories across multiple slides using footage we already created to market the property.

What I like about this approach is that people can see what working with us might actually look like, rather than simply taking our word for it.

We recently sold a property in San Pedro where we hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. We found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and we had to start again.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein)

We eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when we shared the case study, we didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing we’d done. We opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”

I liked that opening because it put the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, we explained how we responded, got the property back in front of buyers, and ultimately closed.

We’ve used the same approach to tell different stories, including a transaction in Hesperia, California, where we coordinated a sale for sellers who had moved out of state, and a humorous carousel about a San Diego transaction that generated 15,741 views.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein)

Not every transaction needs an extraordinary twist. Sometimes the interesting part is a problem you solved, a decision you made, or the work that went into making the experience easier for your client. The challenge is recognizing those moments and figuring out how to communicate them.

The storytelling portion generally takes me about 15 minutes, although gathering information and designing the finished post take additional time.

Before writing, I go through the transaction and take inventory of everything we’ve done. I want to know how many open houses we hosted, how many people attended, how many postcards we mailed, how much content we published and how many views our videos generated. I’ll also look at offers received and anything else that helps explain how the sale unfolded.

This has made me more conscious of documenting our work as we’re doing it. It’s difficult to communicate the effort behind a sale if you can’t remember the specifics, and having those numbers also makes it easier to evaluate what worked.

I then gather content we’ve already created, whether that’s property videos, walkthroughs, open house footage, or photographs. Repurposing footage gives that content another life, but agents could create something similar using listing photos.

Once I have everything together, I open ChatGPT Voice and talk through the transaction. I’ll explain the sellers’ circumstances, our approach, the decisions we made and anything unexpected. I don’t organize my thoughts beforehand because I find it more helpful to get everything out and work through the story conversationally.

What I’ve found particularly useful is having ChatGPT ask follow-up questions to identify the most compelling angle. Sometimes what I initially find interesting isn’t what another homeowner would care about, and that back-and-forth helps me consider their perspective.

Once we’ve found the angle, we work on the writing, particularly the opening two slides because Instagram can serve both to your audience. Lately, I’ve preferred carousels with moving video backgrounds, but we’ve also created Reels and experimented with humor. I’ve shared an editable version of our Canva template for anyone who wants to try the format.

If you want to try this with one of your transactions, open ChatGPT Voice and use this prompt:

“Interview me about [Address] I recently closed. Ask me one question at a time about the seller’s goals, our marketing strategy, the decisions we made, challenges we encountered and the outcome. Help me identify the most compelling part of the story and why another homeowner would care. Once we’ve found the angle, help me write a seven-slide Instagram carousel with a strong opening and a natural narrative. Use specific details and results, avoid generic sales language, and don’t invent anything.”

We’ve also been sharing these case studies in emails to our database, giving us another opportunity to demonstrate our experience to homeowners and agents who may eventually refer us business.

If you’ve been in the business for any length of time, you probably have dozens of transactions worth revisiting, with interesting stories buried in them. You don’t need a new closing every week to share those experiences, and you don’t need to make every transaction sound more dramatic than it was.

There’s tremendous value in helping people understand the work we do, particularly when so much happens behind the scenes. If we’re already investing all this time and effort into helping our clients, it seems like a missed opportunity not to share more of it.

Use this FREE Canva template to replicate these results.

Krys Benyamein is a Realtor with Allstars Realty in Southern California. Get connected on Instagram or LinkedIn.

#5391. Formal verification startup Sequent raises $2.2M to prove code obeys its safety rules

Formal verification startup Sequent Inc. today announced that it has raised $2.2 million in new funding to take its Alan proof platform out of early access.

Founded in London in January, Sequent offers a platform that uses artificial intelligence to find mathematical proofs that code obeys the safety rules its engineers set. Decentralized exchange Curve Finance is its first paying customer.

Curve also figures in how Sequent got started. Chief Executive Charles Cooper, who leads development of Vyper, one of the two main programming languages for Ethereum, inadvertently introduced a flaw into the Vyper compiler in 2021. Though the bug was fixed within months, programs already running on the blockchain could not be updated, leaving older Curve pools and other projects exposed when attackers used the flaw to take more than $50 million in July 2023.

Following the incident, Ramana Kumar, now Sequent’s chief technology officer and formerly an AI safety researcher at Google DeepMind, offered to help prove the Vyper compiler correct. Kumar co-created CakeML, a compiler proved correct all the way down to the instructions a computer runs.

Cooper believes the lesson reaches far beyond crypto, saying that “smart contracts taught us that anything that can be exploited will be.” Banks, governments and companies running older systems have relied on keeping their code private, according to Cooper, who said AI-powered cyberattacks are now eroding that protection.

Alan works today on Vyper smart contracts, with support for Solidity and Solana in development and general software in Rust, C, TypeScript and Python to follow.

For now, engineers using Alan write rules for their code such as “no user can withdraw more than their balance” in plain language, and the job of finding a mathematical proof is handed to AI. Nothing the AI comes up with is taken on trust, as each proof has to get through HOL4, a checker Kumar has helped build for more than a decade.

For two-coin StableSwap pools holding standard tokens, Alan was used to prove that no user can take more than a set limit from depositors, whatever they do and in whatever order. The work also found minor accounting and rounding errors, none of which breached the limit. The founders are now proving the Vyper compiler itself, since the Curve proof does not cover the compiler where the 2021 flaw sat.

Along with AI computing costs, the funding will pay for engineering, sales and marketing hires. Subscriptions to Alan start at $99 a month for individuals, with auditor plans priced at $200 a month and team plans starting at $500 a month.

Frachtis and Metaplanet Holdings OÜ co-led the pre-seed round. Metaplanet is the investment firm of Skype co-founder Jaan Tallinn, who led Anthropic PBC’s Series A round in 2021. According to Frachtis founder Xavier Meegan, crypto is the right place to start, with “billions already at risk.”

#5389. GoVeda Launches AI IP Intelligence Agent for Innovators and IP Professionals

GoVeda's own IP models work with frontier AI models. In examiner-grade patent analysis tests, the Agent found 81.8% of the references examiners cited, at a small fraction of the cost of traditional IP work.

SINGAPORE, Nov. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- GoVeda today launched its AI IP Intelligence Agent for innovators and IP professionals, now available at www.goveda.com. Users ask any question about a technology, a patent or an idea in their own words. The Agent researches more than 220 million patents from 108 countries and regions, more than 350 million research papers and the live web, then returns a clear answer or a finished report.

For innovators: affordable, from idea to filed patent, no IP expertise needed

Startups, R&D teams and university labs use the Agent to explore a technology, size up competitors, map the landscape, check whether an idea is new and find who could license or buy it. When an idea is worth protecting, GoVeda's end-to-end filing service takes it to a filed patent. Registered patent practitioners back the service, at a fraction of typical professional fees.

For IP professionals: faster, more accurate, lower cost

In-house IP teams, search firms and law firms use the Agent for prior art, novelty, FTO and invalidity searches, landscapes and patent valuation. Most tasks take 15 to 55 minutes, and every patent cited links to its record for review. Teams get a report they can check, edit and deliver, at a fraction of the usual cost.

Hybrid models: better performance, lower cost

Every task uses two kinds of models together. GoVeda's own IP models search, read and count patents, so every answer rests on real patents. They search by meaning and across languages, and GoVeda refined them working with patent examiners on search and examination tools. A frontier AI model from OpenAI or Anthropic plans the steps and writes the result.

In examiner-grade patent analysis tests, the Agent identified 81.8% of the references examiners cited, compared with 40% to 68% for frontier AI models tested on their own. It delivers this at a small fraction of the cost of traditional IP work.

"General AI models can talk about patents, but they miss too much of what matters," said Dr. Tai Cheng, CEO and Co-Founder of GoVeda. "We built our own IP models and paired them with frontier AI models. Now any innovator can get answers they can act on, and IP professionals can deliver more and better work, at a cost both can afford."

GoVeda does not use customer data to train AI models, and its security controls are audited under SOC 2 Type II. Organizations can also deploy GoVeda inside their own infrastructure.

GoVeda is a venture-backed, AI-native company based in Singapore, building the AI infrastructure for innovation. GoVeda provides startups, R&D teams and university labs with an end-to-end solution from idea to filed patent, and helps in-house IP teams, search firms and law firms deliver faster, more accurate work at lower cost. Its AI IP Intelligence Agent, powered by GoVeda's own IP models, draws on more than 220 million patents from 108 countries and regions and more than 350 million research papers.

Power 500 Million Global Innovators. Learn more at www.goveda.com.

#5387. The Must-Have Gifts Grandparents Should Have on Their Radar This Holiday Season

CHARLESTON, S.C., Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- With Black Friday and the holidays approaching, grandparents are on the lookout for gifts their grandchildren will love and products that make family life easier. From fun toys and games to practical family essentials, ZestYears, a national resource for modern grandparenting, is sharing some of the season's best gift ideas. These are products grandparents can feel good about giving, using with their own families, and recommending to friends and relatives looking for great gifts.

What makes these recommendations different is the firsthand experience behind them. Through its Golden Grandparent Awards, ZestYears brings together grandparents and grandchildren nationwide to test products in their own homes. Families share feedback on quality, ease of use, how well products keep children interested, and whether they would recommend them to others. ZestYears uses this feedback, along with considerations such as age appropriateness and value, to identify products worth a closer look.

"There are so many products on the market that it can be hard for grandparents to know which ones are actually worth buying. That's why we put products into the hands of grandparents and grandchildren across the country and ask them to use them in their everyday lives. We look at everything from quality and ease of use to how well a product holds a child's interest and whether families would recommend it to others. Our goal is to take some of the guesswork out of gift shopping and help grandparents find products they can feel confident buying and sharing with family and friends," said ZestYears co-founders Ellie Barziv and Alexandra Breuer.

Great Gifts for Grandkids This Holiday Season

Looking for the perfect gift? Explore this year's standout picks, from toys and games to creative activities, baby essentials and practical finds for the whole family. There's something for every age, interest and holiday wish list.

Lovevery Play Kits (Excellence in Developmental Play Award). Give little ones a head start on learning with these play kits packed with toys and activities designed for each developmental stage. From curious babies to busy toddlers, there's always something new to explore.

MAGNA-TILES (Creative Learning Award). Kids can't get enough of these colorful magnetic tiles! From towering castles to entire cities, the building possibilities are endless, and knocking everything down to start again is half the fun.

We Craft Box (Exceptional Craft & Creativity Award). Everything young artists need for an afternoon of creativity comes in one box, with art supplies and guided projects that kids can proudly show off when they're finished.

Makedo (Early Builder Innovation Award). Who knew cardboard boxes could be this much fun? With kid-friendly construction tools, ordinary boxes become rocket ships, forts and amazing creations kids can proudly say they built themselves.

Stickerbox (AI-Powered Imaginative Play Award). Imagine a sticker of absolutely anything! Kids simply describe their ideas, and this clever voice-activated printer brings them to life as custom stickers to color, collect and share.

Smart Four (Innovation in Strategy Play Award). Four-in-a-row gets a whole new twist! This three-dimensional electronic game challenges kids to outsmart their opponents, plan their next moves and put their strategy skills to the test.

GoChess (Innovative Gameplay Award). This interactive chessboard uses illuminated moves and AI guidance to help kids learn chess, build their skills and take on new challenges as they improve.

CONNETIX Ball Run (Motion-Based Play Design Award). Build it, race it, change it and do it all over again! Kids can create their own colorful ball runs with twists, turns and winding tracks, then experiment to see how far their designs can go.

Dex Language Discovery Camera (World of Words Award). Turn everyday exploring into a language-learning adventure! Kids can use this clever camera to discover what familiar objects are called in another language, making learning new words feel like a game.

Camp Guru (Excellence in Logic-Based Play). This portable puzzle game introduces Sudoku and Meowdo-style challenges, starting with easier puzzles and progressing to more difficult ones as kids improve their skills.

GoBalance Play (Kids Movement & Technology Award). Who says screen time has to mean sitting still? This interactive balance board lets kids control on-screen games by moving their bodies, turning indoor play into an active challenge that builds balance and coordination.

eat2explore (Excellence in Culture & Culinary Exploration). Young chefs can explore foods from around the world with country-themed cooking kits that include recipes and cultural information. It's a fun gift for grandparents and grandchildren who enjoy cooking together.

321Grow (Ultimate Mealtime Essentials Award). Designed for little hands, these cups and dishes help young children practice eating independently. The foldable On-the-Go Snack Mat, with its lidded containers, is loved by families for making snacking on the go easy and contained.

Inglesina Fast Table Chair (Travel-Friendly Mealtime Solution Award). This portable chair attaches to tables, giving babies and toddlers their own seat at family meals. It's especially handy for restaurants, travel and visits to Grandma and Grandpa's house.

Clixo (Excellence in Creative Toy Design). These flexible magnetic pieces snap together, bend and twist into all kinds of shapes and creations. They're easy to use, fun to experiment with and offer plenty of ways to build something new.

Figgy (Style Meets Play Award). More than a play couch, Figgy's modular cushions can become forts, obstacle courses and reading spots. Kids can rearrange them for different activities, while the simple design fits nicely into a family living space.

Tender Leaf Toys Kitchen Range (Little Chefs' Creative Play Award). Little chefs can cook up a storm in this charming wooden play kitchen, whipping up pretend meals, baking treats and serving their favorite dishes. Its beautiful design looks just as good in the living room as it does in the playroom.

AirFort (Ultimate Kids' Play Space Award). A giant fort that inflates in seconds? Kids will love having their own hideout for secret clubs, imaginative games, reading or just hanging out with friends.

Nonnanest SightAware Baby Monitor (Excellence in Baby Monitoring). Keep a watchful eye on your little one with this easy-to-use video monitor, giving parents and grandparents added peace of mind. With a private, Wi-Fi-free connection and no monthly subscription fees, it's a smart choice for families who value safety, security and simplicity.

Lumi Swing (Superior Baby Swing Design Award). Give those tired arms a break! With gentle swinging motions to help soothe babies and a stylish, neutral design that blends into any room, this swing is a gift new parents will appreciate every day.

Baby Brezza (Baby Feeding Solutions Award). Less time preparing and washing bottles! Baby Brezza's innovative feeding appliances take the hassle out of everyday routines, making them a gift new parents will appreciate again and again.

SpongellÃ© (Golden Grandparent Award Winner). Make bath time a little more fun with these colorful, soap-infused sponges that bring plenty of bubbles to the tub. A playful and practical stocking stuffer!

Remy XL Wagon (Best On-the-Go Travel Solution Award). Pack up the kids, snacks and all their gear! This roomy wagon makes trips to the park, outdoor adventures and family outings easier, with plenty of space for everyone to ride comfortably.

Lulyboo Toddler Travel Activity Tray (Kids' Travel Companion Award). Road trips just got more entertaining! This handy activity tray gives little travelers their own space for coloring, games and snacks, with built-in storage to help keep the car organized.

Mimish Sleep-N-Pack (Kids' Sleep Gear Design Award). Sleepovers are even more exciting when kids get to pack their own bags! This clever sleeping bag folds into a backpack they can carry themselves, perfect for weekends at Grandma's, camping trips and overnight adventures.

Biky Air (Children's Cycling Design Award). Few gifts are as exciting as a brand-new bike! With its lightweight frame and easy-to-handle design, Biky Air helps young riders build confidence as they learn to balance, steer and explore on two wheels.

mifold (Best On-the-Go Child Safety Solution Award). A booster seat that fits in a bag? This compact design makes traveling with grandkids more convenient, especially for grandparents who don't keep a bulky booster in the car. Designed for children who meet the manufacturer's size and fit requirements.

Newton Baby (Ready-to-Go Sleep & Play Award). Make room for the littlest overnight guests! This portable travel crib gives babies a comfortable, dedicated space for sleep and play, making family trips and sleepovers at Grandma and Grandpa's house easier.

Baby K'tan (Ultimate Babywearing Comfort Award). All the closeness of a baby wrap without the complicated tying! This soft, slip-on carrier makes babywearing easier, keeping little ones close while giving parents the freedom to use their hands.

IvyGo Diaper Bag (Modern Parenting Design Award). More than your average diaper bag! This stylish bag packs in clever extras, including a hidden nursing cover, feeding support, changing mat and stroller clips, so parents have what they need wherever they go.

Buckle Me Baby (Excellence in Child Safety Design). No more taking winter coats on and off at every car stop! These innovative coats feature front panels that open for car-seat buckling, making chilly outings with little ones easier when used according to the coat and car-seat manufacturers' instructions.

The August Collection (Premium Organic Babywear Award). Soft, cozy and seriously cute! These organic baby clothes feature adorable prints and stylish designs that look great on little ones, making them a gift parents and grandparents will love picking out.

Roshambo Kids (Playproof Eyewear Award). Cool sunglasses made for kids who never sit still! With flexible, durable frames and sun protection, these stylish shades are ready for playgrounds, beach days and family vacations, and make a great little stocking stuffer.

From pancakes and egg bites to mac and cheese, chicken nuggets and meatballs, these are the foods kids love and grandparents will be happy to have on hand! Kidfresh (Healthy Kids' Cuisine Award) offers freezer-friendly breakfast, lunch and dinner favorites with hidden veggies, while Little Spoon (Excellence in Children's Nutrition Award) delivers nutritious, ready-to-heat meals with kid-friendly flavors. Both make it easy to serve foods little ones love, with ingredients parents and grandparents can feel good about.

ZestYears is a national resource for modern grandparenting, offering expert advice, family activities, gift recommendations and practical ideas for spending time with grandchildren. Its Grandparenting Hub brings together resources that grandparents can use in their everyday lives and share with family and friends. ZestYears also operates the Golden Grandparent Awards, a product recognition program that combines hands-on testing by grandparents and grandchildren nationwide with a structured evaluation process to identify products that families enjoy and find useful.

For more holiday gift ideas, family activities and practical advice, visit the ZestYears Grandparenting Hub.

These insights power trans-GEO's end-to-end services, from information architecture design to website redesign, helping clients increase their visibility in AI-generated answers, reach new customers and strengthen their brand value.

*1 GEO (Generative Engine Optimization): The practice of optimizing content and website structures so that a company's information and services are more likely to be cited and recommended in AI-generated search results. Also referred to as LLMO (Large Language Model Optimization).

â  Background and challenges: The risk of missed opportunities in the age of AI searchWith the widespread adoption of generative AI, consumers are increasingly relying on AI-generated answers directly when comparing and evaluating products and services, rather than simply following links in search results. As a result, companies that have traditionally focused on SEO (Search Engine Optimization) now face the risk of missed opportunities if their information is not accurately cited or recommended by AI, preventing them from even being included among the options users consider. Moreover, because AI-generated responses change dynamically, conventional tools that rely on estimated data make it difficult to accurately understand how a company is being evaluated by AI.

â  Profound, the global standard for AI marketingProfound is the fastest-growing AI marketing platform used by 16% of the Fortune 500 like The EstÃ©e Lauder Companies, Comcast, Walmart and U.S. Bank, and innovators like Zoom, Ramp, and MongoDB. Built on 2B+ real user prompts and growing, Profound shows what people ask AI and what the models say back. Profound's AI Marketer proactively pairs that data with your business context to surface opportunities, deploy Agents, and measure the impact to improve with every use.

â  AI search optimization solution "trans-GEO" featurestrans-GEO, offered by transcosmos, uses its proprietary method to provide detailed diagnostics, including assessments of how a company is evaluated by AI and analysis of the factors behind identified challenges, helping visualize the causes of missed opportunities facing the company. Based on these diagnostic findings, trans-GEO provides one-stop support from strategy development and content creation to website optimization and ongoing operations tailored for AI, helping promote appropriate citation and recommendation by AI and creating an environment that ensures companies are included among the options users consider when making comparisons. In addition, leveraging its global network, trans-GEO can also support AI search optimization across multiple languages. Customer interest in this area has been strong. As a result, trans-GEO helps improve the visibility of company information in AI search and maximize opportunities for preferential citation across global markets, languages, and regions, not only in Japan but around the world.

#5385. A former professional athlete on selling real estate to other athletes

While it’s easy to get starstruck when working for an athlete or other high-profile client, Yohann Sangaré, an agent with eXp’s sports and entertainment division, discourages it. “You come as a problem solver, not a fan,” he said.

Sangaré, a French former professional basketball player who played for 16 years across Europe, sometimes avoids reading up too much about his athlete clients’ accomplishments in their prospective sports so that he can focus on the task at hand: Finding them the right home and advising them on large investments.

Sangaré came to the U.S. when he was hired to work for Tony Parker, his former teammate, in San Antonio, Texas; he started as a financial advisor for professional athletes. During COVID, he moved into real estate, specializing in finding homes for athletes instead.

Sangaré explains that the pros tend to make a lot of money for a short period of time, and for that reason they’re usually interested in buying investment properties (often right after they’ve found homes for themselves and their family members). A big part of their real estate agents’ job, then, is to keep their eyes on investment properties with the potential for strong returns.

Athletes have specific needs. “As a rookie, they’re just starting out, and they may not want to buy,” Sangaré told Taylor Anderson at eXpcon in Salt Lake City last month. Depending on the length of the contract, a rental might be a better idea. “There are times you tell people now’s not the right time to buy. If they feel you’re working in their best interests, they will trust you,” said Sangaré, who is part of eXp’s relatively new sports and entertainment division (which several brokerages offer).

You have to be patient when working with athletes, he said, since their situations are tied to ever-changing contracts; of course, players can be traded, and have to move quickly. You also have to be prepared to wait and work with them as they grow in their careers.

What you don’t have to be: A major follower of their particular sports. Sangaré admits that as a European, he doesn’t know much about football or baseball, but that doesn’t stop him from working with athletes in those sports. Sometimes not being starstruck helps him work with a more level head, he said.

But you do need to know the nuances of sports contracts. For example, some leagues, like the NBA, offer several-year guarantees, while others, like the NFL, don’t; housing options will vary based on those.

Often the connection to an athlete client comes through their financial advisor or sports agent, Sangaré said. “The sports agent is always talking to the player, and he’ll know to reach out to you when someone gets traded,” he said.

But that can be a long road. Sangaré said it can take anywhere from five months to two years from starting a relationship with a sports agent to seeing any traction with a player, but you want to start that relationship early since once their clients do start to get traded, they’ll undoubtedly be approached by many other real estate agents. One practical tip he gives is going to the NBA Summer League in Las Vegas and taking agents out for coffee or lunch. “You have to be present where they’re present,” he said.

And when you do get connected to the client, make sure you don’t start with a sales pitch. “You can’t try to sell them something right away,” Sangaré said; instead, you want to counsel them on how they can protect themselves and what they really need to know when buying a home — whether as an investment property or to live in.

#5381. Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

Want to price more precisely? Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers said no. Learn three steps to add failed listings to your next CMA.

When agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds. Look at what’s coming soon, active and pending. Adjust for condition, location, square footage and amenities. Figure out where our house fits.

But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.

Expired. Canceled. Withdrawn. Earlier in my career, I looked at these failed listings all the time. Then the market changed. When inventory became tight, and buyers were competing for homes, digging through failed listings often wasn’t necessary to determine where a property would sell.

Now the market is shifting again; pricing must be more precise, and I’m sharpening my approach by bringing an old tool back into my pricing process.

A sold comp tells us where a buyer said yes, but a failed listing can help us figure out where buyers said no. And in a buyer-favored market, that’s valuable information.

Imagine you’re pricing a home, and the recent comparable sales range from $600,000 to $625,000. Then you expand your search.

Suddenly, you know considerably more than the sold comps alone told you. Other sellers have already tested the upper limits of pricing, and buyers responded. It’s essentially a series of pricing experiments someone else conducted for you — and they paid the carrying costs.

One of the most interesting things buried in MLS history is the pricing journey. A property might show a final list price of $649,000 and an eventual sale of $630,000. Dig deeper, and you may discover this:

$725,000 → $699,000 → $675,000 → canceled → relisted at $649,000 → sold for $630,000.

That’s a different story. The sale tells us what one buyer eventually paid. The listing history tells us buyers had previously rejected that house at $725,000, $699,000 and $675,000.

It also illustrates something sellers don’t always understand: Getting to the right price eventually isn’t necessarily the same as pricing correctly from the beginning. After months of market exposure and multiple reductions, buyers may stop asking, “Could this be the house?” They start asking, “What’s wrong with it?”

When I find a comparable property that sat for 90 days without selling, I want to know what did sell during those same 90 days. Sometimes we blame the market when the market was functioning just fine. Buyers were buying houses. They simply weren’t buying that one.

Maybe they chose the renovated house at $640,000. Maybe they paid $650,000 for the better lot. They may have even paid more for another property because it offered something the failed listing didn’t. That’s useful information when you’re sitting across from a seller who believes buyers just need more time to appreciate their home.

If buyers repeatedly toured the property and purchased competing homes instead, the market may already have delivered its opinion.

This is where agents have to resist oversimplifying the data. An expired listing isn’t automatic proof that a house was overpriced, and a canceled listing certainly isn’t either.

Listings fail for all sorts of reasons. Sellers change their minds. Job transfers fall through. Repairs surface. Agents get fired. Sometimes a seller receives a perfectly acceptable offer and decides not to move.

So, investigate. Call the previous agent. I might simply say:

“I’m pricing a similar property and noticed yours was on the market last year. Is there anything you can tell me about the activity or why the seller decided not to continue?”

Twenty-seven showings and no offers tell me something. Two showings in four months tells me something different.

There’s one more number worth considering: the cost of the pricing journey.

Find a house that started high, sat, reduced, expired, relisted and eventually sold. Then compare it with similar homes that entered the market closer to where buyers were actually buying.

Sellers often view aspirational pricing as a no-risk strategy: “We can always come down.” Technically, that’s true. But time isn’t free, and neither is market perception.

The next time you’re preparing a CMA in a shifting or buyer-favored market:

We’re very good at studying success in real estate. But as pricing gets harder, I’ve found myself returning to an old habit: studying the failures, too. Sold listings tell us where buyers have been willing to say yes. Sometimes the house nobody bought is the one that tells us exactly where they started saying no.

Roxanne Hale is the associate broker of the Art House Team, brokered by RealtySouth in Birmingham, Alabama. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.

#5380. Europe's €225 Billion Illegal Online Gambling Heist Revealed in New EU27 Report

European Casino Association-commissioned research finds illegal operators extracted 70% of online gambling revenue between 2023 and 2025, with an estimated â¬56.3 billion in gambling tax lost

BRUSSELS, Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Illegal online gambling operators extracted an estimated â¬224.8 billion in gross gaming revenue (GGR) from consumers across the European Union's 27 Member States between 2023 and 2025, according to new research commissioned by the European Casino Association (ECA) and produced by Gaming Compliance International (GCI).

The report, Online Gaming 2023â2025: Illegal Gambling in EU27 Europe, estimates that illegal operators captured approximately 70% of the EU27's â¬320.8 billion online gambling marketplace over the three-year period, extracting more than twice the â¬95.9 billion recorded by regulated operators.

The estimated gambling tax lost to European governments over three years reached â¬56.3 billion.

Illegal gambling captures 78% of marketplace growth

Between 2023 and 2025, the EU27 online gambling marketplace grew by â¬49.7 billion in annual GGR. Illegal operators accounted for â¬39.0 billion of that increase, capturing 78% of marketplace growth.

By 2025, illegal operators were extracting â¬91.6 billion annually, equivalent to more than â¬250 million every day, and controlled approximately 72% of the online marketplace.

Despite growth in regulated gambling revenues, the regulated sector's market share declined from 33% in 2023 to 28% in 2025.

A growing failure of public policy outcomes

The findings raise questions about the effectiveness of Europe's gambling regulatory and enforcement systems.

Regulated gambling provides governments with mechanisms to protect consumers, support legitimate commerce, enforce safeguards and collect taxation. Illegal operators compete for those same consumers while avoiding the licensing obligations and regulatory oversight required in the jurisdictions they target.

One marketplace, two competing industries

GCI's research examines the total online gambling marketplace, incorporating both locally regulated and illegal operators.

Its monitoring covers consumer audiences, their online activity and the wider infrastructure through which gambling is discovered, promoted and accessed, including websites, apps, search, AI, affiliates, social media, advertising, streaming and payments.

The report recorded 6,238 illegal operator destinations targeting EU27 consumers in 2025, compared with 4,921 in 2023.

The reported US$6.3 billion Binance heist shocked the world, yet illegal online gambling extracted an average of â¬6.24 billion from European consumers every month over three years. That's more than the value of the Binance heist, on average, each month, across 36 months.

Unlike a single theft of assets, gambling GGR measures stakes minus winnings across multiple transactions and events. This illustrates the scale of economic value extraction, not equivalent criminal losses.

Erwin Van Lambaart, Chairman of the ECA said:

"These findings demonstrate the enormous scale of illegal gambling operating alongside Europe's regulated businesses.

"Across three years, illegal operators extracted â¬224.8 billion while European governments missed out on an estimated â¬56.3 billion in gambling tax. Protecting consumers and legitimate businesses requires action against the operators and networks that undermine national regulatory systems."

Ismail Vali, President of GCI and founder and former CEO of Yield Sec said:

"The Binance heist shocked the world but why aren't we more outraged by what is likely the biggest heist in European history.

"Illegal online gambling isn't some separate marketplace operating beyond the regulated industry. Consumers experience one marketplace, but two industries compete for their money - one operating within national laws, the other outside them.

"Europe cannot protect its consumers, businesses or public finances by policing only the operators who follow the rules. We need to confront the entire marketplace and stop the criminal extraction of value from European economies."

#5379. Make it 8: Connecticut joins first responder homebuying push

Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.

The “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing. To qualify, first responders must have completed two years of service and purchase a primary residence within the community they serve.

In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.

“Connecticut’s police officers, firefighters and EMS personnel dedicate themselves to protecting our families and communities, and we want to make sure they have the opportunity to build their own futures here,” Governor Ned Lamont said in a prepared statement on Tuesday. “By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them.”

The program is part of Public Act 26-12, a state bill that aims to increase the number of first responders with a number of incentives, including college tuition reimbursement and improved labor protections.

“The people who protect and serve our communities should be able to afford to live in those communities, and this program with help them do it,” Comptroller Sean Scanlon said in a written statement. “Helping the people who put their lives on the line for us every day buy their first home is literally the least we can do, and I’m proud to have worked with Governor Lamont and legislature to make this a reality.”

Seven other states also have down payment assistance programs for first responders. Florida, Nevada, Georgia and South Carolina provide flat amounts, ranging from $10,000 to $35,000. Texas, Maryland and Ohio’s programs are percentage-based and offer assistance ranging from 2.5 percent to 5 percent of the purchase price.

The terms of each program vary. Most states forgive the assistance after five to seven years, but Nevada requires homebuyers to repay the funds within 30 years. And like Connecticut, Ohio also offers a 0.25 percent mortgage rate discount.

“Homeownership offers more than a place to live. It creates stability, strengthens connections to community and provides an opportunity to build wealth over time,” CHFA CEO and Executive Director Nandini Natarajan said in an announcement. “Through First Responders’ Time to Own, we’re helping the people who answer the call for our communities take an important step toward achieving their own homeownership goals.”

First responders often fall through the cracks of housing assistance programs because they don’t earn enough to afford market-rate housing but earn too much to qualify for federal housing vouchers.

Inman explored this dilemma last September in a feature on workforce housing in resort towns like Jackson Hole, Vail and Tahoe. These towns can’t operate without first responders and other essential workers in the hospitality and retail sectors. However, rental and for-sale home prices have far outpaced what these workers earn, forcing them to commute long distances from more affordable towns or take on second and third jobs to survive.

The solution for some of these towns has been investing in workforce housing, which caps prices for households that earn between 60 percent and 120 percent of their area’s AMI. Most workforce housing is rent-only, but some states are extending the programs to include for-sale properties.

“I think the fact that workforce housing can be necessary or is a thing in the first place is really an indictment of the state of housing affordability in the country today,” Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel said. “I think it’s important to ground any conversation about workforce and affordable housing in that reality. It’s a market failure and a policy failure that someone could be a doctor, a teacher or another kind of professional and cannot afford to pay the market rent or own a home outright.”

Windermere Principal Economist Jeff Tucker said workforce housing isn’t a panacea for affordability and works within an ecosystem of other housing and economic policies, such as upzoning, to create a more equitable market.

Tucker’s comments came a month after the Senate introduced the ROAD to Housing Act of 2025, and three months before the House introduced the Housing for the 21st Century Act. The bills were eventually combined into the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed in June.

“A broad package of necessary reforms to make more housing construction possible in much of the country is a really important component of a long-term solution to the housing affordability challenges we face,” Tucker said. “Our current housing shortage took years to develop. So it’ll take years to build our way out of it.”

Trusted Partner Providing Fiber Optic Solutions for ISP & System Integrator.

DUBAI, UAE, Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- FICER Technology, a manufacturer of high-performance fiber optic solutions, announces its strategic participation in GITEX GLOBAL 2026. Aligning with the theme "THE GLOBAL RESET 2027: Through a New Lens," FICER demonstrates its in-house manufacturing capabilities at the Dubai Exhibition Centre from 8th to 11th December at Booth H1-9 (S1, South Hall). Guided by the main theme "Universal Compatibility, Infinite Connectivity," FICER targets system integrators (SIs) and internet service providers (ISPs) across Dubai and the Middle East. The company delivers the essential optical components required to meet modern digital economy demands and build advanced infrastructure.

Driving AI, Data Centers, and Backbone InfrastructureThe Artificial Intelligence and IoT sectors demand high network connectivity, resilience, and data throughput. To support SIs managing computational tasks, 800G and 400G core optical transceivers are needful. These high-capacity modules serve as building blocks for high-density server environments. Addressing modern digital infrastructure challenges, the F520 OTN DWDM System and Digital Coherent Optics (DCO) solutions designed to be the optimal transceiver choice for backbone, metro, and Data Center Interconnect (DCI) networks. Utilizing these cross-compatible components, regional SIs and data centers optimize architectures without requiring total infrastructure overhauls.

Empowering ISP Regional Operation NetworksTo support ISP regional operation networks and SI partners, FICER offers 25G to 100G single-fiber BiDi (bidirectional) optical modules. Designed to pair perfectly with diverse switch equipment, these transceivers enable high-speed, bidirectional transmission over a single fiber. This architectural advantage doubles the usable capacity of existing fiber plants without initiating new cable construction. Operators deploy the released strands to expand transmission limits and absorb rising traffic across networks.

Advancing Digital Industries and Edge ConnectivityIndustry digitalization depends on connectivity reaching the network edge. To support this shift, XGSPON/25G-PON access networks are being deployed. Building on the existing optical distribution network, telecom operators elevate capacity for IoT-dense applications without laying new fiber. This architecture enables ISPs to converge enterprise services and mobile backhaul onto a unified fiber plant. FICER delivers the optical layer driving regional digital transformation.

Transcending standard brand positioning, FICER maintains robust in-house manufacturing operations. Holding a commanding market share in Taiwan, FICER extends its integrated manufacturing advantages to OEM/ODM clients. Guided by the mission "Fiber First. Compatibility Always", FICER combines technical expertise with a partner-centric approach, empowering customers to build efficient, future-ready optical networks.

#5377. Mortgage application payments reveal slight homebuyer affordability gain in October

MBA's Purchase Applications Payment Index fell 0.3% to a reading of 161.6 in October, signaling slightly better affordability. Median payments rose to $2,236, but a lower median loan amount of $315,424 helped offset higher rates.  AI Summary

Homebuyer affordability improved slightly in October as lower purchase loan amounts offset higher mortgage rates, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA)’s Purchase Applications Payment Index (PAPI), released Tuesday.

The index, which measures mortgage payments relative to borrower income, decreased 0.3% to a reading of 161.6 in October, down from 162.1 in September. A lower index reading indicates improving affordability.

The improvement came despite the national median mortgage payment for purchase applicants rising to $2,236 in October, up $21 (or 0.9%) from $2,215 in September. The median purchase loan application amount fell to $315,424 from $324,022, helping offset a 37-basis-point increase in mortgage rates.

“While the median mortgage payment rose $21 in October, payments as a share of earnings edged lower — slightly improving affordability,” Edward Seiler, MBA’s associate vice president of housing economics and executive director of the Research Institute for Housing America, said in a statement.

Affordability remains weaker than a year ago. The median mortgage payment increased 9.7% from $2,039 in October 2025, while earnings grew 1.6%. As a result, the PAPI was up 8% year over year.

“Looking ahead, lower mortgage rates and stronger earnings growth would give prospective buyers more room in their budgets,” Seiler said.

The median mortgage payment for Federal Housing Administration (FHA) borrowers increased to $1,944 in October, up from $1,906 in September and $1,789 a year earlier. For conventional loan borrowers, the median payment rose to $2,258, up from $2,244 in September and $2,063 in October 2025.

Among borrowers applying for lower-payment mortgages, those in the 25th percentile, the median monthly payment increased to $1,536 in October from $1,525 in September.

The PAPI for Black households decreased to 162.4 in October from 162.9 in September. For Hispanic households, it fell to 149.6 from 150.1, while the index for white households declined to 162.8 from 163.3.

Idaho had the highest PAPI reading in October at 269.8, followed by Nevada at 243.0, Rhode Island at 233.1, Arizona at 215.2 and Utah at 202.7. At the opposite end of the spectrum, Louisiana had the lowest reading at 119.8, followed by Washington, D.C., at 121.5, Alaska at 126.2, Iowa at 127.6 and Connecticut at 131.6.

The MBA’s mortgage payment-to-rent ratio also edged higher, increasing to 1.44 at the end of the third quarter from 1.43 at the end of the second quarter. The increase indicates that mortgage payments for home purchases rose slightly relative to rents.

The U.S. Census Bureau reported that the national median asking rent increased to $1,541 in the third quarter from $1,531 in the second quarter. The ratio of mortgage payments for lower-payment applicants to median asking rents remained at 0.99 in September.

Separately, the MBA’s Builders’ PAPI showed that the median mortgage payment for new-home purchase applicants increased to $2,375 in October, up from $2,307 in September.
