#5374. Lower mortgage rates could bring buyers back. What market will they return to?

Mortgage rates could fall below 7%, but what does that mean for local housing markets? HousingWire Data examines housing inventory, home asking prices, price reductions and pending home sales to reveal how housing affordability and buyer demand could shape opportunities heading into 2027.  AI Summary

The possibility of mortgage rates falling below 7% before the holidays is back on the table. In Tuesday morning’s Analyst Insights update in HousingWire Intelligence, HousingWire Lead Analyst Logan Mohtashami noted that the 10-year Treasury yield had reached 4.89%, approaching the 4.85% threshold he is watching, though mortgage spreads still need to improve.

But for housing professionals hoping to reengage buyers who stepped away from the market, mortgage rates are only part of the equation.

The homes available, the prices sellers are asking and the competition buyers face may look considerably different from when those buyers last searched.

Nationally, active single-family inventory stands at 894,692 homes, approximately 8% higher than a year ago. New pending listings increased 5.7% in the week ending Nov. 20, while new listings increased 1.2%.

That increase in contract activity is encouraging, but the broader picture remains more complicated.

HousingWire Data shows that 44 of 57 large metro areas (77.2%) recorded an improving ratio of new pending listings to new listings over consecutive four-week periods, even as pending activity remained below year-ago levels.

During the comparable period in 2025, just three of 54 qualifying metros (5.6%) showed that same combination.

An improving relationship between incoming listings and new contracts does not necessarily indicate strengthening buyer demand. And if lower mortgage rates do bring buyers back, the opportunities they encounter will vary considerably by market.

Consider Denver and Kansas City, two metro areas averaging nearly identical numbers of new pending listings per week but offering buyers different inventory and pricing environments.

Over the four weeks ending Nov. 20, Denver averaged 497 new pending listings per week, while Kansas City averaged 491. Both markets are experiencing substantially weaker contract activity than a year ago.

That’s where the similarities begin to fade.

Denver’s housing market offers buyers a different landscape heading into the holidays, with more available inventory, lower asking prices than during the spring and widespread price reductions.

For buyers who paused their home searches earlier this year because of affordability, Denver’s changing inventory and pricing conditions provide a reason to revisit their options, even before mortgage rates move meaningfully lower.

Kansas City’s median asking price has declined from its summer peak as price reductions have become more prevalent, although median asking prices remain above year-ago levels.

Kansas City offers buyers considerably more selection than a year ago. And while asking prices have moderated since the summer, higher median asking prices compared with last year could offset some of the affordability gains from lower borrowing costs.

Both markets offer more available homes than a year ago, but the pricing environments are different.

In Denver, a decline in mortgage rates could coincide with lower asking prices and more available homes. In Kansas City, greater selection and recent pricing adjustments may create opportunities, even though the median asking price remains higher than it was a year ago.

Changes in median asking prices can reflect shifts in the composition of available inventory, not just changes in individual home prices. That’s why examining inventory, asking prices and price reductions together provides a more useful assessment of local buying conditions than any one metric alone.

Another consideration is whether contract activity is already beginning to strengthen, even with mortgage rates above 7%.

In Denver, weekly new pending listings increased across the four most recent reporting weeks:

Cincinnati, Ohio, recorded a similar pattern, with weekly new pending listings increasing from 397 to 459 over the same period.

But Cincinnati presents a different inventory and pricing environment. Its median active list price is up 1.9% year over year, and the market has 2.44 months of inventory, compared with 3.01 in Denver.

While both markets have recorded three consecutive weekly increases in contract activity, buyers returning to Cincinnati could encounter a tighter inventory environment than those returning to Denver.

Neither market has recovered to last year’s level of contract activity, and several weeks of increases are not enough to establish a sustained recovery, particularly heading into the holidays.

Still, these are developments worth monitoring. If contract activity continues to strengthen while new listings decline seasonally, competition for available homes could increase.

Housing professionals don’t need to wait for mortgage rates to fall below 7% to start preparing for that possibility.

The more immediate opportunity is to understand how local market conditions have changed since buyers last evaluated their options.

For buyer’s agents: Revisit the searches of clients who paused their homebuying plans earlier this year. Has available inventory expanded in their price range? Are more homes experiencing price reductions? Changing market conditions may create opportunities worth exploring before rates move lower.

For listing agents: More available inventory means more competition for sellers. Monitor new pending listings alongside active inventory and price reductions to help sellers evaluate whether their pricing strategy remains competitive as buyer activity changes.

For mortgage lenders: Reengaging prospective purchase borrowers doesn’t have to begin with a conversation about mortgage rates. Understanding how available homes and asking prices have changed in a borrower’s target market can help make that conversation more relevant. Revisit purchasing power using current local asking prices and different mortgage rate scenarios.

For brokerage leaders: National mortgage rate movements can provide a reason to launch buyer reengagement campaigns, but local housing conditions should inform the messaging. A market with expanding inventory and declining asking prices presents a different opportunity than one with tighter inventory and strengthening contract activity.

Using HousingWire Intelligence, you can recreate the charts above for your own metro area, city or ZIP code.

Select single-family homes, choose the one-year view and examine four metrics together:

Use the one-year view to understand seasonal patterns, then narrow your analysis to the most recent three or six months to identify changes in market conditions.

Looking at these metrics together can help you distinguish between a market offering greater selection and potential affordability opportunities and one where renewed buyer activity could increase competition for available homes.

Mortgage rates may give buyers a reason to reconsider their plans. Understanding how local market conditions have changed gives housing professionals a reason to reach out before they do.

Source: HousingWire Data. Metro-level analysis reflects single-family housing data using four-week averages through Nov. 20, 2026, and comparable periods in 2025. The national weekly figures reflect the week ending Nov. 20. Large metro areas were defined as those with at least 3,000 average active listings and 100 average weekly new pending listings. Qualifying metro areas may differ between comparison periods. New pending listings represent homes entering contract, not closed transactions. Median active list prices reflect asking prices and may be influenced by changes in the composition of available inventory.

#5373. What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

Taylor Swift, classical or silence? Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.

Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers. One is a carefully curated playlist, while the other is silence.

Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.

None could point to hard numbers showing a playlist moved a home faster or for more money. What they did offer was a clear set of rules from the agents who use music, and an equally firm argument from those who won’t touch it.

Ben Jacobs, co-founder of the Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman in New York City, thinks music raises more questions than it answers. He said he’s not a fan of playing music during showings.

“Buyers may wonder if the agent is trying to mask something, whether it’s street noise, construction nearby, sounds within the building or even a noisy appliance,” Jacobs told Inman. “You want buyers to experience the home as it actually is, without anything distracting from their ability to evaluate the space.”

His co-founder, Jessica Chestler, said music has its place. That place is just not a private showing.

“Music can be wonderful for setting a mood at a cocktail party, listing launch or special event, but during a showing, I think there’s something to be said for letting the property speak for itself,” Chestler said.

Megan Sullivan works at the same brokerage, and she uses music for the very reason Jacobs avoids it. Sullivan sells large estate homes across Fairfield and Westchester counties out of Douglas Elliman’s Greenwich, Connecticut, office. Some of those homes sit within earshot of things a seller can’t fix.

“I actually do like incorporating music into certain showings, particularly when a property is impacted by outside noise from planes, trains or automobiles,” Sullivan said. “Thoughtfully selected background music can help create a more welcoming atmosphere and soften those distractions, allowing buyers to focus on the overall experience of the home. I think it’s very property-specific.”

Jeffrey Hensel is a broker associate with North Coast Financial, a California hard money lender that funds fix-and-flip and probate deals. He looks at it from the investor side.

“Dead silence can amplify every creak, clank, and drip in an otherwise quiet home,” he said. “Background music masks these sounds and provides some white noise to help set a calm mood.”

Agents in the pro-music camp mostly aren’t trying to cover anything up. They simply want buyers to stay longer.

Sandra Daniels of Harry Norman, Realtors | Forbes Global Properties serves the East Cobb and Marietta area outside Atlanta. She’s currently listing a $3.9 million estate in The River Club in Suwanee, Georgia.

For those showings, she rotates light classical piano, The Macarons Project and a Spotify playlist called “Nora Ephron + Nancy Meyers Dinner Party.”

“Put a buyer in a home with a glass of Champagne or a cup of coffee and the right music playing, and that cozy, inviting atmosphere encourages people to stay, relax and feel at home,” Daniels told Inman.

Daniels also has a low-tech trick for vacant listings she expects to sell in the first week. She bought an old-school CD player and a few classical CDs. She leaves it on repeat through the first weekend of showings and stops by each evening to turn off the lights and music and lock up.

Natalia Bassova, founder and CEO of Resort Real Estate in Breckenridge, Colorado, saw the same effect at a luxury mountain listing. The home looked great, she said, but it showed cold.

“By adding some background instrumental music, it gave the buyers more time to spend in the home. They spent more time in the kitchen and great room areas,” Bassova said. “The property didn’t change, but the atmosphere did.”

For mountain and luxury homes, Bassova plays acoustic and piano music, including Ludovico Einaudi and The Piano Guys. For condos and new construction, she switches to soft contemporary instrumentals.

Agents who play music disagree on genre, but almost all agree on one thing: avoid lyrics.

“If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact,” Bassova said. Her never-play list covers anything with strong lyrics, politics, swearing or heavy bass.

Andrea Seeney is a global real estate advisor with Atlanta Fine Homes Sotheby’s International Realty and a trained opera singer and classical pianist. She compared lyrics to a seller’s personal effects.

“Acoustic performances are best because they set a tone and allow the buyer to fill in the blanks with their own thoughts,” Seeney said.

She leans toward jazz and usually plays Spotify’s Coffee House radio or its Ella Fitzgerald playlist. She says music works on buyers through memory: a song can take someone back to a time and place they enjoyed, “and that memory then reflects positively on the home.”

Hensel takes the lyrics rule a step further, to genre itself. If an agent plays hip-hop or country for a buyer who doesn’t listen to it, he says, that signals an assumption about who the buyer is. That can create friction neither side notices. His pick is quiet cocktail-lounge jazz like Miles Davis or Bill Evans, at a steady tempo and volume.

He also cited retail research by psychological scientists Adrian North and Lorraine Sheridan of Curtin University and Charles Areni of Macquarie University. It found that shoppers who heard classical music rated merchandise as higher quality and were willing to spend more.

Some agents ignore the rulebook completely.

Rachel Kilmer, an agent with ReeceNichols Real Estate in Kansas City, Missouri, plays Taylor Swift at nearly every open house. She swaps in country for more rural listings.

“In Kansas City, she’s a conversation starter,” Kilmer said. “People come in, and it’s, ‘Are you a Swiftie?’ ‘No, but I love the Chiefs!’ It really helps loosen up the conversation.”

She added, “I’m the one sitting there listening to it for two hours!”

Monica Shea, a broker with KW Aspire in Colorado Springs, Colorado, builds whole open houses around a theme, and the music follows.

She played the Eras Tour set list at a Taylor Swift–themed open house and the Frozen soundtrack at a hot cocoa bar event. A Halloween open house got not-too-spooky Halloween music. For regular showings, she has sellers put on a YouTube channel with seasonal background music and scenery.

Shea’s never-play list puts her directly at odds with a few other agents: smooth jazz. Shea says she never plays “anything that sounds like the Weather Channel.”

Marcel Finkelstein of Team BlackStar at eXp Realty hosts open houses every Sunday across Monmouth County, New Jersey. He sees music as more of an icebreaker than a staging tool.

His Apple Music rotation includes lounge instrumentals, vocal-free dance-pop and Bon Entendeur. It also has Afro house from DJ Alex Niyazov and the warm trumpet and sax of Fausto Papetti and Paul Mauriat.

He uses the same approach whether the listing is a $600,000 two-bedroom condo in Manalapan or a $2 million six-bedroom in Colts Neck.

“I want the atmosphere to feel calm, comfortable and welcoming, rather than like a sales presentation,” Finkelstein said.

Finkelstein added that his Instagram followers also know how much he loves music.

“Every week, I share new songs and incorporate music into my stories and posts about homes,” he said. “It’s a personal interest that carries through into how I present properties.”

On setup, agents who play music give similar advice. Keep the volume low enough that buyers can ask questions and the agent can hear their feedback. Use one good speaker rather than several.

Bassova puts hers in the middle of the home, and Seeney puts a small Bluetooth speaker in the kitchen. When sellers have a Sonos system, Daniels connects to it from her MacBook or iPad. Otherwise, she brings her own Bose speaker.

Kilmer runs her music from an iPad instead of her phone. “That way, incoming calls and texts don’t interrupt the music,” she said.

As for proof, none of the agents Inman spoke with track music as a performance metric. Bassova said she gets buyer feedback that certain homes feel relaxing, but nothing tied to days on market or offers.

So the evidence is anecdotal, and the playlists don’t agree. Agents can’t even settle on jazz. Both camps share one goal: the buyer should notice the home, not the soundtrack.

As Bassova said, “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact.”

#5372. Leekr Technology Brings Automotive-Grade Brake-by-Wire Solutions to Support Mass Production of Autonomous Vehicles

SHANGHAI, Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Leekr Technology, a leading provider of intelligent chassis solutions, is accelerating its expansion into overseas autonomous vehicle markets, bringing its automotive-grade brake-by-wire technology, which has been proven in high-volume production in China's intelligent electric vehicle market, to low-speed autonomous vehicles. It offers DHB-P (Two-box: Decoupled Hydraulic Brake-by-Wire System) and IHB-P (One-box: Integrated Intelligent Braking System) to meet the braking requirements of autonomous logistics and sweeper vehicles.

Varying vehicle loads, emergency braking demands, and prolonged operating hours pose three major challenges for their braking systems. For low-speed autonomous transport vehicles, Leekr Technology's brake-by-wire systems dynamically adjust braking force based on vehicle mass and payload variations, in coordination with the vehicle control strategy, ensuring reliable braking under full load and smooth braking when unladen.

The systems support active braking, with a braking response time of less than 150 ms, and work with automated driving systems to execute emergency braking commands, helping to reduce collision risks. Automotive-grade design, safety redundancy, and system self-diagnostics help maintain reliable braking during extended unattended operation. Its solutions have been adopted in series-production vehicles by leading autonomous logistics and sweeper vehicle OEMs in China.

DHB-P (Two-box) is designed for mainstream OEM production programs. Featuring a fully decoupled hydraulic architecture with motor-driven active pressure generation, the system applies braking force in response to vehicle control commands without requiring brake pedal input. It supports integration with Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS). The system supports human-machine collaborative driving and is compatible with both human-driven and autonomous driving modes.

For vehicles requiring higher integration and more advanced active safety functions, Leekr Technology offers the IHB-P (One-box) Integrated Intelligent Braking System. It combines the electronic brake booster (eBooster) and Electronic Stability Control (ESC) functions in a single unit.

To meet the safety requirements of advanced automated driving, IHB-P can be paired with an independent Redundant Brake Unit (RBU). If the primary braking unit (IHB-P) fails, the RBU can take over braking control to bring the vehicle to a safe stop, meeting the braking redundancy requirements of SAE Level 4 automated driving and low-speed autonomous vehicle applications.

Leekr Technology is the first company in China to achieve mass-production deployment of an IHB-P + RBU redundant brake-by-wire solution in autonomous vehicles. In Europe, it will provide OEMs with customized brake-by-wire solutions and engineering delivery services.

#5371. Your real estate listing is stuck and a price drop will not fix it

Some stalled condo listings are constrained by building level compliance and HOA financials, not pricing or marketing. Leaders can protect the seller by pausing the listing, extending the agreement, and pushing repairs to regain financing eligibility.  AI Summary

There is a category of stuck listing that is going to become more common over the next few years, and most agents have not been trained for it. It is the listing that cannot sell for a reason that has nothing to do with price, photography or effort. It is the listing blocked at the building level, and if we keep coaching agents to treat every slow listing with a price reduction, we are going to watch good professionals burn good listings for no reason.

This came up on one of our Power Agent coaching calls. An agent brought me a four-unit situation. The condo had been on the market for 86 days. She had lost two solid buyers. One was all cash, and the all-cash buyer still walked. Any time an all-cash buyer walks, leaders should pay attention, because the one thing you cannot blame is financing.

The building had a balcony and structural-compliance issue, the kind of inspection-and-repair requirement that has spread across the country since Surfside and that states like California have written into law for decks and balconies. The repairs had not been started. A new management company had taken over months earlier and was still, in their words, figuring things out.

Because the work was un-started, the building landed on the list that does not qualify for conventional Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac financing. The financed buyers were gone instantly. The all-cash buyer pulled the association financials, saw thin reserves and un-started repairs, read it correctly as a poorly run building, and decided the headache was not worth it.

Powerfact: Structural-compliance problems do not lower a home’s price. They remove a home’s buyers.

That distinction matters for anyone leading a team, because it changes the coaching. When a building cannot get conventional financing, the buyer pool does not shrink, it collapses to cash buyers willing to tolerate a troubled association. We just watched one of those rare buyers say no. Telling that agent to drop the price would have been coaching malpractice. The price was never the lever.

Here is the plan I gave her, and it is the plan I would want every leader teaching.

Take it off the market, temporarily. Days on market is a public number, and a climbing one negotiates against your seller before an offer is ever written. Pull the listing before the clock becomes the story.

Then, stay hired. This is the step that separates an advisor from an order-taker. Taking a listing off the market should not end the relationship, it should restructure it. The agent and I built a new listing agreement long enough to cover the repair timeline plus fresh marketing afterward at a likely new price.

If repairs take a couple of months and the sale takes several more, that is an eight or nine month agreement, not a renewal of the old 90 days. The property comes off the MLS and is not shown, but the agreement stays active. The agent keeps her position. The seller keeps a professional who is still working.

Then, advocate for the whole building. I told her to get in front of the management company and the association board, the president and the vice president, and push to expedite repairs that are hurting all 54 owners. This is where a top producer builds a reputation that compounds. When you are the agent pushing a stalled building back into compliance, every owner in that building knows your name, and so does every agent who tried and gave up. In a 54-unit building, that is 54 future listing conversations you just earned by being the one who showed up and did the work nobody else would touch.

We also talked through the rent-instead question, because these sellers had already relocated and were carrying the unit. Renting for a year while the building gets sorted is a legitimate option, but it has to be coached with the worst case on the table. In a tenant-friendly jurisdiction an eviction can run six to nine months. Florida’s landlord rules are workable. Other markets are not.

This property sits in California, and I told her plainly that I do not know California’s specifics well enough to promise a timeline, so she needs to find out. Because if the tenant will not leave and removal takes six months, the one-year rental really delivered about six months of clean cash flow. Leaders, this is the kind of worst-case math we owe our sellers, and it is exactly the math an anxious agent skips to avoid an awkward conversation.

The larger point for the industry is this. Compliance-driven financing blocks are a growing reality, and they reward the agent who can diagnose, not just discount. The old reflex of lowering price until something moves does not clear a building-level obstacle, and agents who only know that one move will lose listings they could have saved. The professionals who win in this environment are the ones who can look a seller in the eye and say, the problem is not your price, the problem is your building, and here is the plan to fix it.

That is the advisor our clients actually need. Serve, don’t sell. In a market with this much noise, the agent who clings to a dying listing looks desperate, and the one who calmly takes the sign out of the yard, extends the agreement, and goes to fix the real problem looks like exactly what they are. The one in control.

Darryl Davis, CSP, is a national speaker, real estate coach, and the bestselling author of How to Become a Power Agent® in Real Estate. Learn more at darrylspeaks.com.

#5370. NAR’s latest data, must-have AI tools, Compass’ 15 new lawsuits

Congratulations, you’ve made it to Friday again this week. But before you head out for the weekend, we’re bringing you a quick catch-up on the biggest headlines and the most helpful how-tos for your business. So, Take 5 and peruse our top editor picks for this week and why they matter to your business.

P.S. Don’t miss The Download, our weekly column that breaks down one of the week’s top stories and equips you with what you’ll need to meet next Monday head-on.

Homeownership is slipping further out of reach for young Americans, according to the National Association of Realtors’ 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers. The report, released on Thursday, revealed that the share of first-time homebuyers rose 1 percent year over year to 22 percent. Despite the small gain, first-time buyer activity remains near historic lows (21 percent) and 18 percentage points below pre-2008 trends (40 percent). Same as last year, the median age of a first-time homebuyer was 40 — roughly a decade older than the typical median age in the 1980s.

Why it matters: This annual report gives you a pulse on national real estate trends and how you might want to pivot your strategies. For example, as noted above, the median age of the first-time homebuyer is 40, and the share of single women homeowners has risen to 20 percent. A longer nurture campaign might be in order (ahem, see below), and if you’re not already marketing toward single women, perhaps you should. Read the full report for more.

EXTRA: The buyer who can’t close for a year is your best asset in 2026

AI has been the topic of conversation for the past couple of years. And there’s a lot of talk. So how do you suss through the noise and find what works for your business? Jimmy Burgess has created a no-nonsense list of seven AI tools that are actually worth your time.

Why it matters: Burgess shares not only his top tools but also how to use them. These tools will help you turn prompts into better questions, find the questions your future clients are asking, remember the details that matter, evaluate your AI search visibility, turn one video into multiple pieces of content, make video editing easier and use AI as a strategist rather than a writing assistant. Don’t feel overwhelmed. You don’t have to use all of them at once.

Krystopher Benyamein recently sold a property in San Pedro where his team hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. They found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and they had to start again.

They eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when they shared the case study on Instagram, they didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing they’d done. They opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”

That opening puts the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, they explained how they responded, got the property back in front of buyers and ultimately closed.

Why it matters: In today’s market, there are many stories of buyers backing out of deals. This approach allows you to create content that keeps you top of mind, show sellers exactly how you work and reach a wider audience. Benyamein shows you how to do it and shares a FREE Canva template to help get the job done.

VA loans often get passed over for conventional loans. Inman’s Nick Pipitone spoke with Fathom Realty’s Lindsey Schmidt, an Army veteran who served in Iraq, about why VA financing still carries a stigma among sellers and listing agents, how she gets around it and why VA assumptions remain one of the most misunderstood tools in the market.

Why it matters: Military members often have to move. Understanding and busting myths about VA loans can help you get ahead of objections before making an offer, which will help you get more deals across the finish line and get more service members into homes.

Compass has been busy, creating and formalizing policy around employees in association leadership positions and how Compass brokerage agents cooperate on private listings.

The company announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it says can reach $15,000.

Why it matters: Compass International Holdings is currently in litigation with 16 total MLSs across 18 federal lawsuits. Not only is this big news that’s making waves throughout the industry, but its ripple effects could impact your MLS’s rules, if they haven’t already.

EXTRA: What Compass’ leadership ban signals for agents and associations

#5368. Why 16 MLSs want a united front against Compass in the battle over private listings

MLSs sued by Compass asked the JPML to consolidate or coordinate pretrial proceedings across 16 antitrust cases and 2 SDNY declaratory judgment actions. Compass plans to challenge the SDNY cases and says each MLS rule is local and distinct.  AI Summary

Compass International Holdings may have filed 16 separate antitrust lawsuits against 16 separate MLS, but according to court documents filed earlier this week, those MLSs are seeking to combine these lawsuits into one.

In a motion filed on Monday to stay the lawsuit Compass filed against it, California Regional MLS (CRMLS) told the court that it and the other MLSs Compass has filed lawsuits against have asked to consolidate or coordinate the pretrial proceedings for the various Compass v. MLS lawsuits currently pending across the country in federal court in the Southern District of New York (SDNY). If the panel declines to select New York, the motion identifies the Western District of North Carolina and the Middle District of Florida as alternative venues for the consolidated litigation.

According to the motion, the MLSs have also asked to include the two declaratory judgement lawsuits nine MLSs have already filed against Compass in the SDNY.

“Compass has chosen to wage the same legal fight in courts across the country, creating unnecessary costs and the risk of conflicting rulings,” Richard Haggerty, the CEO of OneKey MLS, said in a statement. “Each of the 16MLS organizations are challenging that approach. We believe these cases belong before one judge, and we will continue defending the cooperation rules that ensure no brokerage gains an unfair advantage by withholding publicly marketed homes from the shared marketplace.”

This request comes after Compass informed the SDNY court that it plans to file a motion to dismiss the declaratory judgement lawsuits or to sever and transfer each MLS’s claims to the district where Compass has brought its own antitrust case against that MLS.

After months of posturing and clashes over policies, the legal dispute between Compass and the MLSs kicked off in earnest this September when Compass sent letters to MLSs across the country demanding that they stop fining agents for publicly marketing office exclusive listings. Later that month, Compass CEO Robert Reffkin told a room full of MLS executives gathered at the Council of MLSs (CMLS) that he would sue any MLS that refused to give in to Compass’s demands.

Despite Reffkin’s threats, it was actually CRMLS that made the first move, filing a lawsuit in early October seeking a declaratory judgment that its policies on listing cooperation are “fair, procompetitive, and legally sound,” according to a company announcement. CRMLS has since been joined by New York’s OneKey MLS in this lawsuit, while MLSListings, Arizona Regional MLS, bridgeMLS, Canopy MLS, REcolorado, Hive MLS, and Doorify MLS have filed their own lawsuit, also in the SDNY, seeking the same judgements as CRMLS and OneKey.

In the midst of these lawsuits hitting the court docket, Compass filed its own lawsuit against CRMLS, alleging that its rule unlawfully restrict how homeowners and their agents can publicly market properties outside the MLS.

Roughly a month later, Compass reiterated those same claims in 15 separate lawsuits filed against 15 MLSs. MLS defendants in those lawsuits include bridgeMLS, Bay East MLS, Contra Costa MLS, MLSListings, The MLS-CLAW, San Diego MLS, Canopy MLS, Hive MLS, Doorify MLS, Arizona Regional MLS, Recolorado, NorthstarMLS, Houston Association of Realtors, Stellar MLS and OneKey MLS.

In an emailed statement a Compass spokesperson told HousingWire that the filing is “a procedural request  that does not change the substance of [Compass’s] claims.”

“Each MLS applies its own rules, and the impact of those rules on agents, home sellers, and buyers is specific to its local jurisdiction,” the spokesperson added.

It remains to be seen if court will allow the MLSs to consolidate their lawsuits. This is not the first time real estate industry defendants have sought to consolidate similar lawsuits. Several real estate brokerage defendants in the copycat commission lawsuits attempted to consolidate their cases, but their request was rejected.

#5367. NAR saved for his $541K exit; now it won’t pay, ex-CFO says

License under the Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 Generic license.

Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.

Pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005. To avoid booking the full expense when a senior vice president retired, NAR created a Compensation Reserve that let it steadily set aside funds throughout the executive’s tenure, which it would release at retirement. Pierpoint helped establish the reserve in 2005 at the direction of former NAR CEO Dale Stinton, court documents said.

Pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind. The former CFO said he was key in executing the buyer-broker commission settlement payout, which totaled $418 million. The first settlement payment, totaling roughly $200 million, was issued in February 2025, with subsequent payments of $72 million per year until the full $418 million is paid.

Pierpoint said he notified NAR of his impending retirement in late 2024 and requested his retirement payout. However, six days before his last day with NAR, Pierpoint alleged that a Grant Thornton auditor named White — there is no first name listed in the court documents — emailed him and said that “NAR had been ‘unable to locate any policy or verify any consistent practice’ concerning the Compensation Reserve or ‘the payout to executives of a full year of salary upon retirement.'”

White also allegedly said that the Compensation Reserve “was not used to fund” the exit packages of eight other senior vice presidents who retired before Pierpoint, which are listed in the court documents as L.J., F.S., B.M., D.H., J.G.,  J.B., D.G. and B.G. Real Estate News said L.J., D.G. and B.G. are likely former general counsel Laurie Janik, former SVP of talent development and resources Donna Gland, and former senior vice president and CEO Bob Goldberg.

As a result, Grant Thornton said it was “unable to approve the payout of a full year’s compensation without any concrete proof that such act is mandated by an employment agreement, policy or plan.”

Pierpoint claimed NAR had the funds to pay his retirement benefit and provided a ledger outlining what the Association allegedly reserved from December 2014 to December 2024. He also said the trial balances NAR provided to outside auditors, including Grant Thornton, included evidence of the Compensation Reserve’s existence and purpose.

“NAR carried its obligation to Pierpoint at approximately 97.6 cents on the dollar three months before it refused to pay him anything,” the complaint read. “The practice NAR now claims it cannot verify is documented in NAR’s own ledger, its own year-end schedules, its own payroll records and its own audit files, and was paid to every one of Pierpoint’s predecessors who retired. NAR did not stop believing in its obligation; it stopped wanting to pay it.”

Pierpoint’s counsel accused NAR of shirking its obligation to pay the former CFO due to its financial woes after the settlement. In December 2025, former NAR president Kevin Sears said the buyer-broker commission settlement saved the Association’s finances — the other option was to file an appeal and declare bankruptcy.

“John Pierpoint helped guide NAR through an extraordinarily challenging period in its history, including the financial consequences of the antitrust litigation,” said David Fish, an attorney with Workplace Law Partners, P.C., who represents Pierpoint. “After nearly four decades of service, he expected the organization to honor the same retirement compensation practice it had followed for other senior executives.”

“We believe the evidence will establish that the financial pressures following the antitrust verdict did not relieve NAR of its obligation to pay compensation earned by its employees,” he added.

Pierpoint’s counsel is requesting that NAR pay the $541,059 retirement payout, statutory damages of 5 percent of the unpaid amount for each month it remains unpaid, attorneys’ fees and costs, and prejudgment and post-judgment interest. They also seek a jury trial.

NAR denied Pierpoint’s claims, saying that the former CFO has “[mischaracterized] a varied set of individual arrangements with departing executives as a uniform and guaranteed retirement benefit.”

“Mr. Pierpoint was not entitled to the payment he now seeks, and NAR’s decision was unrelated to its antitrust settlement or its financial condition,” an NAR spokesperson told Inman in an emailed statement. “NAR is committed to appropriate financial controls and responsible stewardship of its members’ dues dollars. NAR pays compensation and benefits that are actually owed, not just because a former executive requests payment. No such obligation exists here, and we intend to vigorously defend against these claims through the appropriate legal process.”

#5366. Mortgage rates whiplash is in full effect, with jumbo loans shedding 25 bps this week

Mortgage rates moved lower this week after recent increases, but demand indicators remain soft. MBA reported applications down 5% week over week and affordability about 8% weaker than a year ago, while the vast majority of interest rate traders are pricing a Federal Reserve hike in December.  AI Summary

The seesaw pattern for mortgage rates that’s been the story for much of the second half of 2026 reared its head again this week as rates for major loan types declined, reversing some of the increases from prior weeks.

At HousingWire‘s Mortgage Rates Center on Tuesday, rates for 30-year conforming loans averaged 7.53% — down 5 basis points from a week ago. Rates for 30-year loans through the Federal Housing Administration (FHA) dropped 7 bps to 7.30%, while rates for 30-year jumbo loans plummeted 25 bps to 7.62%.

Rates in the mid-7% range continue to weigh on homebuyer demand and affordability metrics. Last week’s application index from the Mortgage Bankers Association showed that total applications were down 5% on a weekly basis. MBA data released Tuesday found that affordability is about 8% weaker than a year ago, even though it improved slightly from September to October.

“Higher mortgage rates weighed on application activity last week, with the 30-year fixed rate rising to 7.35%. Purchase applications were down 18% from a year ago, reflecting continued affordability challenges and softer homebuyer demand. The direction of mortgage rates in the coming weeks will be key to the housing market’s momentum heading into 2027,” MBA president and CEO Bob Broeksmit said in a statement.

Dan Ribler, vice president of capital markets and strategy at national reverse mortgage lender Longbridge Financial, said that the October jobs report should’ve sent rates higher. Nonfarm payrolls increased by 165,000 positions last month and the unemployment rate remained steady at 4.1%, indicative of today’s healthier labor market conditions in relation to 2025.

Ribler noted that the jobless rate has been below 5% every month since September 2021, unemployment claims are lower than a year ago and the Federal Reserve‘s “own description is the labor market is very strong.” But strong employment trends have been overshadowed by stubborn inflation, which continues to run well above the central bank’s 2% annualized target.

“Inflation has been above 2% year over year 57 months in a row,” Ribler remarked. “The Fed has, by the way, under this administration, reiterated the 2% hurdle and that they’re going to be tough on inflation. They’re certainly talking the hawk talk, saying we’re going to keep inflation under 2%.

“But man, I don’t know about you, if my kid breaks curfew 57 nights in a row — and I say I’m going to punish you one of these times and I never do anything about it — at some point, he stops believing me, right?”

Inflation is likely to prompt the Fed to raise rates next month. The CME Group‘s FedWatch tool reveals that a 25-bps hike in December is all but certain, with 96% of interest rate traders saying that the federal funds rate will rise to a range of 4% to 4.25%. It was last at that level in September 2025.

Much of the housing and mortgage industry headlines in the past week have cast a shadow over any potential market improvements in 2027.

Selma Hepp, chief economist at Cotality, said in a statement that existing home sales have fallen to their lowest level since August 2010. She also pointed to a Realtor.com analysis, which found that the typical repeat buyer will pay about $1,100 more per month if they choose to sell and move.

“A meaningful housing recovery requires rates to come down and, importantly, stay down long enough to improve affordability and unlock turnover,” Hepp said. “Until then, the adjustment is likely to come through weaker sales and softer home prices rather than widespread homeowner distress.

“The number worth writing is the $1,100. That’s the jump in monthly payment a typical repeat buyer takes on just to move house. It’s the clearest explanation yet of why nobody is selling.”

New home sales have been equally grim, with September’s seasonally adjusted annual rate of 676,000 sales representing a 5.3% decline from a year ago. Higher rates have also prompted homebuilders to remain cautious about creating more supply, with U.S. Census Bureau figures showing that single-family housing starts were down 3.2% year over year in September. Monthly gains in total starts were largely tied to the multifamily sector.

“Challenging affordability has been weighing on the resale market. Newly pending sales fell 17% in October, the largest year-over-year drop since 2023,” Zillow senior economist Kenny Lee said in a statement. “Single-family homebuilders have been navigating the same challenge. While homebuilders have been adapting to the softer market by offering concessions and building smaller homes, the 2027 spring home-shopping season could see a slow start as buyer demand continues to wane.”

The relative lack of sales has weighed on mortgage origination volumes, with ATTOM data for the third quarter of 2026 showing that the roughly 730,000 purchase loans closed during that period were the lowest figure for any third quarter in 14 years.

Refinance activity was also bleak, with the roughly 561,000 refis in Q3 down 19% year over year. Refi lending was down from Q2 2026 in nearly 90% of the metro areas analyzed by ATTOM, with the largest declines in major metros like San Jose, San Francisco, Dallas, Austin and Louisville, Kentucky.

#5365. Huawei and CMA Jointly Launch National Payment Solution to Accelerate Global Payments Transformation

SINGAPORE, Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- At the Singapore FinTech Festival 2026 (SFF 2026), Huawei and CMA Small Systems AB (CMA), a member of the Huawei Global Financial Partner RONGHAI Program, jointly launched a National Payment Solution.

Frank LU, Director of Central Bank Integrated BU Solution Sales Dept., Huawei, and Maxim Neshcheret, Regional Director, Asia, CMA Small Systems AB, attended the launch ceremony. By combining CMA's software capabilities in national payment systems with Huawei's ICT infrastructure capabilities across computing, storage, networking, cloud, and data centers, the two companies aim to provide end-to-end joint solutions for central banks and financial institutions, accelerating the modernization of national payment systems.

Combining Strengths to Build Resilient National Payment Systems

As digital transformation continues to reshape the global financial industry, payment systems are evolving toward real-time processing, greater efficiency, and enhanced interoperability. This evolution is placing higher demands on system performance, security, business continuity, and infrastructure resilience.

With more than 30 years of experience in financial market infrastructure, CMA has extensive expertise serving central banks, commercial banks, clearing houses, and securities depositories, with core capabilities spanning RTGS, ACH, IPS, and securities depository systems. Huawei, drawing on its extensive ICT expertise, provides financial institutions with full capabilities spanning computing, storage, networking, cloud, and data centers.

The jointly launched National Payment Solution deeply integrates CMA's proven payment software with Huawei's highly reliable ICT infrastructure across computing, storage, networking, cloud, and data centers, providing customers with an integrated solution spanning payment applications and underlying infrastructure. The solution supports high-availability and disaster recovery deployments to ensure the stable operation and business continuity of critical payment systems. It also enables phased implementation and flexible expansion based on evolving business requirements. In addition, through the Huawei Global Financial Partner RONGHAI Program, the two companies have established a collaborative mechanism covering joint solution development, project delivery, and customer services. This helps reduce system integration and project governance complexity while delivering solutions tailored to the needs of customers in different countries and regions.

Deepening Partnership to Expand Global Financial Markets

The joint launch marks another important milestone in the deepening partnership between Huawei and CMA. In 2025, CMA joined the Huawei Global Financial Partner RONGHAI Program. In September 2026, the two companies signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) during HUAWEI CONNECT 2026, further defining their collaboration in technology integration, joint solution development, market expansion, and customer services. The latest launch marks a further step in their partnership, advancing from ecosystem collaboration to joint solution development and market collaboration.

Launched in 2024, the Huawei Global Financial Partner RONGHAI Program aims to deepen collaboration with financial industry partners and accelerate customers' digital and intelligent transformation.

Looking ahead, Huawei will continue to work closely with CMA to deepen joint innovation and market collaboration in national payment systems, bringing their joint solutions to more markets worldwide and contributing to the modernization of global financial infrastructure.

#5363. FHFA raises conforming loan limit to $855,400 in 2027

FHFA will increase the 2027 baseline conforming loan limit by 2.71% to $855,400 for one-unit properties, with a $1,283,100 ceiling in high-cost areas and higher caps in Alaska, Hawaii, Guam and the U.S. Virgin Islands.   AI Summary

The baseline conforming loan limit will rise 2.71% in 2027 to $855,400 for one-unit properties in most parts of the country, according to the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA). Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac will be authorized to buy loans up to that balance in the vast majority of U.S. counties.

The $855,400 cap is an increase of $22,650 from 2026 and reflects slower home price growth tied to a weaker housing market and higher-for-longer mortgage rates. The annual adjustment was 3.25% last year and above 5% in each of the prior two years.

Under the Housing and Economic Recovery Act of 2008 (HERA), the national “ceiling” for high-cost areas is set at 150% of the baseline. For 2027, that ceiling will be $1,283,100 for one-unit properties in markets where 115% of the local median home value exceeds the baseline limit. Conforming caps first surpassed $1 million in these high-cost areas in 2022.

Special statutory provisions apply in Alaska, Hawaii, Guam and the U.S. Virgin Islands. In these areas, the 2027 baseline loan limit for one-unit properties will be $1,283,100, while the ceiling will be $1,924,650.

“Due to rising home values, the CLL will be higher in all but 24 U.S. counties or county equivalents,” the FHFA said in a statement.

Each November, FHFA publishes new conforming loan limits for the coming year. Increases resumed in 2016, after home prices returned to pre-Great Recession levels, a condition required by HERA. The statute also prevents the ceiling from declining in years when home prices fall; the cap only moves higher when national prices increase year over year.

This year’s adjustment is tied to FHFA’s third-quarter 2026 House Price Index (HPI), which tracks changes in average U.S. home values over the prior four quarters. Nominal, seasonally adjusted, expanded-data HPI showed house prices rose 2.72% on average between the third quarters of 2025 and 2026, essentially matching the 2.71% rise in the baseline conforming loan limit.

The new limits expand the amount of mortgage debt that can qualify for conventional financing backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. Loans above FHFA’s limits are classified as jumbos, a segment still dominated by banks and portfolio lenders that set their own credit standards and capital requirements.

Mortgage lenders once again anticipated FHFA’s announcement and raised their internal conforming loan limits ahead of the official release to compete for volume. But they were conservative.

Rocket Mortgage was an early mover, lifting its conforming loan limit to $845,000 for single-family homes in 48 states in September. CrossCountry Mortgage adopted the same level.

Pennymac set its internal limit at $850,000, while United Wholesale Mortgage increased its one-unit cap for conventional and Department of Veterans Affairs loans to $847,440.

BEIJING, Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Gaotu Techedu Inc. (NYSE: GOTU) ("Gaotu" or the "Company"), a leading technology-driven education company in China focused on enabling lifelong learning through AI-powered solutions, today announced its unaudited financial results for the third quarter ended September 30, 2026.

Third Quarter 2026 Key Financial and Operating Data

(In thousands of RMB, except for percentages)

[1] For a reconciliation of non-GAAP numbers, please see the table captioned "Reconciliations of non-GAAP measures to the most comparable GAAP measures" at the end of this press release. Non-GAAP income (loss) from operations and non-GAAP net income (loss) exclude share-based compensation expenses.

[2] Gross billings is a non-GAAP financial measure, which is defined as the total amount of cash received for the sale of course offerings in such period, net of the total amount of refunds in such period. See "About Non-GAAP Financial Measures" and "Reconciliations of non-GAAP measures to the most comparable GAAP measures" elsewhere in this press release.

Nine Months Ended September 30, 2026 Highlights

First Nine Months 2026 Key Financial and Operating Data

(In thousands of RMB, except for percentages)

Larry Xiangdong Chen, the Company's founder, Chairman and CEO, commented, "This quarter, our net revenues increased by 18.3% year over year to nearly RMB1.9 billion, and we achieved GAAP operating profitability in a third quarter for the first time. Our performance reflects solid improvements in resource allocation and management efficiency, alongside our continued focus on high-quality products and services. Deeper integration of AI and digital tools also elevated efficiency across teaching, services, and operations. This enabled us to unlock operating leverage while maintaining high delivery standards, enhancing the scalability of our business model and strengthening our long-term earnings potential. We also remain committed to returning value to shareholders: as of November 24, 2026, we had repurchased approximately RMB780.5 million under our aggregated share repurchase programs.

'One Customer Commitment' defines how we serve learners across different stages of life. Our comprehensive product portfolio empowers us to accompany users throughout their learning journeys, and the trust we earn through every high-quality delivery is what keeps them choosing Gaotu at each step of their growth. Over time, this trust will strengthen our competitive advantage and support sustainable value creation for shareholders. "

Robin Bin Luo, COO of the Company, added, "Profitable growth remained our focus in the third quarter, guiding our resource allocation strategy and dynamic adjustments across products and channels. Gains in user acquisition efficiency were a key driver of operating margin expansion, underscoring stronger execution in product selection, channel management, and cost control. We also continued to refine our business portfolio, concentrating resources on businesses with clear market demand, differentiated competitive strengths, and attractive operating returns. As businesses with stronger unit economics contribute a growing share of revenue, we expect to see greater operating leverage, supporting more sustainable growth and improved profitability."

Financial Results for the Third Quarter of 2026

Net revenues increased by 18.3% to RMB1,868.4 million from RMB1,579.0 million in the third quarter of 2025, which was primarily driven by continued year-over-year growth in gross billings as a result of our sufficient and effective response to the strong market demand. Our high-quality educational products and learning services also gained wider recognition of our product and service offerings.

Cost of revenues increased by 18.1% to RMB632.2 million from RMB535.5 million in the third quarter of 2025. The increase was mainly due to the expansion of instructors and tutors workforce, increased server and bandwidth cost, higher rental cost, and increased learning materials cost.

Gross profit increased by 18.5% to RMB1,236.2 million from RMB1,043.5 million in the third quarter of 2025. Gross profit margin increased to 66.2% from 66.1% in the same period of 2025.

Non-GAAP gross profit increased by 18.4% to RMB1,236.7 million from RMB1,044.5 million in the third quarter of 2025. Non-GAAP gross profit margin increased to 66.2% from 66.1% in the same period of 2025.

Operating expenses increased by 1.1% to RMB1,235.1 million from RMB1,221.5 million in the third quarter of 2025.

Income from operations was RMB1.1 million, compared with loss from operations of RMB178.0 million in the third quarter of 2025.

Non-GAAP income from operations was RMB8.5 million, compared with non-GAAP loss from operations of RMB168.6 million in the third quarter of 2025.

Interest Income, Net and Realized Gains from Investments

Non-GAAP net income was RMB23.1 million, compared with non-GAAP net loss of RMB137.7 million in the third quarter of 2025.

Net operating cash outflow in the third quarter of 2026 was RMB794.8 million.

Basic and diluted net income per ADS were both RMB0.07 in the third quarter of 2026.

Non-GAAP basic and diluted net income per ADS were both RMB0.10 in the third quarter of 2026.

As of September 30, 2026, the Company had 155,503,808 ordinary shares outstanding.

Cash and Cash Equivalents, Restricted Cash, Short-term and Long-term Investments

As of September 30, 2026, the Company had cash and cash equivalents, restricted cash, short-term and long-term investments of RMB3,128.0 million in aggregate, compared with a total of RMB3,972.5 million as of December 31, 2025.

In November 2022, the Company's board of directors authorized a share repurchase program ("2022 Share Repurchase Program"), under which the Company may repurchase up to US$30 million of its shares, effective until November 22, 2025. In November 2023, the Company's board of directors authorized modifications to the share repurchase program, increasing the aggregate value of shares that may be repurchased from US$30 million to US$80 million, effective until November 22, 2025.

In May 2025, the Company's board of directors authorized a new share repurchase program ("2025 Share Repurchase Program"), under which the Company may repurchase up to an aggregate value of US$100 million of its shares during the three-year period beginning upon the completion of the Company's 2022 Share Repurchase Program.

As of November 24, 2026, the Company had cumulatively repurchased approximately 39.0 million ADSs for approximately US$109.3 million under the aforesaid two share repurchase programs.

Gaotu is a leading technology-driven education company in China focused on enabling lifelong learning through AI-powered solutions that cultivate interest and drive continuous growth. The Company provides AI-powered, product-led learning solutions for learners from pre-school to adulthood. By combining rare, high-caliber teaching resources with AI-enhanced tools and content, Gaotu creates engaging and effective learning experiences delivered through both online and offline channels. AI and data analytics permeate throughout the Company's operations to adapt content and teaching methods to individual learner needs, enhance efficiency and drive sustained learning progress.

The Company uses gross billings, non-GAAP gross profit, non-GAAP income (loss) from operations and non-GAAP net income (loss), each a non-GAAP financial measure, in evaluating its operating results and for financial and operational decision-making purposes.

The Company defines gross billings for a specific period as the total amount of cash received for the sale of course offerings in such period, net of the total amount of refunds in such period. The Company's management uses gross billings as a performance measurement because the Company generally bills its students for the entire course fee at the time of sale of its course offerings and recognizes revenue proportionally as the classes are delivered. For some courses, the Company continues to provide students with 12 months to 36 months access to the pre-recorded audio-video courses after the online live courses are delivered. The Company believes that gross billings provide valuable insight into the sales of its course packages and the performance of its business. As gross billings have material limitations as an analytical metrics and may not be calculated in the same manner by all companies, it may not be comparable to other similarly titled measures used by other companies.

Non-GAAP gross profit, non-GAAP income (loss) from operations and non-GAAP net income (loss) exclude share-based compensation expenses. The Company believes that these non-GAAP financial measures provide meaningful supplemental information regarding its performance and liquidity by excluding share-based expenses that may not be indicative of its operating performance from a cash perspective. The Company believes that both management and investors benefit from these non-GAAP financial measures in assessing its performance and when planning and forecasting future periods. These non-GAAP financial measures also facilitate management's internal comparisons to the Company's historical performance. A limitation of using non-GAAP measures is that these non-GAAP measures exclude share-based compensation charges that have been and will continue to be for the foreseeable future a significant recurring expense in the Company's business.

The presentation of these non-GAAP financial measures is not intended to be considered in isolation from or as a substitute for the financial information prepared and presented in accordance with GAAP. For more information on these non-GAAP financial measures, please see the table captioned "Reconciliations of non-GAAP measures to the most comparable GAAP measures" set forth at the end of this release.

The accompanying tables have more details on the reconciliations between GAAP financial measures that are most directly comparable to non-GAAP financial measures.

#5361. FHFA maps out FICO 10T rollout with broad eligibility by late 2028

FHFA has approved the FICO 10T credit score model for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. It has also outlined a multiyear road map to phase it in while retiring Classic FICO by late 2028.  AI Summary

The Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) has approved the FICO 10T credit score model for use by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. It also released an implementation road map that would make FICO 10T broadly eligible and retire Classic FICO by September 2028.

The staged rollout, announced Tuesday, mirrors the VantageScore 4.0 timeline and is meant to give lenders, mortgage insurers and loan origination system providers time to analyze historic FICO 10T data, rework pricing and risk models, and update technology before a full transition, according to the agency.“The timeline below prepares lenders, mortgage insurers and loan origination system providers for the final step in credit score modernization: lender choice between FICO 10T and VantageScore 4.0,” the agency said. At the Federal Housing Administration (FHA), VantageScore 4.0 and FICO 10T are expected to go live alongside the existing Classic FICO in January.

Bob Broeksmit, president and CEO of the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), issued a statement of support following the announcement.

“We welcome this milestone as it moves us closer to the industry’s and FHFA’s goal of transitioning to true competition with two modernized credit score models,” Broeksmit said. “We appreciate FHFA’s desire to provide a clear and transparent roadmap for this process. Given the industry’s experience with the just-completed adoption of VantageScore 4.0, MBA will work with FHFA and industry stakeholders to expedite the implementation timeline responsibly.

“MBA and its members will continue to engage with FHFA to establish meaningful competition for both credit scoring and credit reporting. Continued reforms to end the tri-merge requirement will further improve our credit reporting system and lower costs for borrowers. Today’s announcement is a critical next step.”

The FHFA initially validated both FICO 10T and VantageScore 4.0 for use at the government-sponsored (GSEs) enterprises in October 2022. In July 2026, Fannie and Freddie released historical performance data for FICO 10T along with additional VantageScore 4.0 data, a key prerequisite for lenders and investors to back-test new score models and recalibrate credit policy.A FICO 10T pilot is expected to begin around December 2027. In this “launch and refine” phase, lenders will deliver a subset of loans underwritten with FICO 10T while FHFA, the GSEs and industry stakeholders monitor data quality, pricing and delivery performance.

Based on pilot results, FHFA expects upfront pricing grids and private mortgage insurer eligibility requirements, or PMIERs, to be updated to reflect the new score model. That step will be critical for secondary market execution and risk transfer structures that currently rely on Classic FICO.

A limited FICO 10T rollout is targeted for April 2028, followed by a scale-up and transition phase that leads to broad eligibility around September 2028. During this final stage, FHFA plans to confirm industry readiness, fully implement Uniform Loan Delivery Dataset (ULDD) Phase 5, expand FICO 10T use across GSE channels and retire Classic FICO.

FHFA emphasized that dates after November 2026 are targets and are subject to change.

In October, Fair Isaac Corp. said it will hold its wholesale mortgage price at $10 for a bundle of its credit scores for lenders and brokers enrolled in its Preferred Program. The $10 price is available through participating tri-merge credit report resellers to lenders that commit to FICO under the program. It covers both Classic FICO, which has been the mortgage standard for nearly three decades, and FICO Score 10T, the company’s trended-data model.

FICO is also preparing a new subscription-based pricing model for mortgage credit scores in 2027, sources told HousingWire.

VantageScore 4.0, by comparison, has been offered at 99 cents per score, or at no additional charge when purchased alongside a FICO score through Equifax, Experian and TransUnion, which jointly own VantageScore.

Bank of America Global Research, using data from Recursion, found that more than 170 lenders now pull VantageScore 4.0. Despite that breadth of use, only a small share of conventional loans are actually priced with VantageScore 4.0. In October, 20% of issuance reported a VantageScore 4.0, yet only about 8% of total issuance used the score model for pricing, according to the research.

Editor’s note: This story was updated with a statement from the MBA.

#5360. What will Social Security look like in 2027 and beyond?

Social Security recipients will get a 3.6% COLA in 2027 but also face a 2032 insolvency deadline, rising senior hardships and competing policy responses. The Senior Citizens League urges Congress to lift the payroll tax cap, restore Medicare funding and expand benefits, while a new Senate bill would instead borrow from general revenues to avoid benefit cuts, a move budget watchdogs say could add $190 trillion to federal debt over 75 years.  AI Summary

With potential program insolvency looming in 2032, the next few years for Social Security are being defined by conflicting pressures — including the 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) in 2027, quickly rising financial obstacles for older Americans, and yet another proposal in Congress that could either stabilize benefits or sharply increase federal debt levels.

Earlier this month, The Senior Citizens League forecast a 3.6% COLA for 2028, matching the Social Security Administration’s recently announced 3.6% COLA for 2027. But Morningstar noted this week that the 2027 COLA — the largest since 2023’s 8.7% adjustment — will translate into smaller take-home increases once Medicare costs are deducted.

Most Social Security beneficiaries are enrolled in Medicare Part B, and premiums are automatically deducted from monthly checks. Morningstar reported that the standard monthly Part B premium will rise by $6.50 next year to $209.40, a 3.2% increase. That will allow most beneficiaries to keep more than 3% of the 3.6% COLA after the deduction.

Morningstar calculated that a retiree receiving the average October benefit of $2,092 would see a net benefit increase of about 3.29%, assuming they pay the standard Part B premium and have no other changes in deductions. A higher-income retiree with a $3,500 monthly benefit would see a net increase of roughly 3.41% under the same assumptions.

The COLA is based on the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W), which compares the average readings for July, August and September on a year-over-year basis. Analysts cited by Morningstar noted that CPI-W may understate seniors’ actual cost pressures, particularly for healthcare, and pointed to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics’ CPI-E index for older households, which has historically risen faster than CPI-W.

The Senior Citizens League (TSCL) said the projected 3.6% COLA for 2028 is likely to arrive against a deteriorating backdrop for older adults, including senior homeowners who may still be making monthly mortgage payments. The group said that seniors are now the country’s fastest-growing homeless population and that many forgo vision, dental and hearing care due to costs.

TSCL’s release emphasized that Social Security’s primary trust fund is projected to reach insolvency in 2032, triggering automatic benefit reductions if Congress does not act. The Medicare Part A hospital insurance trust fund is projected to become insolvent in 2033, the group said.

That timing elevates the stakes for the next Congress, which will be led by Democrats after their decisive victories in the recent midterm elections. Senators elected in the current cycle will serve from Jan. 3, 2027, through Jan. 3, 2033, overlapping the projected insolvency date. TSCL framed these terms as a key window for any reforms to prevent automatic benefit cuts for millions of retirees.

In its agenda for the 120th Congress, TSCL called on lawmakers to:

TSCL pointed to Social Security Administration projections, which show that eliminating the taxable wage cap would add “decades” to the trust fund’s life. And the organization’s internal polling indicates broad bipartisan support among seniors for lifting the cap.

As advocacy groups push for revenue-raising reforms, a new proposal in the Senate would instead rely on federal borrowing to preserve full benefits.

Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), the chairman of the Senate Budget Committee, has introduced the Stop Scaring Seniors Act. The bill would allow the Department of the Treasury to transfer general fund dollars to Social Security’s retirement trust fund once it becomes insolvent, according to a press release published last week by the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB).

Under current law, Social Security can only pay benefits from dedicated payroll tax income and trust fund reserves. When the retirement trust fund’s reserves are exhausted — currently projected to be in less than six years — benefits would be cut by about 22% without legislative changes.

CRFB estimated that backfilling Social Security with general revenue under Johnson’s bill would increase federal debt by $190 trillion over the next 75 years on an inflation-adjusted basis, equal to roughly 165% of gross domestic product.

“Paying for Social Security out of the general fund would absolutely explode the national debt, costing a whopping 165% of GDP over 75 years before even considering the economic implications,” CRFB President Maya MacGuineas said in the release, arguing that the policy could trigger a debt crisis or unsettle bond markets even before it is fully implemented.

CRFB characterized the bill as avoiding “the real decisions” needed to repair Social Security’s finances and urged lawmakers to pursue a mix of adjustments — potentially through a bipartisan commission — that would close the program’s funding gap without shifting the shortfall onto the federal balance sheet.

The trajectory of Social Security and Medicare benefits has direct implications for housing demand and credit risk among the senior segment.

Net benefit increases closer to 3% than 3.6% may constrain seniors’ ability to absorb higher housing costs — including the required property tax, insurance and association dues associated with reverse mortgages. The impact could be particularly acute in housing markets with rapid property tax growth.

Rising healthcare and prescription costs could drive more senior homeowners to tap their equity through home sales or reverse mortgages. Increased levels of downsizing would alter inventory and product mixes in senior-heavy markets.

A 22% across-the-board benefit cut in the next decade, if Congress fails to act, would likely raise delinquency risks among fixed-income borrowers and could affect investor views of senior-heavy mortgage-backed securities pools. Conversely, large-scale borrowing to backfill Social Security, as proposed in Johnson’s bill, could influence interest rates and broader funding conditions.

Localized affordability pressures could also emerge. Growth in senior homelessness and medical cost burdens might increase demand for affordable and supportive housing. It could also influence municipal planning, tax policy and zoning decisions that shape housing development pipelines.

#5359. ITRI Wins Three R&D 100 Awards for Innovation in Emissions Reduction, Wireless Sensing, and Semiconductor Processing

HSINCHU, Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI) received three 2026 R&D 100 Awards in Scottsdale, Arizona, on November 19. The winners are NâO-CAT: Low Temperature NOx Free NâO Abatement System; Ubiquitous Network-Native Radar (UNR); and IonTwin, a digital twin for semiconductor ion implantation. The recognition marks ITRI's 19th consecutive year of winning R&D 100 Awards, with 72 awards in total. More than 90% of its award-winning technologies have been applied in industry.

"One of the biggest trends this year was a strong focus on process development and prototyping, with roughly one in five entries focused on AI and software. This highlights the potential to speed up core processes, as demonstrated by ITRI's IonTwin, which reduces simulation time from hours to less than 10 seconds," said R&D World Editor-in-Chief Brian Buntz. "I think ITRI's success comes down to execution, simplicity, and excellence. Its strength lies in manufacturing, collaboration with global partners, and consistent execution. Taiwan is also uniquely positioned to turn applied research into real-world solutions," he added.

In response to global trends in AI, semiconductors, and the transition to net zero, ITRI focuses on industry needs and draws on expertise across disciplines to translate advanced research into commercially valuable solutions. This year's award-winning technologies deliver advances in greenhouse gas emissions reduction, wireless sensing, and semiconductor process efficiency, with proven industrial applications.

NâO-CAT is an NâO removal technology that uses low-temperature catalysis to achieve over 99% NâO removal at temperatures below 500Â°C, compared with approximately 10% removal efficiency for conventional electrically heated exhaust treatment systems. Its intelligent exhaust routing and three-stage treatment process also remove particulate pollutants, including PM2.5, while preventing NOâ emissions. Developed and validated by ITRI and Integrated Plasma Inc., NâO-CAT can be integrated with existing semiconductor exhaust treatment equipment, helping manufacturers reduce emissions, energy consumption, and equipment adoption costs while enhancing their competitiveness in sustainable manufacturing.

Ubiquitous Network-Native Radar (UNR) adds sensing and positioning capabilities to existing communications equipment with modular software upgrades. By analyzing changes in wireless signals in the environment, it turns communications networks into sensing systems. This "network-as-a-sensor" approach brings integrated sensing and communications (ISAC), a key technology envisioned for 6G, to conventional wireless infrastructure. UNR achieves centimeter-level positioning accuracy indoors and positioning accuracy within three meters outdoors. ITRI has completed field validation with base station companies in Taiwan, the UK, Spain, and the Netherlands, paving the way for broader ISAC adoption.

IonTwin uses physics-informed AI to complete an ion implantation simulation in under 10 secondsâa task that takes four to five hours with conventional Monte Carlo methods. By reducing test wafer consumption, it lowers process development costs. The system supports both cloud and edge environments, enabling faster decision-making in process optimization. Already deployed at a leading foundry, IonTwin accelerates process development and improves production efficiency.

To explore further commercialization opportunities in the U.S., the ITRI team visited Arizona State University (ASU) and its affiliated innovation facilities including Eyring Materials Center and SkySong Innovations. The team also hosted Taiwan Tech Day to showcase Taiwan's award-winning technologies, facilitating technology matchmaking and fostering TaiwanâU.S. industry collaboration. Participants included Charla Griffy-Brown, director general and dean of Thunderbird School of Global Management at ASU.

The Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI) is a world-leading R&D organization dedicated to innovating a better future. Founded in 1973, ITRI has played a vital role in transforming Taiwan's industries from labor-intensive into innovation-driven. Over the years, ITRI has incubated hundreds of startups and spinoffs, including well-known companies such as UMC and TSMC. Headquartered in Taiwan, ITRI also operates offices in the U.S., Germany, the UK, Japan, and Thailand. For more information, please visit https://www.itri.org/eng.
