#5358. BTR sector fears Treasury rules move the goal line on investor ban

Treasury closed public comments on proposed ROAD act rules for build-to-rent exemptions to the institutional investor ban. Industry groups opposed the 18-month certificate-of-occupancy purchase window and sought clearer definitions for single-plat communities and rehab exceptions.  AI Summary

Earlier this year, build-to-rent projects secured some notable exemptions from the institutional investor ban included in the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. However, while the industry still doesn’t know exactly what the final rules will look like, it just moved a step closer to finding out.

Monday marked the end of the U.S. Department of the Treasury‘s public comment period on its proposed rules for BTR exemptions from the institutional investor ban. Although ROAD explicitly exempted BTR from the ban, some of the proposed rules and language Treasury released in October have left the industry uneasy and unsure of where it stands.

BTR developers and operators say this uncertainty continues to suppress capital flowing into new projects, a trend they expect to continue until the federal government clarifies the rules.

Last month, Treasury released a notice of proposed rulemaking detailing how it would implement the institutional investor ban while protecting BTR communities. The proposed rules would exempt newly built, never-owner-occupied BTR communities if an investor buys them within 18 months of receiving a certificate of occupancy and uses them only as rentals.

Treasury would also exempt communities that include both rental and for-sale homes, allowing builders to sell the rental portion to large institutional investors while marketing the remaining homes to individual buyers. The proposals additionally call for allowing transfers of existing BTR communities between large institutional investors and keeping the renovate-to-rent exemption.

Although the rules appear to protect BTR, industry leaders say the finer details leave several concerns unresolved.

“If you read the law as a layman, you’d say, ‘all right, built-to-rent is carved out.’ But then you get this rulemaking, and it’s like you have to pat your belly and tap your head and hop on one foot for the built-to-rent to not be banned,” Sean Dobson, chairman, CEO and CIO at The Amherst Group, said in an interview with HousingWire TBD.

Over the last month, Treasury received more than 450 letters with questions and concerns concerning its proposed rulemakings. HousingWire TBD reviewed 10 of those letters, from high-profile BTR developers and operators and leading organizations that advocate on behalf of the rental housing industry, including:

These letters detailed the outstanding concerns that the industry still has concerning how Treasury will enforce ROAD. With the institutional investor ban set to take effect on January 7, Treasury has several weeks to finalize and release the rules that BTR operators will have to follow.

Until then, the industry has to wait and see whether, and how, those concerns are addressed.

The chief concern among BTR developers, operators and advocates is the proposed requirement that institutional investors purchase BTR communities within 18 months of receiving a certificate of occupancy (CO). Under the proposed framework, if a developer fails to sell a community by that deadline, they may lose the ability to do so altogether.

That proposal matters because many BTR developers, much like multifamily developers, rely on selling their communities after completion and stabilization to make a profit and move on to their next project.

Richard Ross, CEO at Quinn Residences, argued that the 18-month window is far too limiting. A community may still be under development and lease-up after the first homes receive a CO, so 18 months will almost certainly run out before the full community is ready to sell.

“To build and stabilize a new community takes about 30 months. If I start receiving certificates of occupancy at month 15, I may not receive the final CO for the last home until month 28 or 29. I need enough time to complete and stabilize the entire community before selling it,” Ross said in an interview.

The letters that HousingWire TBD reviewed unanimously opposed the proposed 18-month window. Just like Ross, industry groups argued that the deadline does not align with how rental communities are developed, leased up, financed and sold.

The letter signed by a coalition of 12 BTR developers led by Greystar and Brookfield Residential argued that the deadline would create uncertainty for projects that may not be sold until years after construction. The letter further argued the restrictions would continue to affect financing decisions for future projects.

“A smaller potential buyer pool reduces liquidity and creates greater uncertainty regarding terminal value,” the letter read.

Additionally, the groups argued that Treasury must protect long-term institutional owners’ ability to purchase BTR communities. Otherwise, the federal government would undermine the industry.

“If large institutional investors cannot purchase horizontal multifamily communities (which individual families cannot), the values of those properties will fall and new construction and necessary maintenance and reinvestment will slow,” MBA’s letter read.

To address this, NAA and NMHC, two of the largest rental housing advocacy organizations, requested that Treasury eliminate the deadline or replace it with a provision that institutional investors can purchase BTR communities directly from the builder or developer responsible for construction.

Quinn Residences, AHV Communities and LGI Homes also requested that Treasury remove or substantially extend the deadline. LGI Homes also emphasized the need for production homebuilders to retain the option of renting homes that have not sold.

Treasury’s proposed rulemaking describes the three activities that could qualify an institutional investor as a covered entity as “purchases, constructs, or constructs and retains”. This matters because BTR developers often build and retain homes as rental properties before selling stabilized communities to finance future developments.

Treasury’s language is ambiguous, leaving open the possibility that BTR developers could be treated like institutional investors.

The National Rental Home Council made this a central argument in its letter, distinguishing between an investor buying a home from someone else and one acting as the builder. The organization urged Treasury to recognize that developers who build and retain homes as rentals operate differently from investors who purchase newly built homes from third parties.

Up for Growth Action made a similar argument, urging Treasury to differentiate between creating new rental housing and acquiring existing housing.

Several letters argued that Treasury’s proposed rule does not clearly distinguish single-plat rental communities, where multiple homes share one parcel and common ownership, from individual single-family homes. They worry the rule could inadvertently restrict the development, ownership or sale of these communities by treating them as collections of individual homes subject to the institutional investor ban.

In response, BTR advocates argued for clearer rules for single-plat communities and those mixing renters and owners, while NRHC asked whether buildings with three or more attached units could count as single-family homes.

The letters also raise concerns about the proposed exception for investors that purchase distressed homes, substantially rehabilitate them and rent them out. Treasury’s proposed rules would allow institutional investors to purchase existing homes in need of extensive repairs, as long as they spend 15% of the purchase price on improvements.

However, several of the letters argued that the 15% threshold is too high. They further argued that the rule could be hard to enforce for homes that are difficult to inspect before purchase, homes in jurisdictions without applicable local codes, and homes with problems that aren’t obvious upfront.

Rental housing advocates disagreed on how flexible the rehabilitation threshold should be. While some groups advocated for increasing the threshold, NMHC, NAA and RETTC support the 15% benchmark while advocating for more flexibility in identifying problems and applying older building standards.

The common theme is that industry leaders want the exception to work for genuinely distressed properties without requiring investors to predict every hidden problem before purchasing a home.

Several letters raise implementation issues beyond those five main concerns, including:

#5356. As cities act to shred housing’s red-tape, Boston homes in on parking

Cities are targeting costs and delays through zoning and permitting changes, including Boulder's 90-day affordable review deadline and Allentowns affordability requirement for tax breaks. Boston joined the trend with a 9-4 vote to remove parking minimums, subject to further approvals.  AI Summary

Boston is an expensive place to build housing, and it is one of the priciest places in the country to live. Its City Council has taken a step toward scrapping one costly requirement: parking.

Cutting parking is one path cities are taking to lower construction costs. Others are chasing review time, density and tax incentives, and the changes are landing at the city and county level.

Boulder, Colorado, set a 90-day deadline for deciding affordable housing applications. Allentown, Pennsylvania, tied a tax break to affordable units. Lake County, Illinois, outside Chicago, opened all its residential zones to accessory dwelling units.

These local moves come as states test how far they can push cities to build in the name of approving housing affordability. California, Texas and Florida have passed laws that override local zoning authority. Lawmakers there have had to keep tightening them to head off workarounds.

Illinois and North Carolina may be next. Gov. J.B. Pritzker’s housing reform plan, which stalled this year, is expected to return in January.

A shift in political winds in the Tar Heel State may mean lawmakers try once again to pass broad reform after failing multiple times. But they did eliminate off-street parking requirements across most of the state.

More than 120 cities have eliminated parking mandates, according to the Parking Reform Network, an advocacy coalition.

Boston could be next. The city’s average asking rent was $3,065 a month in the third quarter, the fifth highest of the 90 markets Cushman & Wakefield tracks, behind San Francisco, New York, San Jose and Long Island. Home construction fell by 14,000 units between 2024-2025 and 2025-2026, according to this year’s Greater Boston Housing Report Card.

The council voted 9-4 on Nov. 18 to remove parking requirements for new residential construction. The zoning commission must now approve the measure before it goes to the mayor.

Abundant Housing Massachusetts, the Commercial Real Estate Development Association, the Greater Boston Real Estate Board and the Environmental League of Massachusetts Action Fund support the measure.

Five years ago, Mayor Michelle Wu signed off on a zoning amendment to remove off-street parking requirements for affordable housing. Wu, who has championed zoning reform, hasn’t said whether she supports the current measure.

“We will evaluate the implications of eliminating parking minimums citywide,” spokesperson Marcela Dwork said in a statement.

Boston’s transportation department says a garage space can cost up to $50,000, but the Pioneer Institute put underground spaces in Boston at $106,000 to $152,000 in late 2025.

Opponents argue the policy leaves out residents who need cars. But real estate professionals in Boston and elsewhere in the country note that such changes don’t mean parking vanishes.

“It’s about letting each Boston project respond to real demand, not one-size-fits-all formulas,” Reginald Jones-Booker, a Berkshire Hathaway agent, wrote on LinkedIn. “Developers can still include parking where it makes sense, but the mandate would no longer force every new home to meet a fixed minimum.”

Boulder’s council unanimously approved an ordinance on Nov. 19 that sets a 90-day decision deadline for complete applications. It applies to projects in which at least half the homes are affordable to low- and middle-income households.

Site reviews there have taken a median of 277 days over the past two years, according to Boulder Reporting Lab. Staff, not the Planning Board, will decide requests for extra height or reduced open space, and neighbors can appeal.

The rules take effect Dec. 19. They are meant to keep Boulder eligible for Proposition 123, a 2022 voter-approved measure that sends state income tax revenue to affordable housing in cities that commit to growing their affordable stock by 3% a year.

Billy Joel’s 1982 hit “Allentown” made the Lehigh Valley city a symbol of a fading industrial America. Bethlehem Steel, the region’s anchor, ended most steelmaking in 1995 and was dissolved in 2003.

Those days are long gone, but the city now faces a different problem: keeping housing within reach as the region grows.

The City Council voted unanimously Nov. 18 to pass a workforce housing ordinance. Developers of projects with 10 or more units who receive a tax break under the Local Economic Revitalization Tax Assistance Act, a 1977 Pennsylvania law known as LERTA, must make at least 20% of the units affordable. Those units are rent-restricted for households earning 60% to 120% of area median income.

The city has no LERTA zone yet, so a council member said the amended version “does not directly impact workforce housing today.”

Lake County amended its Unified Development Ordinance on Nov. 10, effective that day, to allow accessory dwelling units in all county residential zones. It also lowers their minimum lot sizes, adds incentives for conservation developments and creates an “early assistance” process for developers. The rules reach only unincorporated areas.

The county acted while the state stalled. Gov. J.B. Pritzker’s Building Up Illinois Developments plan, known as BUILD, would have legalized accessory dwelling units statewide, allowed missing-middle housing, set permit-review deadlines, ended excessive parking minimums and standardized impact fees.

It failed to advance before the spring session ended, after the Illinois Municipal League and suburban mayors objected to its zoning mandates. Pritzker has said the plan will likely wait until January.

After Pritzker’s plan stalled, Illinois REALTORS revived its Illinois Housing Supply Accelerator Program, launched in August. The program asks local officials to form working groups targeting barriers to building.

Pritzker said in October that he expected BUILD to wait until the full session starting in January. Lawmakers finished the first week of the fall veto session without major housing action. They return Dec. 1-3.

DUBAI, UAE, Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- What do some of Hollywood's biggest blockbusters, Oscar-winning films and celebrated productions at the Cannes Film Festival have in common? Beyond the famous faces and extraordinary storytelling, many share a connection to ARRI, a name one may never have heard of, but whose work one has almost certainly seen.

For more than a century, the German filmmaking technology company has helped shape how movies look and feel on screen. Its cameras have captured everything from spectacular action sequences to intimate moments that bring audiences closer to the characters they love.

Now imagine having some of that cinematic expertise in one's pocket.

Through its Cinematic Imaging Partnership with HONOR, ARRI is bringing selected elements of its professional filmmaking technology to smartphones. And with the HONOR Magic9 Pro Max arriving in the Middle East and Africa, that expertise is becoming accessible to a new generation of creators.

From a Small Munich Workshop to Hollywood

ARRI's story began in 1917, when two young film enthusiasts, August Arnold and Robert Richter, established a filmmaking equipment business in Munich, Germany. Combining their surnames to create ARRI, they began developing lighting equipment, film-processing machinery and other tools for the emerging motion picture industry.

Their ambitions soon extended to cameras. In 1924, ARRI developed its first camera, the KINARRI 35, followed by a breakthrough in 1937 with the ARRIFLEX 35. Its revolutionary mirror-reflex viewing system allowed filmmakers to see precisely what the camera was capturing, helping transform how films were shot.

Over the following decades, ARRI continued developing cameras and lighting technology that gave cinematographers greater freedom to bring their creative visions to life.

Then came another defining moment. In 2010, ARRI introduced its ALEXA digital camera system, which became widely recognised for its exceptional image quality, natural colours and ability to preserve detail in challenging lighting conditions.

Today, ARRI produces professional cameras, lenses, lighting systems and imaging technologies used across film and television productions worldwide. ARRI and its engineers have received 20 Scientific and Technical Awards from the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences.

From the Oscars to Cannes: Behind Cinema's Biggest Moments

Think of the sweeping desert landscapes, atmospheric scenes or breathtaking action sequences that define some of cinema's most memorable moments. Behind many of these experiences is ARRI technology, trusted by filmmakers to capture the visual details that bring stories to life.

Its influence continues today. At the 2026 Academy Awards, six of the ten Best Picture nominees were filmed using ARRI cameras. Guillermo del Toro's Frankenstein, captured entirely on the ARRI ALEXA 65, went on to win three Oscars.

At the 2026 Cannes Film Festival, ARRI cameras were used on 18 of the 22 films in the Main Competition, including Palme d'Or winner Fjord, which was captured with the ALEXA 35 and ARRI Master Anamorphic lenses.

But what makes ARRI so important to filmmakers?

Beyond camera hardware, its expertise lies in how images reproduce light, colour, contrast and natural skin tones. Whether capturing an actor's expression in a dimly lit room or preserving the details of a sunset, ARRI's imaging technology helps filmmakers achieve the visual richness audiences associate with cinema.

And that expertise is now finding its way into smartphones.

Bringing Hollywood's Imaging Expertise to HONOR

Think about the last time you recorded a beautiful sunset, only to discover that the sky looked washed out or someone's face disappeared into shadow. Or perhaps you filmed a special occasion, but the colours looked nothing like what you remembered.

These are among the challenges professional filmmakers have long worked to overcome.

At the heart of ARRI's expertise is ARRI Image Science, which determines how cameras interpret colour, lighting, highlights and shadows.

Through its collaboration with HONOR, selected elements of this technology are being adapted for mobile devices.

This is more than a branding partnership. HONOR contributes its mobile imaging hardware, AI capabilities and image-processing technologies, while ARRI brings its expertise in cinematic colour reproduction, image quality and professional filmmaking workflows.

Together, the companies are working to make sophisticated imaging techniques available in a device people carry every day.

The collaboration also introduces professional features including ARRI LogC3, designed to retain more image information for editing, and ARRI Wide Gamut 3, which supports a broader range of colours. ARRI Looks allows creators to preview different cinematic styles while filming.

From Barcelona to One's Hands: The Partnership Journey

The partnership was announced in March 2026 at Mobile World Congress in Barcelona, bringing together HONOR's mobile innovation and ARRI's century-long filmmaking heritage.

Its first commercial result arrived in August with the HONOR Robot Phone, then the collaboration reached another milestone in September with the launch of the HONOR Magic9 Pro Max in China.

Featuring ARRI branding on its camera module, the flagship introduced an end-to-end professional cinema workflow co-engineered with ARRI.

Its dual 200MP camera system, HONOR Imaging Chip H1 and 4K Cinematic LiveVideo capabilities work alongside ARRI Image Science to give creators greater control over how their footage is captured and finished.

This December, Hollywood Comes a Little Closer

For years, smartphone cameras have competed on megapixels, zoom capabilities and AI-powered features. HONOR's collaboration with ARRI introduces another dimension: bringing the colour, atmosphere and creative control associated with professional cinema into mobile filmmaking.

With the HONOR Magic9 Pro Max making its Middle East and Africa debut, consumers will soon have an opportunity to experience that collaboration firsthand.

The collaboration also reflects HONOR's evolving "Dare to Be" philosophy, which champions bold innovation, individuality and the confidence to challenge conventions. By bringing professional cinema technology into everyday devices, HONOR is encouraging a new generation of creators to explore possibilities once reserved for professional filmmakers.

#5352. Bezos and Bond: Amazon founder played a big role in casting new 007

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:36 pmNovember 17, 2026 at 6:36 pm

Jeff Bezos has a space company, a newspaper, an AI startup that’s raised $14.5 billion and, apparently, a seat in the room when Amazon decides who gets a license to kill.

Speaking Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event, the Amazon founder said he was “heavily involved” in the casting of Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond, a pick Amazon MGM Studios announced Monday.

Amazon got a 50% stake in the Bond franchise when it acquired MGM for $8.5 billion in 2022, then took creative control last year in a joint venture with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson.

Bezos said a large initial pool of would-be Bonds was narrowed to five finalists, who then did “real old-fashioned screen tests”: three scenes apiece, in full costume on real sets with other actors.

The other finalists were Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner, according to The New York Times, which reported that the tests took place in London in late October.

Bezos said the decision-makers got together Friday and spent a couple of hours reviewing the screen tests before settling on Pattinson.

“By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing,” Bezos said. “But there was something special about Rob Pattinson and his performances.” He said the group, including director Denis Villeneuve, reached a quick consensus. It was “kind of immediately undebated.”

Bezos admitted that the group was initially “slightly biased” against Pattinson because he’s already so famous.

“We sort of thought, you know, maybe we should have somebody a little more unknown,” he said. “But in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond.”

#5351. XRP Price Plunges 25%, but Dom Kwok’s $1,000 Calls Remain in Play

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

XRP is having its worst November on record, but one prominent crypto entrepreneur still sees a four-digit price ahead. EasyA co-founder Dom Kwok has reiterated his $1,000 XRP target for 2030, even as the token crashes toward $0.90 and institutional investors pull money from spot exchange-traded funds (ETFs).

XRP has dropped 25% this month, surpassing its previous November record decline in 2019. The token briefly touched $0.862 over the weekend before recovering toward $0.94. It remains below $1, a level XRP has failed to reclaim since November 14.

The timing makes Kwok’s forecast look almost absurd on a chart. Yet the sell-off is now testing a level where historical capitulation, ETF positioning, and XRP’s long-term adoption thesis collide.

The institutional story has taken a serious hit, with spot XRP ETFs recording $30.76 million in November outflows, marking their third consecutive week of withdrawals. Assets across the funds have slipped from around $1.42 billion at October’s end to below $1 billion.

November has also produced no daily net inflow for XRP ETFs so far. That is a sharp reversal from the buying streak that helped fuel institutional optimism earlier this year. Still, cumulative net inflows remain near $1.78 billion since launch. Investors have pulled money recently, but the institutional trade has not disappeared.

Right now, XRP’s chart is already showing signs of trying to stabilize. The token has bounced from its weekend low around $0.86, with buyers defending the $0.90 area. The daily Relative Strength Index sits near 32, following its recent oversold dip below 30.

That is not a confirmed reversal. But XRP does not need a massive catalyst to produce a sharp bounce after a decline this aggressive.

LiquidChain is tackling one of crypto’s biggest problems: liquidity scattered across Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Solana. Its Layer 3 network aims to connect these ecosystems through a unified execution environment, allowing developers to build applications accessing multiple networks without deploying separate versions everywhere.

That could unlock cross-chain trading, liquidity pools, and DeFi applications without the usual bridging complexity. Bitcoin brings capital, Ethereum brings DeFi depth, and Solana offers fast execution. LiquidChain wants developers to access all three through one infrastructure layer.

Alone, you're just another chain.Connected, you're part of something bigger. 👁https://t.co/vqvBcdSQYC pic.twitter.com/oP2E2IDuUQ

The presale has raised $990K toward its $1.1 million target, with LIQUID priced at just $0.014977. Staking is also offered at 1,160% APY, and the project allocates 10% of its 11.8 billion token supply to staking rewards.

The APY will attract attention, but the product is the bigger bet. If LiquidChain delivers its unified liquidity vision, it could offer developers a reason to build beyond a single blockchain ecosystem. That is what makes the project worth watching beyond its presale numbers.

Kwok, a former Goldman Sachs analyst and EasyA co-founder, has publicly said he believes XRP could reach $1,000 by 2030. His thesis centers on institutional adoption, blockchain utility, and the possibility that XRP becomes part of a much larger global payments infrastructure.

That forecast is a long way from today’s price. At $0.94, XRP would need to rise more than 1,000-fold to reach his target. Kwok XRP price prediction is extremely ambitious, but it puts the current price collapse into perspective: Kwok is betting on what XRP could become, rather than what the chart looks like today.

The immediate battle is much less dramatic. XRP needs to hold $0.90–$0.91 before buyers can seriously challenge $0.95. A break above $0.98 would bring the $1 psychological barrier back into reach. Reclaiming $1, followed by the $1.03 area, would be the first convincing sign that the November downtrend is losing control.

Failure to hold $0.90 could send XRP back toward $0.862, with $0.80 becoming the next downside target.

Historical data offers a mixed warning. XRP’s five worst November performances before this year were all followed by December losses, averaging 10.4%. However, the losses varied widely. December 2018 and 2016 were comparatively mild, while 2019 extended the damage with another 14.8% decline.

The pattern is not encouraging, but it is not uniform capitulation either. XRP has already experienced a historic flush, and the next move could depend heavily on whether ETF selling finally slows.

#5350. Battery startup Sila lands potential $1B Panasonic deal, plans Central Wash. expansion adding 500 jobs

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:00 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 7:47 am

Sila, a startup producing next-generation battery materials, announced a long-term customer agreement with Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America potentially worth more than $1 billion. To meet demand from Panasonic and other buyers, the company plans to expand its plant in Moses Lake, Wash., supporting roughly 500 additional manufacturing and construction jobs over the coming years.

Panasonic, a battery supplier to Tesla, will buy Sila’s Titan Silicon anode material for its U.S.-made battery cells. The silicon-carbon composite can replace some or all of the graphite in lithium-ion battery anodes to improve performance.

Sila began operations at its Moses Lake plant last year and has about 100 full-time employees at the site. The facility is still scaling up production, with initial capacity designed to supply batteries totaling about 2 gigawatt-hours — enough for roughly 20,000 to 50,000 EVs, depending on how the material is used.

The expansion will increase that capacity to tens of gigawatt-hours, said Gene Berdichevsky, Sila’s co-founder and CEO.

“This is a really important blueprint for reindustrializing the U.S.,” he said. “We have to take new technology and leapfrog China, not just copy what they’ve done over the last 20 years.”

While the U.S. has expanded battery manufacturing, it still depends heavily on overseas suppliers for core materials and technologies, Berdichevsky said. Sila aims to strengthen that domestic supply chain with higher-performing components.

Batteries support industries central to energy independence and national security. They power EVs, consumer devices, drones, robotics and hardware deployed in space, and provide backup electricity for data centers.

Berdichevsky said Titan Silicon can help a battery store 20%–40% more energy in the same space, cut recharging time roughly in half and deliver more power than a battery using a conventional graphite anode. The anode itself is also much lighter and smaller.

In August, Sila received a conditional federal loan commitment of up to $1.4 billion through the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital to expand domestic battery technology manufacturing. The company must meet financial, legal, technical and other requirements before the loan can be finalized.

The startup previously received a $100 million grant during the Biden administration under a similar initiative to increase U.S. energy independence. Those funds helped build its plant in Washington.

The company has also raised $1.6 billion from private investors, including a $300 million round announced in July. The 15-year-old company is valued at $2.27 billion, according to PitchBook.

Seattle-area startup Group14 also makes a silicon-carbon anode material. It operates a smaller-scale manufacturing facility at its Woodinville, Wash., headquarters and produces commercial-scale volumes at a plant in South Korea.

Group14 has partially completed its Moses Lake manufacturing site but repeatedly delayed the start of production. It now targets mid-2027 to bring the first of two production units online, with no firm completion date for the second. It recently announced plans for a factory in Spain.

Growth is key to bringing down costs and making Sila’s technology competitive in mass-market batteries, Berdichevsky said.

“This is really the beginning of chapter three for our company’s history,” he said.

The first two chapters were inventing the technology and moving from grams to tons of production, he added. This phase is about reaching the mass market. Sila aims to begin manufacturing at the expanded facility in 2028, with output increasing over time.

“None of this is easy,” Berdichevsky said. “It’s not the inventing technology; it’s the manufacturing of it that’s really really hard, and we’re going to try to more than 10x the scale from what we’ve already done.”

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5349. On a $1,000 Social Security check, Medicare’s 2027 premium hike eats 18% of the COLA raise—and hits small checks the hardest

In 2027, Social Security recipients will get their biggest cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) in four years. January’s benefits will be 3.6% higher, lifting the average retired worker’s monthly check to about $2,170, according to the Social Security Administration’s 2027 COLA announcement. The larger adjustment reflects persistent inflation in 2026.

Most COLA announcements fail to emphasize that Medicare takes its slice first. Starting in January, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced on Nov. 17 that the standard Part B premium rises by $6.50 to $209.40 a month. For most retirees, that premium is deducted straight from their Social Security benefit.

Although $6.50 doesn’t sound like much, it absorbs about 9% of the average retiree’s raise. And because the premium is a flat amount, the smaller the check, the bigger the share it takes.

For a retiree collecting the 2026 average of $2,095 a month, the 3.6% COLA adds about $75. After the higher premium, roughly $69 remains, so Medicare claims about 9% of the increase.

Lower down the scale, the bite grows. A $1,000 monthly benefit rises by $36, but only $29.50 survives the premium hike, an 18% haircut on the raise. At $1,500 a month, the COLA is worth $54 and the net gain is $47.50, meaning 12% of the raise goes to Medicare.

Bigger checks barely feel it. A $2,500 benefit gains $90 and keeps $83.50, losing 7% of the increase. At $3,000 a month, the raise is $108, the net gain is $101.50, and the premium takes just 6%.

That math applies to retirees who pay the standard premium out of their benefits. Higher-income enrollees pay income-based surcharges on top of it, while states cover the Part B premium for about one in five Medicare enrollees with low incomes and savings.

By recent standards, this year’s hike is mild. The 3.2% premium increase is smaller than the COLA for the first time since 2023; in 2026, the premium jumped 9.7% against a 2.8% COLA.

Even though COLAs are treated like bonuses or raises, they’re not. As David Herbert, director of economics & economic freedom and a senior research fellow at the American Institute for Economic Research (AIER), told The Hill, “It’s meant to make sure that Social Security recipients are receiving the same amount of spending power as they did in the past. It’s not actually going to make them wealthier or have an easier time buying things that they weren’t already going to buy.”

Seniors appear to agree. In an AARP survey conducted before the announcement, 80% of Social Security recipients said a projected 3.5% COLA in 2027 would not keep up with rising prices. When the final number landed, some retirees dismissed it as too little to offset soaring costs.

It seems as though seniors are right. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported 3.7% annual inflation for September 2026, its most recent annual figure. The 3.6% COLA will not keep up, especially since the higher payments don’t start until January.

By then, seniors will have absorbed higher prices since March, when inflation hit 3.3% and outpaced the 2026 COLA of 2.8%. It peaked at 4.2% in May. In other words, a 3.6% COLA is a small improvement, but it comes too late.

Against the backdrop of higher benefits and costs looms Social Security’s insolvency. The 2026 Trustees Report found that starting in the fourth quarter of 2032, the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) Trust Fund will no longer be able to pay 100% of scheduled benefits. Instead, recipients would receive only 78% of them.

Part of the funding shortfall comes down to demographics. According to the trustees’ projections, about 2.6 workers paid in for every beneficiary in 2025, compared with 41.9 in 1945. The trustees expect the ratio to keep falling, to about 1.9 workers per beneficiary by 2075.

With fewer workers paying into Social Security, “Congress is going to have to step in and do something,” said Herbert. “What is going to be left over for people who are not quite at retirement but are hoping at some point to see any form of a return on investment on this money that we’ve been sending the federal government for our entire working lives?”

That job falls to the new Congress, which convenes in January and has roughly six years to act before automatic cuts kick in. In the meantime, Herbert advises those a decade or two from retirement to start saving and investing. More importantly, workers shouldn’t plan on receiving full Social Security benefits in retirement.

#5348. ‘This seems like an extreme privacy violation.’ Surprising messages from the Muse AI agent are unnerving Meta’s own employees, report says

Meta employees have raised concerns about the company’s Muse AI agent after receiving unprompted notifications that tapped into private information, according to internal posts seen by Reuters.

In one example, a Meta staffer reported that Muse sent her a reminder on her personal phone to respond to a message from her sister on the encrypted messaging service Signal.

A Meta colleague also shared that he got unsolicited chats related to apps he had not connected and discovered Muse was set up by default with permission to access push notifications on Android phones, Reuters reported.

Another employee posted that during his chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, Muse said, “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”

Other random Muse messages also took Meta workers aback, including a question about parental control over access to their child’s data and a conversation about picking up a coffee table that raised concern over “possible cross-account context leak.”

In response to the internal posts about Muse, a member of Meta’s Superintelligence team said the agent appeared to be hallucinating, owing to built-in prompts that were designed to engage users between sessions, according to Reuters.

“These (hallucinations) unfortunately bias towards the most uncomfortable topics, like finances/security/safety, which sucks,” he said, adding that other cases involved “crypto-related things too, like giving people updates on their Bitcoin balances.”

The random, out-of-context messages were confirmed as hallucinations.

As for the Muse messages that referred to encrypted Signal chats, the spokesperson pointed out that Android users have the option to grant apps notification access, which they must opt in to and is not specific to Muse.

“With Mac, to allow Muse to work on your behalf, you not only need to click allow for accessibility and screen recording, but after that it takes you to a settings screen where you once again need to confirm and turn this on,” Meta explained.

Since Muse was launched in September, it’s been downloaded more than 10 million times, becoming one of the fastest-growing apps ever. It’s also key to the social media giant’s plan to generate billions of dollars in revenue from AI.

But other companies are blocking Muse and other AI agents. For example, JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said the bank won’t allow agents to access customer accounts and act on their behalf.

Similarly, Amazon won’t let Muse shop on its e-commerce platform and is already fighting to keep out Perplexity’s AI agents.

The process of raising those barriers, however, also entails network upgrades that may be contributing to a sudden surge in outages.

In recent weeks, companies like Chase, Wells Fargo, United Airlines, Apple, and Microsoft saw temporary service disruptions. U.S. officials have said there’s no evidence of cyberattacks, suggesting software patches were deployed before all the bugs were worked out.

Because AI tools can find vulnerabilities faster than companies can safely fix them, the pressure to fix them right away is straining systems that were never designed for that speed, Sen. Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, told the Financial Times.

In an interview with Fortune’s Catherina Gioino, Mark Giles, director of Downdetector parent company Ookla Research, said there’s nothing linking the outages.

“This is a big blip, but it’s kind of on par for the course for what we’re seeing in terms of those longer-term trends,” he said. “Most of the time they’re fairly self-contained and remedied quite quickly. It’s the ones where you can’t withdraw money or you can’t access your emails that really get the headlines.”

Jason Ma is the weekend editor at Fortune, where he covers markets, the economy, finance, and housing.

#5347. ‘Absurd ambition’: Pulumi expands into software delivery with AI agents that ship and fix code

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 8:57 amNovember 18, 2026 at 9:01 am

Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle company talked about building for years but always found too big to take on.

The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting new software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks.

“The ceiling on what we can accomplish is no longer limited by the speed at which we can build software,” said Joe Duffy, the company’s co-founder and CEO, recounting the message he delivered to the Pulumi team. “It’s limited by how ambitious we’re willing to be and how big we’re willing to dream.”

The ambition is all the more notable because Pulumi is getting smaller. The company has about 100 employees, down from about 130 last year. Duffy said there were no layoffs, and that AI has changed people’s roles and made the company more efficient.

Annual recurring revenue per employee more than doubled over the past year, he said. The company isn’t profitable yet, but it has had a few months of positive cash flow this year. Pulumi hasn’t raised money since 2023, when it landed a $41 million round led by Madrona, bringing its total to about $99 million over the company’s lifetime.

Pulumi’s co-founders include Duffy and Eric Rudder, both Microsoft veterans. They started the company in 2017 to let engineers manage cloud infrastructure such as servers, networks and permissions by writing code in everyday languages like Python and TypeScript.

The new products take that approach further:

To decide whether a change is safe to ship, Pulumi Delivery can use Jev, an AI model from TypeSafe AI that estimates the odds of specific risks the team asks about in a planned change. If a risk is higher than the threshold the team sets, the release stops.

Duffy said he first noticed TypeSafe in May when it signed up as a Pulumi customer, because he liked the name. A few months later, Jev took off and TypeSafe used Pulumi to expand worldwide.

“Now even the call on whether a change ships can be made by a model,” said Daniel Gafni, a member of the technical staff at TypeSafe AI, in the Pulumi announcement. “That’s exactly the kind of decision we built Jev to make.”

Both products are available now in public preview. Some features, including Jev decision gates and setting up agents, require Pulumi’s paid Pro or Enterprise plans.

Lucky timing: Pulumi’s founding bet on everyday programming languages turned out to suit AI agents, which are trained to be very good at writing exactly that kind of code.

“I wish I could say I predicted that 10 years ago, but it turns out in this case, what’s good for humans is also good for agents,” Duffy said.

AI agents now handle 40% of the operations on the Pulumi platform that people used to do, up from 15% in April and none in January, Duffy said. Agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Pulumi’s own Neo are making infrastructure changes on their own.

Duffy said many companies building AI coding tools stop once the code is written and reviewed. “For them, life stops at the merge,” he said. The new products cover the steps after that, from testing through release.

Plenty of company: Pulumi won’t have this market to itself. Duffy pointed to Harness, which calls it the “agentic SDLC” (short for software development lifecycle), and GitHub, which pitched “agentic software delivery” at its Universe conference last month. He said Cursor aspires to solve the problem and Anthropic built its own internal system.

The new products could replace some of the work now done by tools such as Argo CD and GitHub Actions, along with lots of homegrown scripts, he said.

“This is an industry-changing moment, and somebody has to solve this problem,” Duffy said. “And I think we are exceptionally well poised to do so.”

Bring your own bot: Neo, the infrastructure agent Pulumi introduced last year, is now just one example of a Pulumi agent. Customers can set up as many as they want, each with its own job, instructions and tools. They can also bring their own agent, such as Claude Code or Codex, and run it in Pulumi’s cloud.

Neo itself, which ran mainly on Anthropic’s Claude, can now use models from OpenAI or Google, too. “It’s not just Anthropic anymore,” Duffy said.

Agents can start work from an alert in PagerDuty, Datadog or Honeycomb, on a schedule or on request, and they report back to teams in Slack.

Pulumi has briefed about 50 customers, and about a dozen are in a private beta. Duffy said no launch in the company’s history has gotten a warmer reception, and he named Moderna among the customers eager to get it.

Pulumi has thousands of customers overall, including major companies such as BMW, Snowflake and Wiz.

The business: Pulumi’s gross margins have stayed in the high 80s to low 90s even as agents drive up usage, Duffy said. Many customers run Pulumi from inside their own Claude Code sessions, which means they’re paying both Anthropic and Pulumi.

Duffy said Pulumi wasn’t out looking for money when it raised its last two rounds. Investors came to the company, and each deal came together in about 48 hours.

Madrona’s Tim Porter has joined the board, Duffy said, taking the seat previously held by the late Soma Somasegar, who led Pulumi’s first investment.

About 40 of the company’s 100 employees are in the Seattle area, working out of an office at Two Union Square. Duffy said Pulumi is hiring more people locally because in-person work still matters when building new products.

Despite the smaller headcount, Pulumi is still hiring, including sales reps in nearly every region of the world. Inside the company, Duffy said Pulumi is having a lot of success with “product-minded engineers who can think from our customers’ point of view, who can think like engineering managers, commanding a team of agents.”

Asked whether a sale or more funding was in the cards, Duffy said Pulumi aspires to be a long-term successful business. “There are a variety of ways to get there,” he said. “But we want to get there on our own terms.”

Rockstar is calling its new release the biggest entertainment launch in history — and the numbers are highway robbery.

GTA VI has a long way to travel to catch its predecessor, though. Take-Two says GTA V has sold nearly 235 million units.

#5344. Home design’s future depends on how homes support everyday life

Accessibility, ergonomics, and sustainability may deserve as much attention as aesthetics as America’s population ages and housing stays short.

This article has been reviewed by the Quartz editorial team. The content may be licensed for reuse.

The 2026 residential design conversation is placing considerable attention on tactile materials, minimalist interiors, natural stone, and visually distinctive finishes. According to Houzz Research’s 2026 U.S. Houzz Emerging Summer Trends Report, searches for sandstone increased by 257%, while interest in Venetian plaster rose by 94%, reflecting growing interest in sensory-rich interiors. These preferences offer insight into evolving tastes, although they also raise a broader question about how aesthetic priorities relate to everyday usability. As homes receive growing focus for their visual presentation, practical considerations such as accessibility, ergonomics, and long-term functionality may deserve an equally prominent place in the design process.

That question extends into the growing market for smart-home technology. Voice assistants, automated lighting, connected appliances, and app-controlled systems are becoming familiar elements of residential innovation. Pew Research Center’s 2026 report found that 35% of U.S. adults have a smart speaker, while 18% have an AI-enabled smart doorbell. These figures illustrate consumer exposure to connected technology, while also inviting consideration of what innovation means beyond digital convenience. Technology may contribute more meaningfully to residential wellness when it also addresses everyday needs, including water quality, hygiene, accessibility, and household efficiency.

Those considerations become particularly relevant against America’s demographic and housing challenges. The AARP 2025–2026 Policy Book estimates that the population aged 65 and older could increase from 57 million in 2022 to 82 million by 2050. Meanwhile, Realtor.com’s March 2026 Housing Supply Gap $GPS Report estimates that the national housing shortfall reached 4.03 million homes in 2025.

Together, these developments raise questions about the suitability of existing housing and the priorities guiding new construction. Bathrooms with difficult thresholds, inaccessible fixtures, and limited mobility accommodations may create additional challenges for older residents. Designing for different stages of life, from infancy through advanced age, could become an increasingly important consideration.

For Steve Scheer, president of Brondell, a home wellness company developing products for water filtration, hygiene, bathing, and indoor air quality, the relationship between these challenges points toward a broader discussion about residential planning. “Housing innovation involves more than the introduction of connected devices or visually distinctive interiors,” he says. “It also encompasses the physical environments and everyday products people depend on.” Brondell’s product categories provide examples of how practical functionality, accessibility, and resource awareness can inform decisions about residential living.

According to Scheer, the discussion begins with understanding how people interact with their homes throughout the day. Products used for drinking, bathing, washing, and personal hygiene can influence everyday routines, making their design relevant to broader conversations about preventive living. “Consumers want solutions that fit naturally into their lives,” Scheer says. That perspective raises an important consideration for manufacturers. Usability can depend on details such as the placement of controls, the accessibility of fixtures, and the physical effort required to operate everyday products.

Ergonomics consequently becomes an important consideration in product development, particularly when everyday fixtures need to accommodate people with different physical abilities. Brondell’s bidets and toilet seats, for example, incorporate side controls and remote operation that may help individuals with limited mobility maintain greater independence in the bathroom. Similar principles inform its kitchen faucets and shower products, where reach, control placement, and ease of operation influence everyday usability.

Brian Inami, Brondell’s Vice President of Product Development, emphasizes the importance of translating human needs into practical engineering decisions. “Smart product design begins with understanding how people will actually use something in their daily lives. Every detail, from the placement of a control to the way a fixture operates, can influence accessibility, comfort, and the overall experience,” Inami says.

Consumer preferences also raise questions about how functionality and appearance influence purchasing decisions. Brondell’s reverse-osmosis filtration portfolio offers an example. “We have two reverse-osmosis systems that reflect different design priorities. One places greater emphasis on filtration capabilities, while the other gives more attention to aesthetics and integration into the kitchen environment,” Scheer says. “It’s interesting to see how consumers respond to these different features, particularly how visual design influences their preferences.”

This instance highlights the importance of communicating technical specifications in accessible terms. Scheer emphasizes that helping consumers understand filtration performance may allow them to make more informed decisions about their household needs.

These considerations also connect to sustainability. Bidets may reduce reliance on toilet paper through water-based hygiene, while household filtration systems can offer an alternative to single-use plastic water bottles. Both examples demonstrate how everyday products can contribute to personal wellness and resource conservation. For Scheer, sustainability forms part of a broader understanding of healthier living, where individual well-being and environmental responsibility can inform the same product decisions.

Beyond individual products, these principles extend to residential development. America’s housing shortage creates an opportunity to reconsider how new homes and apartment buildings accommodate the people living in them. Alongside housing availability, developers may wish to consider the role of communal gardens, shared indoor facilities, and accessible outdoor spaces. These environments can encourage interaction, help residents build relationships, and contribute to a greater sense of belonging. Residential planning consequently has a social dimension, with community spaces influencing the experience of living in a development.

Scheer identifies three priorities for future home innovation: intentional design, sustainability, and greater consideration of an aging population. “Manufacturers can incorporate ergonomics and impactful design during product development, while architects and developers can account for accessibility and communal experiences during initial planning,” he says. “Designing for people across different life stages, from young children to older adults, can also help create homes that accommodate changing needs.”

Essentially, residential innovation may increasingly be evaluated through its contribution to everyday life. Technology and aesthetics will continue influencing design preferences, while accessibility, practical performance, and environmental responsibility may become equally important considerations.

As demographic changes and housing pressures influence residential planning, the opportunity lies in creating environments that support independence, encourage responsible resource use, accommodate different abilities, and foster human connection. These considerations may help define a broader vision of what homes and communities can contribute throughout people's lives.

#5343. Defense tech VC hit a record $37.9 billion last quarter. Two investors say it looks like 2021

When it comes to defense tech, it’s a FOMO-YOLO market, two prominent investors in the sector said onstage this week at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit.

“I’m a long-term optimist, and I’ve been doing this for 30 years, but I see activity in the capital markets that reminds me of 2021,” said Mina Faltas, founder and CEO of Washington Harbour Partners.

“There are a lot of new entrants into the space. The death of SaaS and the disruption from AI has shifted capital into areas of deep tech, space, robotics, energy, and defense,” he said. “There’s folks deploying capital who aren’t experts in any one of those sectors. So, consequently, we can talk about a bubble.”

The money has arrived fast. Venture capitalists put a record $37.9 billion into defense tech across 269 deals in the third quarter of 2026, up 117.5% from the prior quarter, according to PitchBook data cited by Fortune in its coverage of defense tech CEOs at the forum. Valuations have climbed with it: Early-stage defense startups have fetched 17 to 50 times revenue, Fortune reported this summer.

Even the sector’s biggest winners are uneasy. Anduril cofounder Trae Stephens told Fortune in June that mid-stage defense startups trade at multiples that are “completely disconnected from reality.”

Aidan Madigan-Curtis, a partner at venture firm Eclipse, described the mood bluntly.

“There is a pretty big YOLO sentiment happening right now, essentially in physical tech investing,” Madigan-Curtis said. “There are a lot of tourist investors who are excited about a person, a background, a theme … [and] maybe they’re most excited about who invested in the last round and the signal that that gives, versus a hardcore underwriting of a real set of capabilities that can truly pierce into a market.”

That froth now meets a broader shock. Jensen Huang’s abrupt resignation as Nvidia CEO on Nov. 12, under pressure from the chipmaker’s board, has left the startup ecosystem primed for change and possible disruption.

AI startups are most exposed, but private capital markets more broadly are in flux, including the deep-tech bets now crowding into defense.

For startups, the harder test is selling to the government. It has long been a difficult market to crack, and the Pentagon, which has used the name Department of War as a secondary title since a 2025 executive order, is among the hardest. Part of the trouble is that government isn’t a monolithic customer, even if it looks like one.

“There’s a misconception that the Pentagon is this all-or-nothing type of customer,” said Faltas. “It’s actually not. The building itself is … called the Pentagon. It’s got five corners, and each of those five corners needs to be engaged with, and educated with, and listened to … That requires a very focused ground game.”

Allie Garfinkle is a senior writer and editor at Fortune, where she runs Term Sheet; leads coverage of private capital, investors, and startups; and co-chairs the Brainstorm conference series.

#5342. Latest findings point to fuel supply, not Blue Origin’s engines, in loss of Amazon Leo satellites

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:08 am

Blue Origin’s engines look like they’re off the hook, at least for now.

The two BE-4 engines Blue Origin makes for United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket weren’t to blame for the low thrust in Sunday’s failed launch, according to preliminary findings released Wednesday. Instead, it appears the engines didn’t get enough fuel from the rocket, ULA said.

In its latest update on the investigation, ULA said it had completed an initial integrated review of flight data. Preliminary data indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from “inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines,” ULA said, adding that work remains to determine the cause.

On Tuesday, ULA said early data suggested the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit. It didn’t say then whether the engines played a role.

The BE-4s are made by Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin. Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp said Wednesday on X that he was proud of the BE-4 team for its “rapid response and support of ULA’s investigation” and that the company looks forward to Vulcan’s return to flight.

The finding matters for Blue Origin beyond Vulcan. Its own New Glenn rocket uses seven BE-4s on its first stage, and Amazon has 24 New Glenn launches reserved for Leo.

ULA repeated that Vulcan’s second stage appears to have started normally and that its RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the earlier loss of performance. The six Northrop Grumman solid rocket boosters, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally, ULA said.

The Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the ULA-led investigation. Amazon’s next Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

ULA said it will share more as the investigation continues.

#5341. He Saw a ‘Weird’ Machine on Instagram, Got on a Plane to Try It and Built a $75 Million Fitness Empire

STRONG Pilates co-founder Michael Ramsey shares the making of one of the fastest-growing fitness franchises in the world.

Most people who see something odd on Instagram mutter “huh, neat,” and keep scrolling. Michael Ramsey bought a plane ticket to check it out in person. The former oil and gas marketer, who once ran an F45 studio in Port Melbourne, saw a post about an exercise machine called the Rowformer, and flew from Australia to Orange County to try it himself. Seven years later, STRONG Pilates has more than 130 studios across multiple countries and continents, 57,000 members and more than $75 million in net revenue over the past 12 months.

Ramsey shared how the STRONG brand came together, why some Pilates traditionalists hate it, and why he is totally okay with that.

This wasn’t your original career path. How did you get involved in Pilates?I was working in oil and gas, and I was not enjoying my life too much. I wasn’t highly motivated in corporate. And on the weekends, I was actually running a nightclub with my business partner, Mark Armstrong, who I’ve been in business with for eleven years. And he tapped me on the shoulder and he said, “Hey, I found this really unique boutique concept called F45 Training.” This was about twelve years ago. And so we actually brought the first F45 studio to Melbourne, Australia, and I quit my job in corporate, and for the first time in my life, I felt free, like I was in charge of my own destiny. Not only did I have financial freedom, but I had time as well. We scaled our F45 studios to six very quickly, sold after about four or five years.

What inspired STRONG?My housemate showed me an Instagram post about this Rowformer machine that was created out of Orange County. And to me it ticked a lot of boxes — you’ve got rowing, and you’ve got the Reformer. So I jumped on a plane, took the class and it was one of the most exhilarating, endorphin-led kind of workouts I’d ever done. I’m looking around the room, and there are all these incredibly fit women in their forties and fifties that just looked incredible. And I’m like, “Wow, this, this is awesome. I need to take this back to Australia.” Mark tried it, had the same experience, and then we negotiated global rights for the machine and built a franchise model around it.

Most of us see something cool on Instagram and keep scrolling. We don’t jump on a plane. What does that say about you?Look, to be transparent, it was very opportunistic. I could see, and nothing against F45, but I couldn’t see the lifetime value of the customer increasing over time due to the impact of workouts. So I was on the hunt for something that was low impact, more longevity-focused. How do we keep our members for five, six, seven, ten years? That was a question that I had and the problem I was trying to solve.

How do you turn early adopters into paying clients and repeat customers?You need to respect your product and business enough to have people paying from the start. There’s this whole thing in the fitness industry about free trials, and do they work or do they not work? We are a premium product, and I think once the work is done and the product is ready, you need to respect yourself and your product by charging for every session.

Now, for anyone who’s starting in this space, I would say the first thing to do is just start. Just open, and then learn from your consumer and innovate like crazy. And that’s all we did. It’s a very different product today than what it was seven years ago, and in another seven years it’s gonna be probably even more different, because that’s how it works. If you don’t innovate, you will recede, and you will die.

Was there an innovation that came from customer feedback and made you think, “Oh yeah, that’s a good idea”?The big one was the TV screens. Our male audience, as soon as we put TVs in, their trial-to-member conversion went through the roof. You’ve got to imagine, seven years ago, a lot of men hadn’t even experienced Pilates before. They were terrified to jump on a reformer. So the TVs, although they’re not liked by the traditionalists, gave us a huge uptake, particularly with male consumers. It was huge for us.

Your Instagram handle is just “Strong.” How on earth did you get that?Do you remember when domain names were getting really expensive? Like imagine strong.com. It’s probably worth half a million dollars. I had some friends that were trying to open businesses and trying to get these domain names, and I thought, “Well, I’m gonna start acquiring one-word Instagram names,” because Instagram was really taking off at the time. And so I had Strong, I had Cultivate, I had Ram. So I just held onto them. And then when I went to Orange County and I did the workout, I thought, “How does this workout make me feel? Not only do I need to be physically strong, but I need to be mentally strong to get through this.” And so it just made sense to call it STRONG Pilates, and now we’re here. At one point, it was getting tagged every 30 seconds all around the world, and I would just sit there watching it.

#5340. ‘Voluntary, revocable’: The fine print behind Anthropic founders’ $112 billion giving pledge

Anthropic’s record-setting IPO may have created one of the largest pools of charitable capital ever assembled. Its size depends on a stock that has swung more than $30 a share in its first three sessions.

The Claude maker priced 980 million shares at $83 on Nov. 18, above its marketed range of $70 to $78, raising a record $81.3 billion and valuing the company at about $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis. The stock opened at $111.50 on Nov. 19, closed its first day at $97.17, then fell 8.5% to $88.91 on Friday.

On Monday, as the Nasdaq jumped roughly 6% on Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO, Anthropic went the other way. Shares closed down 1.4% at $87.64, about 5.6% above the IPO price.

TechCrunch estimated Thursday that Anthropic’s charitable commitments could be worth about $156 billion at roughly $95 a share, where the stock traded early in its debut. The figure combines the company’s Public Benefit Fund, employees’ pledged shares, and Anthropic’s match on those pledges.

Because all three are paid in stock, the total moves with the share price. At Monday’s close, the same math yields about $144 billion, down $12 billion from Thursday. At the $83 IPO price, it would be roughly $136 billion.

Even the lower figures are enormous. By TechCrunch’s count, Americans gave $617 billion to charity in all of 2025, so Monday’s value equals nearly a quarter of a year of U.S. giving.

The largest piece is the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a wholly owned LLC the company announced in October. Anthropic’s S-1 filing shows it contributed 846.8 million shares to the fund, 5% of fully diluted shares as of June 30, a stake worth about $74 billion at Monday’s close.

The fund can grow. Anthropic says its board may add another 2% of the company for every 50% increase in value above a set baseline; TechCrunch reported that baseline is the $83 IPO price, which would put the next trigger near $124.50 a share. The company said it will disclose more about the fund’s governance and valuation milestones in the coming months, and it has not announced a distribution timetable.

The second channel is employees. About half of Anthropic’s staff take part in its equity donation program, and the company matches pledged shares 3-for-1 for longer-tenured employees and 1-for-1 for newer ones, according to plan documents filed with the S-1. TechCrunch estimated employees have pledged about $23 billion in stock, which would draw roughly $53 billion in matches at $95 a share.

That money is closer to moving, but not yet. Most holders face a lockup of up to 180 days, which could end sooner after first-quarter 2027 results, and many employees cannot sell or gift most of their shares until next spring, the Associated Press reported. Shares parked in donor-advised funds, which have no annual payout requirement, may take even longer to reach working charities.

The third channel is the least certain. Anthropic’s seven cofounders have pledged to give away 80% of their personal equity, a commitment the AP valued at $112 billion at the IPO price. But the S-1 describes the pledges as “voluntary, revocable expressions” of intent that are not legally binding, and timing, amounts, and recipients remain undecided. TechCrunch’s $156 billion estimate excludes them.

The cofounders also face the longest lockup: up to 365 days from the Nov. 18 prospectus, or earlier after third-quarter 2027 results, with a portion of their shares eligible for release around the 180-day mark.

Some money is already committed. Earlier this month, Anthropic pledged $50 million to a donor-advised fund at the San Francisco Foundation for Bay Area nonprofits through 2027. The first $500,000 went to the SF-Marin Food Bank, GLIDE, the Interfaith Winter Shelter, and the San Francisco Firefighters Local 798 Toy Program, and a company spokesperson told TechCrunch the gift did not come from the Public Benefit Fund.

Anthropic has also committed $200 million to study and address AI’s effects on the labor market. In June, it pledged $150 million to Claude Corps, a fellowship that places early-career workers at nonprofits to help them use AI.

Separately, Anthropic has given $40 million this year to Public First Action, a bipartisan group that advocates for AI safeguards. That is policy spending, not charity, and Anthropic says it will not use equity held by the Public Benefit Fund for lobbying or political giving.

The next test for the share price comes Dec. 15, when up to 303 million shares can become eligible for sale under the prospectus’s lockup schedule, followed by another 303 million on Jan. 5. For charities, the date that matters more is spring 2027, when employee pledges and the company’s matches can start to move.

Until then, Anthropic’s philanthropic promise is marked to market every trading day. A return to the $115 debut high would lift TechCrunch’s measure to nearly $190 billion; a slide below $83 would take it under $136 billion.

#5339. Tech Moves: Microsoft names 2 leaders, loses 1; DoorDash VP departs; BluePill, Glacis get execs

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 18, 2026 at 12:47 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 11:47 am

Yang was most recently a senior director with Microsoft Research, working on grid technology. Her team built a grid dataset and released small foundation models to help users operate and expand electrical infrastructure.

Yang thanked her community at the tech giant, adding, “I hope the relationships and collaborations we’ve built continue well beyond Microsoft, and that we find many new ways to work together.”

In her new role, Mellen said she will lead strategy for protection and threat intelligence, “helping shape what intelligence we produce, how AI can improve its speed and quality, and how we turn that knowledge into better protection for customers.”

— Agility Robotics, the Salem, Ore., company that had its Nasdaq debut earlier this month, has announced three leadership changes:

— Former tech executive Drew Sheriff has been named CEO and president of the Space Needle and Chihuly Garden and Glass. Sheriff was previously a vice president at DoorDash and has held leadership roles at Amazon, Starbucks and Parachute Home. His roles focused on customer experience, product growth, strategy and marketing.

“His skill set is the ideal background for charting how we attract customers and how we delight customers in this new age,” Jeff Seely, board chair for the Space Needle and Chihuly Garden and Glass, told the Seattle Times.

— Microsoft has named Caroline King as director of its Washington state community and philanthropy team, with a focus on advocacy work across housing, affordability and other priority issues.

King is the founder and past CEO of Washington STEM, an organization that coordinates research, advocacy, policy, philanthropy and partnerships to support science, technology, engineering and math education in the state. She most recently served as a leader on the governing body of an international school in Luxembourg.

— Longtime Amazon and Microsoft tech exec Scott Wiltamuth has retired — mostly.

Wiltamuth joined Amazon in 2011 as an AWS vice president overseeing a large organization building developer and management tools. In 2018, he took a seven-month leave for colon cancer treatment. After returning, he sought a director-level position and thanked company leaders for helping him find a better fit. “Their flexibility and creativity enabled me to extend my AWS career,” he said.

Wiltamuth launched his tech career at Microsoft in 1993 and left nearly 19 years later as director of program management for Visual Studio Pro.

He now spends time with his wife and family, traveling, golfing, swimming and reading. “I don’t plan to pursue another full-time operational role,” Wiltamuth said, “but may do some part-time work.”

— Adam Nygate has exited Palo Alto Networks to co-found and lead a stealth startup based in Seattle. He was founder and CEO of Huntr, a platform launched in 2019 where security researchers could submit information on AI and machine learning vulnerabilities. Protect AI acquired Huntr, and Palo Alto Networks later acquired Protect AI.

“Huntr was a bet that open source gets safer when vulnerabilities are visible to the people who can fix them, even when that made life uncomfortable for vendors who’d rather keep things quiet,” Nygate said in a post announcing his career change and impending new baby.

— BluePill, a Seattle-based marketing startup that helps brands predict consumer behavior, has named Mike Weis as chief revenue officer and head of sales.

Weis has 40 years of experience in consumer packaged goods, retail and commerce, beginning his career as a Pacific Northwest leader at Unilever and holding executive positions at Catalina and Quotient Technologies. Recent roles include adviser at Contento2, eGateway Capital and And1 Advisors.

“Beyond the incredible résumé, Mike is one of the kindest, most genuine, and most passionate people I’ve met. Someone who has accomplished so much, yet brings so much humility, curiosity, and energy to every conversation,” said Ankit Dhawan, CEO and founder of BluePill.

— Glacis, a Seattle startup that builds tamper-proof records of AI behavior, has named Caer Mistral Sanders as a technical co-founder. Sanders has launched startups and joins Glacis from Thoughtworks. Before that, she held leadership roles at Wayfair and Onshape. As a teenager, she published a book on mixed-reality control systems and won a world robotics championship.

In a post announcing the new role, Sanders said she has designed medical record systems, researched robot communication, patented cryptographic technology and built widely used AI platforms. “This is the first time in my career I get to bring all of those skills to bear on one problem, and I couldn’t be more excited!” she added.

— The PNW Battery Collaborative has welcomed Jason Demeny as its director of communications. Demeny is a marketing leader whose past employers include Crusoe, Patch, Qualtrics and Apptio. Earlier in his career, he spent more than a decade at Microsoft over two stints, most recently leading teams that served the Azure Partner Experience group.

The nonprofit PNW Battery Collaborative brings together startups, innovators and researchers focused on energy storage.

— Tom Wheeler, former chairman of the Federal Communications Commission, has joined the advisory council for Known, a Bellevue, Wash.-based company building accountability infrastructure for autonomous AI. Wheeler led the FCC from 2013 to 2017.

Known, previously called Identity Digital Innovation Labs, spun out of Identity Digital in September.

— Versium has promoted Matthew Baumgartner to vice president of engineering. The Redmond, Wash.-based company provides data and software that help businesses identify potential customers, fill in missing contact information and target their marketing. Baumgartner has been with Versium since 2018.

— Charlie Trillingham has been named communications manager for the University of Washington AI and Machine Learning for Engineering programs and the UW NSF AI Institute for Dynamic Systems. He previously served as a marketing and communications lead for the Buerk Center for Entrepreneurship within the UW’s Foster School of Business.

Editor’s note: Story updated 11/19 to correct that Charlie Trillingham worked for the Buerk Center for Entrepreneurship within the UW’s Foster School of Business, not the Foster School itself.
