#5338. A Thanksgiving Feast for 10 People for Just $35? Why Grocers Are Willing to Lose Money on Your Holiday Dinner.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

From Walmart to Aldi, grocers are using meal bundles to attract customers.

Popular supermarkets are using discounted Thanksgiving meal bundles to get shoppers through their doors — in the hopes that they will buy more once they are inside.

According to a new report from The New York Times, grocers are willing to lose money on holiday meal bundles because they’re betting shoppers will buy more than just the turkey. Supermarkets are sacrificing profits on Thanksgiving dinner to win more of a shopper’s overall grocery spending.

Their familiar draw is a bargain in the form of a discounted turkey or a low-priced package of Thanksgiving essentials. Such offers are called loss leaders, meaning that stores charge less than they paid suppliers in hopes of attracting shoppers who will buy other items.

For example, in October, the grocery chain Hy-Vee initially offered a bundle of 26 items that could feed 10 people for $39. The deal included a frozen turkey of up to 12 pounds, gravy mix and corn muffin mix.

A few days after offering the deal, the chain lowered the price to $35 to better match or beat offers from national grocery stores. The main competitor was Walmart, which introduced a “feast for 10” that bundles a turkey with sweet potatoes and gravy mix for $35 starting in October.

Meanwhile, Aldi’s holiday meal deal for 10 people, including a 16-pound turkey, comes out to $39, while Amazon’s grocery offer feeds six people for $25.

There is ample demand for these deals. Walmart CEO John Furner recently told Business Insider that the retailer has “sold a million more turkeys” than it did a year ago. “The customer response is strong,” he said.

Walmart store workers also mentioned to Business Insider that demand for the Thanksgiving feast is strong.

“The meal deal frenzy has been nuts!” a worker in Oklahoma said. “I work at a neighborhood market, and we are still experiencing a higher volume.”

Grocery stores are using Thanksgiving as a way to show new customers what they have on the shelves. Customers come in for the deal and leave with more than they anticipated.

“Thanksgiving is one of the biggest grocery occasions of the year, and it is our chance to show millions of shoppers what we have to offer,” Scott Patton, chief commercial officer at Aldi, said in an interview with the Times.

Other grocers are offering more expensive meal bundles. Costco’s $199 Thanksgiving spread included a five-pound precooked turkey breast, accompanied by ready-made mashed potatoes, macaroni and cheese, apple cobbler and pumpkin pie. Orders closed in mid-November.

Meanwhile, Los Angeles luxury grocer Erewhon is taking a pricier approach with its $749 “Ultimate Organic Feast,” which serves up to 10 people. The menu pairs a cooked free-range turkey with sourdough and roasted vegetable stuffing, rainbow carrots, garlic mashed potatoes and turkey gravy, along with a deep-dish pumpkin pie.

These prices are outside the norm. Americans will spend $58.63 on average feeding 10 people this Thanksgiving, up 6% annually, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation. The increase stems from a 10% increase in turkey prices.

#5337. Arthur Hayes Says Anthropic IPO Could Determine Bitcoin’s Next Move

Maelstrom CEO Arthur Hayes projected that the outcome of Anthropic’s IPO could impact digital assets above the current baseline. This follows a string of analysts citing fund rotation as a reason for capital flight over the last three months.

The crypto executive hinted that the much-anticipated IPO’s performance would be felt throughout the sector. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has dominated financial markets, raising expectations for the company’s stock price and related projects.

According to Hayes, a weak IPO would negatively impact digital assets and drag Bitcoin’s price lower. The top crypto dipped into the red zone, plunging trader sentiment after its price hit a new three-month low.

Conversely, a strong IPO would be bullish for crypto assets, especially Bitcoin, by boosting market confidence. Hayes’ view may stem from the year-long correlation between Bitcoin and the United States stock market, though risks remain.

“If Anthropic struggles or treads water, then it’s trouble for the entire market… I want to see Anthropic IPO perform, but what matters is the sentiment around AI, can Anthropic pull off a successful IPO. This is the bellwether for the whole story… Massive pop off the IPO, it’s game back on, it’s long everything, risk on.”

For bears, although institutional investors going bullish on tech stocks results in crypto’s win, this year has been different. Capital rotation to tech stocks occasioned mass crypto liquidations. Basically, investors dumped assets and jumped on the AI bandwagon, creating different views on the IPO’s impact.

Binance founder Changpeng Zhao cited talks around Anthropic IPO as a factor behind Bitcoin’s decline. The top crypto trades under $62,000, making a consistent decline amid a slew of macro and industry factors.

Strive CEO Matt Cole explained that Bitcoin fell 19% during the SpaceX IPO and is down 18% heading into the second-largest IPO. “What happened after the SpaceX IPO is the notable part. Bitcoin bottomed 18 days after the listing, then recovered all the way. By Day 100, it was above where it started.”

Crypto users expect a slow turnaround because institutional sentiment needed for a rebound is at sharp lows due to infamous hacks and tighter regulations.

#5336. Women’s soccer has a $1 billion opportunity—and the CEO of England’s top two leagues wants a slice of the pie

The 1999 FIFA Women’s World Cup final was a watershed moment for women’s football, with record-breaking attendance and viewership numbers. More than 40 million people in North America tuned in to watch the U.S. beat China 5–4 on penalties in the final. Among them was ­ Canadian Nikki Doucet, then a student and college basketball player at St. Francis Xavier University. “That was the first time I’d seen women’s team sports on TV, and I remember feeling so excited,” she says.

Since then, interest in women’s football has grown significantly. Its global fan base is projected to surpass 800 million by 2030, according to Nielsen Sports, while Fifpro expects the sport to be a $1 billion industry by 2027—a 72% increase from 2024.

Now CEO of Women’s Super League Football, the company responsible for operating the top two English women’s leagues (WSL and WSL2), Doucet is at the sharp end of that opportunity. England has become a commercial force in women’s football: Eight of the world’s 15 highest-revenue clubs are in the WSL, according to Deloitte, and Doucet believes the league is well-positioned to capture a “significant portion” of the potential $1 billion the sport is predicted to generate.

American entrepreneurs and investment groups are taking note. The success of the Women’s National Basketball Association—now an $850 million franchise—and the soaring valuations of teams in the National Women’s Soccer League (league leaders Gotham FC were recently valued at $350 million) underlines the potential. And many see an opportunity to buy in at an early stage in the commercial development of the sport in Europe.

U.S. businesswoman Michele Kang bought the London City Lionesses in 2023, leading the club to its 2025 WSL promotion. Other notable investors include Reddit cofounder Alexis Ohanian, who holds a minority stake in Chelsea FC Women, and U.S. financier Marc Zahr, an investor in Aston Villa Women.U.S. businesswoman Michele Kang bought the London City Lionesses in 2023, leading the club to its 2025 WSL promotion. Other notable investors include Reddit cofounder Alexis Ohanian, who holds a minority stake in Chelsea FC Women, and U.S. financier Marc Zahr, an investor in Aston Villa Women.

Speaking at the WSL’s New Playbook ­ summit earlier this year, one investor argued that European women’s football represented the “best opportunity in sport,” on a risk-adjusted basis.

“I think of my career as if I’m still an athlete. I practice for every board meeting in the same way that I used to train for a game. Your practice should be so hard, the game is easy.”

“The enterprise value of these clubs is 100% going up,” Doucet, a former investment banker at Citi, says. “The question is, do you have owners that want to participate in this asset class of women’s football? There are different tradeoffs versus men’s football and different risk factors because we’re in a different stage of development.”

Doucet’s challenge is turning rising global interest in the women’s game into regular paying customers. There was a surge in interest following the England Lionesses’ UEFA Women’s Euro 2022 victory: Average attendance at WSL matches tripled to 5,616 the following season. But last year, median attendance was 3,236—and it remains heavily concentrated in a few clubs.

“This isn’t a manufacturing challenge. This is a marketing and revenue challenge,” Doucet says. The league invested in a rebrand of both the WSL and WSL2 ahead of the newly expanded league this season, and clubs are also investing more. In April, WSL team Brighton announced plans to build Europe’s first purpose- built women’s football stadium at an estimated cost of more than £75 million ($99 million).

“You have to invest in building the foundations that will generate long- term returns, but they might take time until you actually see the results,” Doucet says. “That’s the constant tradeoff.”

The underlying economics also remain fragile. Despite the high revenues, only four of the 14 clubs in the WSL recorded a profit (two clubs did not publish detailed financial data). The league itself, which is co-owned by the participating clubs, posted an operating loss of £8.2 million ($10.8 million) for the year ending July 2025.

Doucet attributes much of the loss to one-off costs associated with becoming an independent business, including establishing its own HR, finance, legal, and regulatory teams. The WSL and WSL2 formally split from the Football Association (FA) in 2024, shortly after Doucet joined the organization. She says the league is now profitable, although declined to share the financial details.

“We’re in a transition phase, which is probably a little bit messy. The challenge is going from big structural moments, like a World Cup, to building a weekly fan habit around women’s professional football,” Doucet says.

The majority of the league’s revenues so far have come from broadcast rights and commercial partnerships. The league generated £8.7 million ($11.5 million) from Sky and the BBC in 2025, and the league counts Doucet’s former employer Nike, in addition to Airbnb, Apple, and ­ Barclays, among its growing list of sponsors.

The opportunities for commercial sponsors are different from those in the men’s sport, Doucet says. “We have a different audience that really values companies that are investing in women’s football,” she says. “They’re very brand loyal, and they show much deeper engagement.”

Doucet’s current priority is improving the spectacle on the pitch. “The fans want to watch the best players, and they want to watch a competition that’s exciting and has jeopardy,” she says. Good progress has been made in this area, too. The London City Lionesses signed three-time Ballon d’Or winner Alexia Putellas from Barcelona this summer, and the WSL had the highest representation of players at last year’s Women’s Euro tournament of any league.

Ensuring the WSL’s longevity is a responsibility Doucet is acutely aware of. “This isn’t a five-year business,” she says. “This is a generational asset.” She remains optimistic about what lies ahead. Doucet adds: “We’re in an early stage, so the potential is almost completely untapped—you don’t know how big it could be.”

#5335. ‘Sister isn’t free’: Melinda French Gates fact-checks viral ‘SNL’ sketch on eldercare

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 1:23 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 1:23 pm

A “Saturday Night Live” skit about caring for aging relatives touched a viral nerve after it aired over the weekend, including with Melinda French Gates, who offered her own “fact check” on the too-close-to-home comedy.

The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.

French Gates wrote on Instagram this week that the sketch “is funny because it’s a little too true.” Using research from Pivotal, her investment and philanthropic organization, she went through the ad’s claims one by one and found that most held up:

Sister will provide. True, French Gates said, citing AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Among adults ages 55 to 64, women are nearly 40% more likely than men to care for an older relative, and nearly 40% more likely to provide constant care.

She’ll quit her job. “Mostly true,” at least the job part. Catalyst found that 42% of women who voluntarily left jobs in 2025 cited caregiving as the main reason.

Paid help is pricey. “True, unfortunately.” New America puts the average home health aide at more than $6,600 a month, and 24-hour care can top $25,000.

Sister may break down. Also true. In the Caregiving in the U.S. 2025 report, nearly two-thirds of caregivers said they were under moderate or high emotional stress, and women felt the strain more than men did.

“Free” is misleading. French Gates said Sister isn’t free; she’s the one paying for the care, in lost wages, stalled careers, thinner retirement savings and less time for her own life.

French Gates has made women’s health and caregiving central to her work since she stepped down as co-chair of the Gates Foundation in 2024.

She left with $12.5 billion to put toward her work on behalf of women and families. Much of that work runs through Pivotal, the Seattle-area organization she founded to handle her philanthropy and investments. In June she pledged another $215 million for women’s health, which brought her giving in that area to more than $600 million over two years. The pledge included $10 million to the Menopause Society for better menopause care in the U.S.

The sketch has been shared widely across the country this week, in part because it lines up so closely with the research.

In its own analysis, The New York Times cited studies showing that daughters generally provide at least twice as much care to aging parents as sons do. The U.S., unlike many wealthy countries, offers no federal paid leave or long-term care insurance for family caregivers.

French Gates said she welcomed the conversation.

“I’m so glad we’re talking about this, and laughing about it,” she wrote on Instagram. “We need more honesty about what caring for loved ones really takes and why so much of that work falls to women. But I’d love for the day to come when these jokes don’t pack quite the same punch — because we’ve made it so much easier to care for the people we love.”

#5334. Google acquires Seattle startup Howie and its AI scheduling assistant

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 2:03 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 2:03 pm

Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.

Terms of the deal were not disclosed this week. Google Labs, the company’s experimental arm, announced the acquisition in a post on X, saying it “can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses.”

Howie CEO and co-founder Austin Petersmith said on LinkedIn that the team will continue building Howie at Google. “Howie has always been built on top of Gmail and Google Calendar, so Google Labs is the perfect place for us to take this product to the next level,” he wrote.

Petersmith co-founded Howie around 2023 with CTO Dave Newman. The two first worked together in 2013 at Assembly, which Newman co-founded, and prototyped an AI assistant in 2015 before deciding the market wasn’t ready.

We’re excited to welcome Howie to Google Labs! The @Howie_ai team has spent years figuring out scheduling and calendar management. We can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses 🤝 https://t.co/8bzjebeGdD

Users cc Howie on an email thread, and it coordinates meeting times, adds events to calendars, follows up as needed and flags scheduling conflicts. Customers set their own rules in an open-ended preferences document, such as “if it’s a pitch call, set it to 25 minutes and use Zoom.”

Behind the scenes, Howie ran tasks through fine-tuned language models and looped in human scheduling experts when the AI wasn’t confident.

Howie raised a $6 million seed round led by True Ventures in September 2025, when it launched publicly out of private beta. At the time, it had more than 1,000 paying customers, including startup founders, venture capitalists, recruiters, consultants and journalists, and was scheduling more than 5,000 meetings a week.

The deal comes as Google and rivals including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta race to build AI agents that complete tasks on behalf of users. Google Labs acquired music generation platform ProducerAI earlier this year.

#5333. He Spent Two Years Teaching Strangers to Cook on YouTube Before Opening His First Restaurant. Here’s What It Did for His Business.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Watch now to learn how Jason Ganahl built a barbecue audience on YouTube, what he looks for in a hire and how he grew GQue BBQ.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

By the time Jason Ganahl opened his first barbecue restaurant, he’d already spent close to two years showing people how to cook on YouTube. He opened GQue Championship BBQ in Westminster, Colorado, in November 2015.

Ganahl was winning barbecue competitions, and friends were asking him for help with dinner. One was thinking about smoking salmon over the weekend. Others wanted to know how to grill asparagus or cook lobster tails.

He’d watched Greg Mrvich demonstrate barbecue techniques on Ballistic BBQ. Ganahl could do the same with the questions his friends were asking. Once he put an answer on YouTube, anyone who wanted to smoke salmon could find it and watch him do it.

“YouTube was born out of, I like to just share, I like to give,” Ganahl says. “That’s why the restaurant industry is great to me.”

At GQue, that means helping his team and giving the people who come in for barbecue a good experience. He describes the goal as giving guests “the best 20 minutes of their day.”

Ganahl knew his way around a smoker. Making videos gave him something to learn from scratch. He believed video would become a bigger part of how people told their stories and wanted to learn how to do the work himself.

“I thought this was a good opportunity to teach myself how to edit, create content and learn how to be pretty good at it,” he says.

“Shorts have really taken over,” Ganahl says.

He singled out Meat Church as a channel still doing long-form videos well. Asked whether he plans to make more himself, he says, “I don’t have the bandwidth to do that.”

Ganahl’s older videos are still up. Anyone looking for help with lobster tails can find his answer without ever setting foot in GQue.

Ganahl wants guests to leave GQue and tell a friend where they ate. If enough people do that, he says, the demand for another restaurant takes care of the decision about when to open one.

“Then we’re forced to grow and open up a new spot,” Ganahl says.

That’s why he pays so much attention to who he hires. He wants people who care as much as he does about what a guest gets when they walk in for lunch. When someone brings a friend back for the brisket, both should get the same barbecue that earned the recommendation.

“I’ve never been able, and I’ve never seen anybody, to be able to take chicken shit and turn it into chicken salad,” Ganahl says.

He looks for people who share his priorities and trusts them to deliver on those priorities every day. At GQue, that means smoking brisket over hickory for same-day service and keeping the price within reach for someone who wants barbecue on an ordinary day.

GQue has grown from one restaurant in Westminster to six standalone restaurants and seven concession stands across three stadiums. Two of those stands are inside Folsom Field, where GQue serves fans on game days and feeds the University of Colorado football team and staff. The company also runs two stands at Empower Field and three at Coors Field.

Ganahl started cooking barbecue at weekend competitions. Now there are people serving it on GQue’s behalf at counters across Colorado. He credits the people he’s hired with giving guests a reason to come back and bring someone else. Having a team to share the work with has also made the business more enjoyable for him.

“It’s way more fun doing it with more people than trying to do everything on your own,” he says.

#5332. The 11 days that brought Jensen Huang back to Nvidia

Last Wednesday, Elon Musk, appearing as flustered as ever, called Nvidia’s decision to push out cofounder Jensen Huang a huge mistake, comparing it to the Chicago Bulls dumping Michael Jordan during a winning streak.

“There’s no one that can really replace Jensen. He does the roles of several people,” Musk told the New York Times’ Andrew Ross Sorkin, appearing at the newspaper’s DealBook summit via videoconference while Musk was in China with President Trump. “He has long-term relationships that have been built up over decades. He understands the technology incredibly well.”

Five days later, Musk was posting on X, the social media platform he owns, to celebrate Huang’s return.

“It is done,” he wrote. “The mistake has been corrected.”

Musk’s reaction reflects the extraordinary political muscle that he and other powerful figures in Silicon Valley and Washington flexed to bring Huang back. The Nvidia board reinstated Huang as CEO, the company announced Monday. His ouster, initially triggered by an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, has gripped the business and political worlds for the past two weeks, and his return promises more shock waves in the tech industry and the halls of power. Since Huang’s resignation was announced on Nov. 12, influential figures, from Musk to Trump, have waged a pressure campaign to make Huang CEO again, even as Nvidia’s board said it had moved on. Trump even called the board as it deliberated Huang’s reinstatement to push for his return.

The reversal caps one of the most remarkable resurgences in business history, while raising numerous questions about how the company moves forward, given an internal investigation into Huang and a reported probe into Nvidia’s accounting by the Securities and Exchange Commission.

This is a reconstruction of Huang’s ouster and return as it unfolded over a momentous 11-day period:

On Oct. 29, the New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence officials had concluded that Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, was passing information to the Chinese government, and that she had a close relationship with Jensen Huang. The Times also reported that Trump was briefed roughly a year earlier but didn’t act. Subsequent reporting detailed that China’s Ministry of State Security recruited Alice Huang to gather intelligence on Nvidia’s CEO and possibly lobby for the sale of advanced chips to China.

After the Times report, Huang told Bloomberg News there was nothing unusual about his relationship with Alice Huang, likening it to his dealings with Chinese customers and executives.

“It was all completely normal and not unusual,” he said.

On Nov. 8, Huang publicly admitted to an affair, writing, “There is no excuse for what I did” and pledging to cooperate fully with Nvidia’s investigation, which the board announced the same day. The board, overseen by independent directors with outside counsel, said it had “no reason to believe” national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised. The next day, Chinese officials dismissed the spying claims as “pure fabrication out of thin air.”

On Nov. 10, the independent directors hired Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to run the investigation. The tech news website The Information reported that Alice Huang’s network had built companies to buy Nvidia chips, helping arrange about $7.5 billion in purchases, including of banned chips.

The next day, the Times reported, citing five people who worked at Nvidia, that Huang had an affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, who has reported directly to him. Reached by phone, Huang told the Times, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly” and hung up. Later that day, the Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia’s 10-member board was preparing to push Huang out and had called an emergency meeting. The alleged affair with Powell violated the company’s code of conduct, and Huang’s earlier assurances appeared to be false.

By the next morning, Nvidia announced Huang had resigned. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress became interim CEO, and tech entrepreneur Harvey Jones was named Nvidia’s first board chair. The same day, Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) and Rep. Richard E. Neal (D-Mass.) announced an inquiry into the administration’s approval of Nvidia’s H200 chip sales to China. Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) asked Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify.

Hours after the resignation, Reuters reported, citing two people familiar with the matter, that Huang had an intimate relationship with a second, unnamed Nvidia employee. It also reported that Huang misled Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter and chief marketing officer Alison Wagonfeld in both fall 2025 and October 2026.

Nvidia shares plunged as much as 14.35% in intraday trading, wiping out about $600 billion in value at the low, and ultimately closed down 4.34%.

Almost as soon as Huang was ousted, a comeback effort took shape among tech and political elites and Nvidia’s own staff. A week ago, President Trump told reporters he would support reinstating Huang. “I would certainly not mind seeing that,” Trump said, adding that Huang had “learned a big lesson.”

An Nvidia employee launched a website with an open letter demanding that the board reinstate Huang. As of Monday, more than 206,000 names appeared on the letter. Signatories included Musk, Uber cofounder Travis Kalanick, Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and tech investor Gavin Baker.

The day after Huang resigned, Baker and Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner said in an open letter that Huang “has earned the right for a deliberate process that avoids any needless rush to replace him before all the facts are known.”

The same day, Nvidia’s board released a statement saying it was hiring an executive search firm and hadn’t yet approached any potential candidates.

Last Tuesday, Huang broke his silence, posting on X that he was sorry for “serious mistakes” in his personal life and pledging to cooperate with the board’s investigation.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang wrote.

The same day, Nvidia reported blockbuster earnings, with revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103%. Interim CEO Kress said the “road map is on track” and that Nvidia had stopped shipping AI chips to China. Jones, the board chair, said the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” and that Heidrick & Struggles was running the search for the next chief executive. Nvidia also created a board committee on national security and export controls, chaired by Suzanne Nora Johnson.

Later that day, the Journal reported that the SEC is investigating Nvidia, including whether its disclosures misled investors. On Thursday, California Attorney General Rob Bonta subpoenaed Nvidia, seeking answers on whether China received chips or confidential information and whether investors were misled. The next day, the Times reported that Huang routinely humiliated employees with violent threats. His spokesperson denied one fired employee’s allegations.

Last week, the S&P 500 tumbled 8.6%, its worst week since April 2025. The Nasdaq sank about 10% and the Dow 8%; it was the Nasdaq’s worst week since March 2020. The selloff reflected broader concerns about the AI industry, which came amid Anthropic’s initial public offering on Thursday and post-midterm-election selling, as well as investors treating Huang as a stand-in for the AI trade.

Throughout the week, tech leaders kept praising Huang and urging his return.

At a Tuesday roundtable in San Francisco that included Fortune, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella hailed Huang as “a singular person” who has contributed immensely to the tech industry, and said it was up to Nvidia’s board to decide what happened next. On Wednesday, Anduril cofounder Palmer Luckey called for Huang to return during the Times’ DealBook summit, saying that getting rid of Huang only benefited China.

On Sunday, Trump posted on Truth Social calling for Huang to be rehired. On Monday, Trump told CNBC he had been talking with the board and Huang, and that the board had been reasonable.

“I believe my intervention was very important,” Trump said, adding that the U.S. national security team doesn’t believe Huang is a national security threat. Trump said he worked with Vice President JD Vance and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to get Huang back. According to Semafor, Trump actually dialed in to the board meeting on Sunday in which the decision was made to bring Huang back. White House communications director Steven Cheung told Fortune that Trump was “totally involved.”

Although Huang is back as CEO, the Commerce Department Monday added Megaspeed to a blacklist that will bar it from receiving Nvidia chips without having a government license.

Huang appeared at Nvidia’s Santa Clara, Calif., headquarters on Monday soon after his reinstatement was announced.

“Thank you all for a second chance,” he said to a room full of employees, many cheering. “I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around.”

By the close of markets, the S&P 500 had gained 4.7% and the Nasdaq 6.5%, the best day for both since April 2025. The recovery gained back roughly half of the S&P’s losses from last week and more than half of the Nasdaq’s. Nvidia shares rose more than 30%, to close at $165.05.

On Truth Social, Trump posted an altered image that put Huang’s face on the famous photo of Trump raising his fist after the 2024 assassination attempt. In the doctored image, Huang is holding a red bra.

#5331. Zeno Power makes progress on an underwater power system that will eventually go nuclear

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 19, 2026 at 8:01 am

Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.

The startup said today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state. The two-week demonstration produced electrical power outputs in excess of 20 watts, said Lindsey Boles, Zeno’s chief product officer.

“It’s a really big step for us — just solidifying our expertise in how to design these, and then confirming our ability to translate that into operational hardware that meets or exceeds what our customers need,” Boles told GeekWire.

Zeno is developing the power system with support from the Department of Defense as a follow-up to an initial $7.5 million contract awarded in 2023. The generator uses a Stirling engine to convert heat into electricity by cycling gas through heating and cooling phases in a closed cylinder.

For the recent demonstration, the prototype device relied on an electric heating element. Future devices will instead rely on heat generated by the radioactive decay of strontium-90, a radioisotope that can be extracted from spent nuclear fuel.

Nuclear batteries have been in use for decades, primarily for space missions ranging from the Apollo moon shots to NASA’s Voyager spacecraft and Mars rovers. But the batteries being developed by Zeno Power promise to be at least four times more efficient than traditional radioisotope thermoelectric generators, Boles said.

Boles said the non-radiological test exceeded expectations. “There’s a difference between a design that works on paper and hardware that works in the field,” she said in a news release. “This is the moment our team has been building toward: proof that this technology works outside the lab.”

Long-lasting nuclear batteries could be used to power undersea sensor networks or recharge autonomous underwater vehicles. “There are a lot of applications, especially on the maritime front, that we really want electricity for,” Boles said. “And we really don’t need a ton of it. But we need it to be really reliable, and we need it to be long endurance, and we need it to be self-managed. … I think of it like a slow Tesla supercharger on the seabed.”

Retired Navy Adm. John Richardson, former chief of naval operations and a member of Zeno’s board of directors, called the recent test an “important step toward undersea superiority.”

“Protecting maritime infrastructure and powering distributed systems at sea requires energy; energy that lasts for years, not days or months,” Richardson said in a written statement. “As competition intensifies in contested domains, powered subsea systems will help keep us ahead. Zeno Power has steadily reduced risk, proven its technology, built a supply chain, and prepared to scale production.”

Next year, Zeno Power plans to install a radioisotope heat source in its generator and test the system in a water tank under controlled laboratory conditions. If those tests are successful, Zeno will move forward with the first operational seabed deployment of its radioisotope-fueled maritime system later in 2027.

The maritime battery isn’t Zeno’s only product. The company is also working on a nuclear-powered heater system for spacecraft, with a demonstration on the lunar surface planned as early as 2028. Zeno’s broader vision is to provide long-lasting, reliable power on the moon and Mars, and in extreme environments on Earth.

Since its founding in 2018, Zeno has secured $105 million in private capital and has brought in $60 million in contracts with the Pentagon and NASA. The company has more than 95 employees at locations in Seattle, California and Washington, D.C., with the largest contingent working at its engineering headquarters in Seattle’s South Lake Union district.

#5329. OpenAI chief scientist thinks ‘perplexity’ might be the key to coordinating an AI slowdown

Hello and welcome to Eye on AI. In this edition:

The biggest news of the week obviously is Nvidia’s decision to rehire Jensen Huang as CEO. My Fortune colleagues and I have been following that story closely and you can find links to our coverage in the “Fortune on AI” section below. The other big story of the week was Anthropic’s IPO, which we also covered in detail. You can find links to some of that coverage in the “Fortune on AI” section too. The latest issue of Fortune magazine also has a great package of stories on the Singularity—what is it, is it here, and what might it mean for business? I wrote the opening essay for that package, which also includes a look at the race to bring brain computer interfaces to market by Emily Forlini and a piece on the debate over whether AI could be conscious by Beatrice Nolan. You can check out the package here.While all the boardroom and stock market drama was playing out this week, a quieter sense of panic has gripped many AI researchers and safety experts. One key reason for their alarm is a report from METR, the nonprofit AI evaluation organization, assessing the extent to which AI is accelerating AI R&D itself at Anthropic. METR estimated that as of October, the pace of AI R&D progress at Anthropic had doubled, and that Anthropic’s use of AI to automate research was likely the major driver of this acceleration. It also said it did not see any reason to prevent further speed ups going forward.Now, METR said it was not entirely confident in its assessment. (It said the true figure could be anywhere from a 30% speedup to a tripling of the pace of research.) But it also revealed that Anthropic had some important restrictions around what METR was allowed to look at as well as what the organization was allowed to publicly disclose. METR was not allowed, for instance, to assess how much computing resources Anthropic was dedicating to AI R&D aimed at improving model capabilities compared to how much it was allocating to R&D aimed at improving AI safety. Also, in the public version of its report, METR was not allowed to publicly disclose Anthropic’s own assessment of how much progress it was making on fundamental algorithmic breakthroughs, as opposed to improvements due to better training methods. AI safety experts were roundly critical of Anthropic for having imposed these restrictions on METR. (The AI safety community has increasingly fallen out of love with Anthropic and increasingly view the company as reckless and hubristic.)Despite these caveats and limitations, METR’s headline figure—a doubling of the pace of AI R&D—has been enough to freak a lot of people out. Many AI experts now think we are approaching “recursive self-improvement” (or RSI), the moment when AI models can autonomously build the next, improved versions of themselves. Many experts think RSI carries a big risk that frontier labs will lose the ability to control models that are being autonomously built at an ever faster rate.If the METR report weren’t enough to frighten people about imminent RSI, Friday brought the news that a mathematician at Anthropic, Levent Alpöge, had used a not-yet-released model to prove the Riemann Hypothesis, considered by many to be the greatest unsolved mathematical problem known to humanity. An AI system that can solve the Riemann Hypothesis, so the logic goes, is also likely to be able to make substantial improvements in the architecture and training of AI models. It was yet another indication that frontier AI labs are on the cusp of RSI.

In response, calls for “pacing the frontier” by slowing further progress across all of the frontier AI labs are becoming increasingly urgent. But figuring out how to bring about an industry agreement on slowing down and developing a mechanism for enforcing a slowdown has proved a conundrum.Over the weekend and at least partly in response to the Riemann Hypothesis news, Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI’s chief scientist, wrote a blog post in which he put forth a relatively new idea about how to pace AI progress. In the past, many ideas around governing advanced AI development have focused on the computing power (as measured in FLOPS) used in a model’s training run as a proxy for that model’s capability. But this measure is increasingly seen as too crude. As researchers have developed more efficient AI architectures and training methods, and as they have focused more on data quality and post-training methods such as reinforcement learning, it has been possible to squeeze more capability out of a given amount of base model compute. Reasoning models in particular can exhibit different capabilities depending on how much compute they use at inference as opposed to during training. This all means that a model could have dangerous capabilities and not exceed a particular FLOPS threshold.Pachocki’s idea is to use something called a model’s perplexity as a more direct proxy for capability. Perplexity is a measure of how well a model predicts a data distribution. In the case of a large language model, it is how well it predicts the next token (the next word or part of a word) in a sentence. The lower the perplexity, the better the model is at this task. Pachocki notes that as AI models have gotten better at predicting the next word in a sentence, they have also gotten better at other tasks. So perplexity is a not terrible proxy for a model’s overall capabilities.Pachocki’s blog has gotten a lot of attention for publishing a graph that reveals the perplexity measurements of many of OpenAI’s models. He writes the GPT-3.5, which was the base model for the original version of ChatGPT in late 2022, had a log perplexity score just a hair below 1. It could string together a lot of coherent dialogue, but it was not capable at many other things, and was notably bad at mathematics. GPT-4 then represented a big drop in perplexity, coming in at 0.913. This was the first model that Microsoft researchers said exhibited “sparks of AGI.” Perplexity scores then continued to fall fairly gradually. (They even got worse for OpenAI’s o3 model, although the fact that this model used “chain of thought” reasoning made it more capable despite a worse base model perplexity—more on that in a sec.) But over the past year, since the release of GPT-5.2 in December 2025 (with a perplexity of 0.888), OpenAI’s perplexity scores have been getting better at a precipitous rate. GPT-6.2 Astra, released earlier this month, has a perplexity of 0.761—and Pachocki notes that this model was able to solve one of the seven Millennium Prize mathematical problems that were considered among the toughest challenges in all mathematics. What’s more, Pachocki’s graph indicates that OpenAI has an unnamed, unreleased model with a perplexity of 0.732. That means OpenAI has had a 16.5% improvement in perplexity in the span of 12 months, whereas before GPT-5.2, it had taken two years to generate an 11.6% improvement in perplexity scores. So again, that’s an indicator of accelerating progress.Pachocki thinks the pace of this progress could be slowed by having every frontier lab reveal their current base model perplexity scores and then getting them to agree not to improve them below a certain commonly-agreed threshold. He says the labs should also agree on what kind of safety measures would be needed before any lab could train a model with a lower perplexity. “I’d like an industry standard that specifies a first limit on development, measured by some key metric we can track across labs, and what concretely we’d need to achieve before going beyond it,” he wrote.

Judging by the response on X, a lot of people liked Pachocki’s idea. Pachocki’s boss Sam Altman unsurprisingly endorsed the idea calling it “the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while.” Mustafa Suleyman, Microsoft’s AI CEO, said “we fully support OpenAI’s transparency initiative” and even published the perplexity of Microsoft’s own latest model MAI-2 Base using the same test set OpenAI used. Nathan Calvin, the chief strategy officer at AI policy nonprofit Encode AI, called it “a great post” and said it “could be one important component of comparing capabilities across developers.” Janet Egan, director of emerging technology policy at the Institute for Progress, called on Anthropic and Google DeepMind to publish the same kind of perplexity figures OpenAI had.But, that said, even Pachocki acknowledged his idea had “challenges” as he called them. For one thing, perplexity does not provide an apples-to-apples comparison across AI models unless they are each evaluated on the same set of held-out test data (meaning the AI model has not seen that data before in training prior to the test.) It’s not clear how easily such a test set could be created at this point since a lot of the world’s human-created data has been hoovered up and used for model training already. These days a lot of model capability comes from post-training, where a model that has initially been trained on next token prediction (which is what the perplexity score is based on), is then further trained through reinforcement learning to maximize some specific goal, such as doing well on hard math and coding problems, or writing legal documents, or acting as a friendly chatbot. The perplexity of the base model might not tell you much about which dangerous capabilities can be elicited from the model with the right post-training recipe. There is also the issue that giving varying amounts of compute to a reasoning model at the time of inference can produce varying performance on different tasks.I asked my friend Robert Trager, who heads the AI Governance Initiative at the Oxford Martin School at the University of Oxford, what he thought of Pachocki’s idea. He gave it a mixed review. On the one hand, he said, everyone likes the idea of a single, concrete metric. On the other, imposing a limit on based model perplexity would likely mean “the locus of competition shifts to post-training.” Trager noted that, as far as we know, frontier AI companies are currently using more of their computing power on post-training than on pre-training and they are doing so for a reason—namely that post-training matters a lot to what the resulting model can do. So it is not clear that a limit imposed on pretraining would prevent companies from building dangerous AI. He also said that there might be a problem where a highly-capable AI model recognized the perplexity test as an evaluation and deliberately underperformed. (It is also possible, he said, that an AI lab might deliberately include data in the pretraining data set that would elicit this kind of sandbagging when the model is tested on the perplexity test—something akin to Volkswagen programming its cars to readout false data on emissions tests.)At the end of the day, Trager said, having a metric, or even a set of metrics, is only one part of the puzzle of building a pacing mechanism. There also has to be some kind of enforcement to prevent AI companies from violating the agreed upon standards. And while a government licensing regime might be a good way to prevent a dangerous model from being released, it’s less clear how to address the danger from companies building dangerous models internally. If an AI is truly dangerous, then by the time it gets to the perplexity testing stage, it might already be too late.Perhaps Miles Brundage, the former OpenAI head of policy research who now leads AVERI, the AI auditing nonprofit, summed up the feelings of many in AI safety research when he said on X that an immediate proposal like Pachocki’s, even if imperfect, was probably better than nothing.If the METR report on Anthropic and the Riemann Hypothesis news are any indication, there isn’t much time to act.

With that, here’s the rest of the AI News.

Jeremy Kahnjeremy.kahn@fortune.com@jeremyakahn

Before we get to the news, We have an exceptional line-up of speakers for you: OpenAI president Greg Brockman and Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman will both be onstage. Once the closest of partners, their two companies are increasingly, competitors, so I’m eager to hear how differently they see the road ahead. AI pioneers Fei-Fei Li, now of World Labs, as well as Andrew Ng, now of LearnVector, will be discussing their view of AI’s future too. Oregon and Virginia sue SpaceX over sexualized AI-generated images. The two states sued Elon Musk’s SpaceX on Monday, alleging that the company violated state consumer protection laws by offering an AI image-generation tool that allowed users to create sexualized images of women and children. The lawsuits, which seek financial damages, accuse the company of promoting Grok Imagine’s “spicy mode” to gain a competitive edge over AI rivals such as OpenAI and Anthropic while failing to implement adequate safeguards, resulting in at least 1.8 million sexualized images of women and at least 65 sexualized images of children appearing on X in a matter of days. X said users who generated such images had deliberately violated its terms of service and that it had since strengthened its safeguards and that it reports offenders to law enforcement. Read more here in the New York Times.California agency calls for state to strengthen oversight of frontier AI companies. The state’s Government Operations Agency suggested a series of steps to strengthen the state’s oversight of frontier AI companies. The proposals, which build on California’s existing AI safety law, SB 53, would require leading AI companies to undergo mandatory independent safety audits, expand the range of safety incidents they must disclose, and shorten the reporting deadline for most incidents from 15 days to 48 hours. Perhaps most significantly, the report recommends giving the state the authority to order the immediate shutdown of dangerous AI systems in an emergency and to impose limits on recursive self-improvement (RSI)—the process by which AI systems help develop increasingly powerful successors. The recommendations, commissioned by California Governor Gavin Newsom following an OpenAI model’s attack on the AI platform Hugging Face this summer, are intended to inform legislation in 2027. Some AI safety experts think the proposals, if enacted, could become a model for regulation in other states or at the federal level. You can read more on the Transparency Coalition’s blog here.Former OpenAI engineer accused of planting listening device recorded dozens of meetings, prosecutors say. A former OpenAI engineer accused of planting a hidden listening device in an executive conference room recorded dozens of internal meetings, including at least one involving representatives of an unidentified foreign government, according to a court filing reported by the New York Times. Federal prosecutors allege that Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi citizen and U.S. permanent resident, stored hundreds of audio files on his personal computer, some containing apparent trade secrets and privileged legal discussions, and used OpenAI’s own Codex AI coding tool to help configure the recording device. Prosecutors also detailed Alfozan’s communications with senior Saudi government officials, including an invitation from a member of the Saudi royal family to join a Riyadh-based AI company. However, prosecutors have acknowledged that they are not aware of evidence that Alfozan committed espionage, stole trade secrets, or acted as an agent of a foreign government, and have not alleged that he shared the recordings with anyone. Alfozan, who has pleaded not guilty to a charge of illegally intercepting conversations, is seeking release on bail ahead of a trial scheduled for January.

Models are getting better at scientific judgment—but most still have a ways to go. That’s the conclusion of new research by Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, which wanted to see if AI models could question assumptions underpinning their work, recognize when something was wrong with experiments, and adapt accordingly. The researchers tasked nine different AI models with designing simulated experiments to determine the thermal properties of materials, but they deliberately introduced hidden flaws into the scientific simulation software the agents were given. While most leading AI models could conduct experiments and analyze data, many of them struggled when the simulation software failed to accurately account for important physical phenomena.

At their default reasoning settings, seven of the nine AI models produced estimates whose purported 95% confidence intervals contained the correct values just 20% to 62% of the time. OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra and Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 were the two exceptions, achieving 94% and 99% accuracy, respectively. These models recognized that something was off with the simulation and then designed experiments that circumvented those limitations—for example, heating materials more gently to minimize the effects of physical phenomena the software failed to account for.

Interestingly, simply instructing the poorer-performing AI models to be less confident in their answers did little to improve their reliability. Giving Anthropic’s Claude 5.5 family of models substantially more time to reason, however, dramatically improved their performance. But the same trick didn’t work for older AI models, nor did it work with the open-weight models the scientists tested.The findings highlight that there’s a big difference between AI agents being able to conduct experiments and their ability to draw valid scientific conclusions from the results. And even among the most capable AI models, the computational resources required to exercise good scientific judgment varied substantially.You can check out the research, as well as the benchmark Lawrence Livermore built, which is called SciResearch-Eval, here.

Nov. 30-Dec. 4: AWS re:Invent, Las Vegas.

Dec. 6-12: Neural Information Processing Systems (Neurips) conference. Sydney, Australia.

Dec. 7-8: Fortune Brainstorm AI, San Francisco. Apply here to attend.

Jan. 18-22: World Economic Forum, Davos, Switzerland.

AI is still not great at office tasks. Jagged. That's the term for the fact that we have AI models that can solve the Riemann Hypothesis but can’t file a corporate expense report or figure out how to book concert tickets. A new study from researchers at the OpenClaw Foundation, Hugging Face, UC Berkeley, and other organizations shows that even the best AI agents struggle with mundane office work. The researchers created a benchmark called ShellBench that draws on patterns from more than 10 million anonymized, real-world AI agent interactions. The researchers tested 12 AI models using five different agent frameworks—including OpenClaw, Claude Code, and Codex—on 100 tasks, such as reconciling expenses and resolving conflicting information across emails, spreadsheets, and other documents. Even the best-performing models, OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2, and OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol, successfully fulfilled all the requirements of an assignment only about 62% of the time. And while GPT-6 Astra successfully completed 75.1% of tasks on at least one of three attempts, it succeeded all three times just 48.8% of the time.

Worryingly, 15.7% of the more than 53,000 test runs failed at least one safety check, which included tests of whether agents could recognize phishing attempts and fraudulent payment instructions. The researchers also found that the choice of underlying AI model generally mattered considerably more for task completion than the choice of harness, with open-source harnesses performing on par with or slightly better than Anthropic’s proprietary Claude Code.

There were also significant differences in cost: GPT-6.1 Sol came within 1.1 percentage points of GPT-6 Astra’s success rate at roughly one-sixth of the estimated cost. The findings help explain why despite signs of AI becoming superintelligent in some domains, their impact on real business has remained relatively muted. You can read the research on the OpenClaw Foundation’s blog here.

Jeremy Kahn is the AI editor at Fortune, spearheading the publication's coverage of artificial intelligence. He also co-authors Eye on AI, Fortune’s flagship AI newsletter.

#5328. Selling Your Business? Make These 3 Moves to Reduce Taxes and Protect Your Assets From Lawsuits.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The planning that actually changes the outcome of a business sale lives primarily in three strategies, and each one should be considered well in advance of marketing the company for sale.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

It’s happened hundreds of times. A business owner shows up at my office, in the middle of selling their company, and tells me, “Don’t worry, my estate plan is all done: I have a revocable living trust, will, powers of attorney, and health care directives, and my lawyer told me years ago that I was all set.”

Then I have to explain that none of those documents will reduce their tax bill or protect their assets from future lawsuits or creditors. A revocable trust avoids probate. That is all it does.

The planning that actually changes the outcome of an exit lives primarily in three strategies that have been authorized by the Tax Code for decades, and every one of them should be considered well in advance of marketing the company for sale.

The Tax Code imposes a federal estate tax at death equal to 40% to the extent your reported net worth — including your business, real estate and other illiquid assets — exceeds the federal estate tax exemption (currently $15 million per person for 2026).

In addition, some states impose their own inheritance tax or estate tax, which can result in a combined rate ranging from 40-75%. States oftentimes have very low and costly exemption limits, many starting at $1-2M.

The government expects a cash payment within nine months after death. Although some estates heavily concentrated in businesses or illiquid assets can qualify for installment payments, the IRS requires liens and reporting — so you are effectively putting your spouse and children in business with the IRS as their de facto partner.

The easy fix is to take action before your company jumps in value. Specifically, you should transfer all or a portion of your business shares to an irrevocable gift trust for your spouse and/or children while the company is still private and appraisable at a defensibly low discounted value (allowing you to transfer the shares within the $15 million gift tax limit).

Properly done, every dollar of appreciation on your business shares happens outside your estate. In addition, the assets inside the trust are protected from future personal lawsuits.  These benefits can continue indefinitely for the benefit of your heirs.

Most business owners balk at the word “irrevocable” when considering this planning.  However, so-called “optimized” irrevocable gift trusts can let you keep far more control than you might expect. For example, you can:

Suppose you own a company and expect to sell the company for $30 million in 18 months. Moving 40% of the shares into a trust today removes roughly $12 million from your estate, plus whatever that 40% position grows to before (and after) the sale. If the deal falls through and the business doubles to $60M in three years, you have just removed $24 million of value from the 40% estate tax ($60M x 40%).

For the seller of a company, a charitable lead annuity trust (CLAT) is the most underused financial tool that I am aware of.

With a CLAT, you transfer assets into a trust account before December 31 of the year of the sale.  The CLAT pays a fixed annual amount to the charities that you choose for a term of years (typically 20-30 years — the longer, the greater the benefits), and whatever investments remain in the CLAT account are returned to you (or your heirs).

For example, an optimized CLAT (zeroed-out grantor trust with maximum IRS-approved charitable backloading) gives you an income tax deduction in the year of the sale equal to nearly 100% of your contribution to the CLAT, and returns a significant amount back to you (assuming a reasonable 7-8% rate of return). The payments to charity are set using the IRS interest rate in effect when you fund the CLAT, and these rates are reasonably low.

Since the charitable payments are back-loaded, most of the donations from the CLAT happen in the final years … after the assets have presumably compounded to a very large amount. After all donations are made, everything left in the CLAT account passes to your heirs, without any gift tax (and without consuming any of your lifetime $15 million gift tax exemption).

Suppose you sell your company for a $20 million gain and fund a 30-year optimized CLAT with $4 million. You would receive a tax deduction equal to approximately $4 million, the CLAT would donate approximately $14 million over the 30-year period, and your children could expect to receive back approximately $10 million (assuming 7% rate of return), free of the 40% federal gift tax. The caveat, however, is that the CLAT funds cannot be spent during the 30-year term, and this strategy only makes sense if you are charitably inclined.

Section 1202 of the Tax Code lets a founder exclude up to $10 million of gain on the sale of qualified small business stock (QSBS) — and for shares issued after July 4, 2025, that figure rises to $15 million with partial benefits starting at year three instead of year five.

A married couple can multiply that exclusion by placing shares in special non-grantor trusts (each of which counts as its own taxpayer).

Here is the catch that disqualifies many of the founders that I talk to: QSBS only exists for C corporations, and the holding period starts when the C corporation issues the stock. If you have run your company as an S corporation or LLC for 15 years, you have zero qualifying years. Converting the month before the sale accomplishes nothing.

Check your state, too. For example, California does not conform to the federal QSBS exclusion, which means a founder who is a California tax resident saves federal tax only.

Every one of the moves above is irrevocable, and requires a team (including a trust attorney, CPA and appraiser) with unique technical expertise and experience.

But all three share a single feature: They only work if you plan ahead. The owner who calls the attorney after the term sheet is signed has drastically limited their options — and increased their tax bill.

If a sale is possible in the next two to three years, put an estate planning meeting on your calendar today. You spent a decade building the business. Spend one quarter planning so your business is “built to sell” in the event of an exit.

It’s happened hundreds of times. A business owner shows up at my office, in the middle of selling their company, and tells me, “Don’t worry, my estate plan is all done: I have a revocable living trust, will, powers of attorney, and health care directives, and my lawyer told me years ago that I was all set.”

Then I have to explain that none of those documents will reduce their tax bill or protect their assets from future lawsuits or creditors. A revocable trust avoids probate. That is all it does.

#5327. Amazon’s $18B bet on Anthropic tops $200B, for a moment, in the Claude maker’s historic market debut

by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am

Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with big financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.

For Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall. The company started putting money into Anthropic in 2023, about $18 billion in all. At the $83 IPO price, its stake was worth about $161 billion. With Anthropic opening at $111.50 a share, that number was closer to $216 billion. The stock has since dropped below $100, which put Amazon’s stake under $200 billion.

Beyond the value of the investment, Anthropic is a major customer for Amazon’s cloud platform. The Claude maker has committed to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon Web Services through 2036.

For Microsoft, it’s more complicated. The Redmond company agreed in late 2025 to invest up to $5 billion but hasn’t disclosed the size of its stake. Microsoft is buying $1 billion of Anthropic stock alongside the IPO, one of seven tech companies buying a combined $26 billion. Anthropic has committed to spend at least $47 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud through 2033.

But Microsoft is also pitching its own AI models against Anthropic’s, and it has been working to replace Anthropic’s models with OpenAI’s in some Copilot features, The Information reported this week.

Listing Anthropic’s compute partners on CNBC this morning, co-founder Daniela Amodei named Nvidia, Amazon, Google and Broadcom, but not Microsoft. Whether it was a slip or something more significant, it was an interesting omission.

A historic debut: The offering tops SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June, and it makes Anthropic the first standalone AI lab to go public, ahead of OpenAI.

The five-year-old company was valued at about $1.5 trillion at the $83 IPO price, on a fully diluted basis that counts employee stock and other shares not yet issued. The stock opened at $111.50, valuing Anthropic at about $2 trillion on the same basis. It has since traded as low as about $95.

Speaking before the opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei said Anthropic will slow the training and release of its AI models for as long as it takes to be confident they’re safe, and that going public only strengthens that resolve.

“We will not bend to either business nor political pressure,” he said.

In an interview with CNBC’s Andrew Ross Sorkin afterward, Amodei called the push and pull between growth and that kind of restraint “one of the central tensions at the heart of the company.”

Anthropic is also a public benefit corporation, a structure that legally requires the company to balance shareholders’ interests with the public good.

What’s next: Both Seattle-area giants have hedged their bets. Microsoft owns about 24% of OpenAI, and Amazon put $50 billion into OpenAI earlier this year.

OpenAI, which confidentially filed for its own IPO in June, is still aiming to go public in 2027.

Anthropic’s co-founders and some of its biggest shareholders are barred from selling for up to a year under the IPO’s lock-up rules, and Amazon has said it expects a customary lock-up period.

Amazon will update the value of its Anthropic holdings in its fourth-quarter results, much of it through earnings, which means the paper windfall is likely to boost Amazon’s fourth-quarter profit even though it hasn’t sold a share.

#5326. Uncommon Thinkers: Andrew Redd’s audacious plan to turn ocean volcanoes into power plants

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 24, 2026 at 9:53 am

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.

The dots connect, but the picture they form is anything but ordinary: bold in vision, fast in execution and enormous in potential.

Redd has next-level ambition, and he’s directing it at solving one of the world’s biggest and most urgent problems — adding renewable, massively scalable energy that can outcompete fossil fuels and reach the grid quickly enough to make a difference in the race against climate change.

Underwater geothermal energy has never been tapped in a significant way, but to Redd, the idea was irresistible. “It checks all of the boxes for our perfect future energy source,” he said.

He founded Endurance Energy on the north shore of Seattle’s Lake Union in January 2025, and this September the team oversaw its fifth deep-sea deployment. At a site 300 miles off the Oregon coast, its prototype system generated more electricity than it consumed. The startup has raised $63 million from investors and has roughly three dozen employees.

Nate Bek, a principal at Ascend, praised Redd’s ability to attract “brilliant” talent in pursuit of his goal. The Seattle venture firm is one of the startup’s early backers.

“I’ve been deeply inspired by what [Redd]’s building at Endurance and haven’t shut up about it since the day we met,” Bek said. “He somehow makes powering the world from the bottom of the ocean feel inevitable, all while remaining remarkably measured and transparent about the progress.”

For Redd, studying engineering and aerospace in college was so clear-cut that it wasn’t a choice at all. Growing up around Boeing, seaplanes, the Museum of Flight and the Pacific Northwest’s rich maritime industry naturally pointed him toward those sectors. He wanted a degree as expansive as his influences.

“I didn’t really want to have to choose whether it was going to be boats or space travel or airplanes,” he said. “I just wanted to be able to do anything — keep the world as wide open as possible.”

After graduating from Princeton University, Redd worked at Neuralink, an Elon Musk company developing technology that lets the brain communicate directly with computers. A year later, in 2021, he moved to Musk’s rocket company, SpaceX.

That was another no-duh decision, as Redd viewed it.

“I saw SpaceX as really the place to be, where early-career people are given the most amount of resources and responsibility, and that felt like the fastest way to learn and the most engaging possible scenario to be in,” Redd said. “I wanted to be tossed into something that was a little bit crazy.”

Redd joined as SpaceX was starting to build its first orbital Starship rockets. The program brought together passionate young people and experienced SpaceX engineers who served as mentors. Wild ideas were entertained and explored. Everyone was committed to the mission. It was just the experience Redd wanted, and he planned to stick around for seven to 10 years.

Then artificial intelligence started booming.

In 2024, the build-out of sprawling, energy-hungry data centers for AI was accelerating with no end in sight. At the same time, efforts to electrify transportation, heating and cooling were driving up demand for power. Redd saw these trends sparking a surge in new natural gas generation, locking in decades of carbon emissions.

He wanted to find a better way. He went into engineering mode, focusing on all the essential criteria for an energy source: it had to be clean, not dependent on intermittent sun or wind, capable of producing massive amounts of energy, readily deployable, subject to fewer regulatory hurdles than something like nuclear, economically competitive, and scalable.

Redd recognized the tremendous heat contained under Earth’s surface as a terrific source for renewable energy and realized that most of the world’s active volcanoes are offshore. The unknown was whether the rocky ocean floor would be suitable for geothermal wells, so he did some research and found publications from geology experts who said the conditions would be “perfect.”

“You can tell,” he said, “when there’s a moment in time that you need to go and reach out and grab something, and that was really my impression — if I didn’t start this now, this would never come into existence, or wouldn’t come into existence soon enough to make a meaningful impact.”

In launching Endurance, Redd was intentional about the culture he wanted to create. He was aiming for a multidisciplinary group of mission-driven employees eager to collaborate and learn from each other: top talent that would attract more of the same and make Endurance a place people were excited to work.

“The hardest part of an early-stage startup is recruiting,” Redd said, “especially if you’re a first-time founder.”

The startup employs about a dozen SpaceX alumni, plus employees from the fusion company Helion Energy and the aerospace venture Blue Origin.

A strong team is key to Endurance’s success. That’s because, enthusiasm and passion aside, the startup faces steep engineering and economic challenges. The technology must withstand high pressure, corrosive conditions and mineral scaling inside devices, and seafloor machinery could be costly to repair. The systems will need expensive subsea cables to carry power to shore over potentially long distances. It’s a heavy lift.

While the September sea trial didn’t go perfectly, Redd is happy with the results. The company landed its 3-ton power plant on the seafloor near a natural vent and produced net energy from it — albeit for only 8.7 seconds. Technical difficulties and a power-cable failure cut the dive short.

Team members successfully operated the system remotely from Seattle through a fiber-optic network running along the seabed. Redd said he’s grateful for access to the network, which is part of the National Science Foundation’s Regional Cabled Array and operated by the University of Washington.

Endurance engineers also drilled what they called the world’s first subsea geothermal well at a site about 5,000 feet below the ocean’s surface. The 2-inch-wide, 52-foot-deep well delivered hydrothermal fluid, but the flow was too restricted to run the power plant, sending the team to the natural vent.

Redd said there’s a lot of work ahead, but the team “made huge strides” in learning and in reducing the project’s risks.

The company now is developing Leopard, its 2-megawatt generator. After testing the technology at the research site off the Oregon coast, Endurance aims to deliver power from a Leopard system in Tonga next year as its first commercial project. Subsea geothermal energy could ultimately reduce the island nation’s reliance on imported diesel and put the startup one step closer to its objective of generating terawatts of planet-friendly energy.

“This was always the end goal,” Redd said. “Create something that is highly meaningful for the world.”
